e-mobility in the country. The “GO ELECTRIC” campaign has been 
designed to educate the masses about the Central/State Government policy 
initiatives pertaining to the promotion of e-mobility in the country & 
benefits of EVs over conventional vehicles. The campaign has been 
designed and developed in consultation with the industry like the OEMs, 
State Nodal Agencies, Oil marketing companies (OMCs) and Public Sector 
Units of Government of India.  
 
116. Ministry of Heavy Industries informed the Committee that as per 
Vahan Portal, EV sales in FY 2022-23 were 11.8 lakh units, which are 2.5 
times of EV sold during FY 2021-22. In FY 22-23, 7.2 lakh e-2Wheelers, 4 
lakh e-3Whleers, 47,479 Passenger Cars and 2973 Commercial Vehicles 
were registered, which is about 6 per cent of total internal combustion 
engine vehicle sales in FY 2022-23.  
 
117. For the promotion and penetration of Electric Vehicles, creating 
awareness regarding the environmental and economic benefits of 
adoption/migration to Electric Vehicles among the people is necessary. 
It's equally important to convey the initiatives taken by the Central & 
State governments to promote e-mobility in the country. The Committee 
recommends that awareness campaigns, events, etc. at the local level in 
coordination with urban local bodies/municipalities, etc. should be 
organised in the regional languages in the States to promote Electric 
Vehicles and their wide acceptance by general public. Print, Audio 
Video, Radio, and Social Media modes should also be utilised to enhance 
the outreach. 
 
118. According to a report of NITI Aayog, Indian Gig force is expected 
to rise to 23.5 million by 2029-30, from the current workforce of 7.7 

42 
 
million. Most of the delivery start-ups especially in food & grocery 
delivery employ gig force on a large scale, which could be a potential 
driving agent for increasing the Electric Vehicles penetration in the 
country, particularly in 2-Wheeler segment. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry should take steps in coordination with 
the stakeholders to make the vehicle fleet of 2-Wheelers in these start-
ups/companies mandatorily to be Electric Vehicles in order to achieve 
the 30 per cent target of EV penetration by the year 2030.   
PM e-Bus Sewa: 
 
119. According to a release of Press Information Bureau, the Union 
Cabinet has approved the PM e-Bus Sewa for augmenting the city bus 
operations by e-Buses on Public-Private Partnership (PPP) Model. The 
Scheme would have an estimated cost of ₹57,613 crore, out of which 
support of ₹20,000 crore will be provided by the Central Government. The 
Scheme will support bus operations for 10 years. The scheme will cover 
cities with a population of 3 lakh and above and priority will be given to 
cities not having organised bus services. Through this scheme, e-Buses will 
be deployed on PPP Model in 169 cities and Infrastructure will be upgraded 
in 181 cities under the Green Urban Mobility Initiatives. Cities will also be 
supported for development of charging infrastructure under Green Urban 
Mobility Initiatives.120. The Committee is of the view that support to bus 
priority infrastructure shall not only accelerate the proliferation of state-of-
the-art, energy efficient electric buses but also foster the innovation in the e-
mobility sector as well as development of resilient supply chain for electric 
vehicles. It will also bring in economies of scale for procurement of electric 
buses through aggregation for e-buses. Adoption to Electric mobility will 
reduce noise and air pollution and curb carbon emissions.  
121. The Committee observes that in phase-2 of FAME Scheme, only 9 
major cities having population of over 4 million were targeted in 
aggregation model for e-buses and very few States have earlier 
participated in operational cost model. With the announcement of PM 
e-Bus Sewa, the Committee is hopeful that the Scheme will help 
transform urban mobility landscape in smaller cities also. The 
Committee recommends that the concerned Ministry(ies) should strive 
for the early implementation of the scheme so that the benefits of the 
scheme will proliferate in an efficient manner and timely. 
 
******* 

43 
 
 
Recommendations/Observations at a Glance 
 
1. The Committee notes that the initial targets were revised by 
bringing down the number of vehicles to be supported under the 
FAME-II Scheme. The Committee is of the opinion that in order to 
facilitate the transition momentum to Electric Mobility, more number 
of electric vehicles need to be supported and, therefore recommends 
that the Ministry should broaden the scope and extend the FAME-II 
Scheme for at least 3 more years in consultation with the Industry 
stakeholders to make the Scheme more inclusive.  
(Para 25) 
 
 
2. The Committee notes that initially the Government had the target 
of supporting 55,000 e-4 Wheelers under the FAME II Scheme, but the 
revised targets have reduced the number of vehicles to the committed 
funds only i.e. for 11,000 e-4 Wheelers. Though 2 Wheelers is a 
dominant category, share of 4 Wheelers is also significant in the 
automotive sector of the country. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry should increase the number of electric vehicles to be supported 
in the 4 Wheelers category and also include private e-4 Wheelers in the 
domain of FAME II Scheme with a cap based on the cost and battery 
capacity of the vehicle. 
(Para 26) 
 
3. The Committee notes that reduction of subsidy w.e.f. 1st June, 
2023 in case of e-2Wheelers has negatively impacted their sales. It also 
notes that the budget constraint was the major reason behind the 
reallocation of funds and for the revision of targets under the FAME-II 
Scheme. As there is an instant need to decarbonise the transport sector, 
the Committee recommends that the Ministry should restore the 
subsidy on e-2Wheelers and, if required, project enhanced budget 
allocations in order to maintain the momentum and pace of electric 
vehicles penetration, so that the desired target could be achieved by 
2030.  
(Para 31) 
 
4. During the deposition before the Committee, the issue of e-
Quadricycle was discussed and the Committee was informed by a 
stakeholder that e-Quadricycle will give a big fillip to last-mile 
connectivity and, based on a study, CRISIL had indicated that India 

44 
 
could be one of the largest manufacturers of e-Quadricycles, which 
would help in reducing two lakh tones of CO2 emissions. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry should develop an ecosystem 
to include e-Quadricycle in the FAME-II Scheme as the e-Quadricycle 
would not only help reduce CO2 emissions but would be an employment 
generation initiative for the youth of the country. 
(Para 32) 
 
5. A safe, reliable and cost-effective public transport system would 
definitely have a positive impact on improving the air quality in urban 
areas as well as reducing the number of private vehicles on road. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry should allocate more funds 
for developing a decarbonised mass public transport system and also 
project for enhancement of the budgetary allocation for e-Buses under 
FAME Scheme so that it does not suffer due to shortage of funds.  
(Para 35) 
 
6. The Committee is of the opinion that frequent changes in the 
policies relating to Electric Vehicles create uncertainties in the market 
as well as in the EV Industry. This will also creates doubt in the minds 
of people and the end users about the Government actions which may 
negatively impact the growth of the EV industry. The Committee 
recommends that the Government should strive towards formulation of 
a consistent and stable national policy on Electric Mobility so that a 
propitious environment is created for the EV industry in order to 
promote sustainable and clean transportation system in the country. 
(Para 36) 
 
7. The Committee is of the view that the proposal of stakeholders 
hold merit and recommends that the Ministry of Heavy Industries in 
consultation with Industry partners should expand the scope of FAME-
II or any future Scheme to incentivize installation of charging stations to 
individual investors in order to achieve the goal of setting up of 
charging stations throughout the length and breadth of the country as 
well as to eliminate road anxiety among potential customers. The 
Committee also recommends that Women Self Help Groups and 
Cooperative Societies may be given assistance to open and operate 
Charging Stations. They may be provided an assured return by the 
Government from its own funds. 
(Para 40) 
 
 

45 
 
8. The Committee recommends that keeping in view the importance 
of EV Mobility as a key ingredient of reducing the pollution level in the 
country, the Ministry of Heavy Industries should play a proactive role 
through BHEL in providing EPC solutions to support electric vehicle 
(EV) charging stations, including solar based EV charging stations and, 
if required, more funds may be allocated to BHEL to facilitate 
popularizing the EV Mobility. Every Public Sector Undertaking and 
Government institutions may be asked to participate in the installation 
of Charging Stations in their own premises for the use of the vehicles 
coming to their premises. 
(Para 41) 
 
9. Ensuring Domestic Value Addition (DVA) is an important aspect 
of the PLI Scheme for Automobile and Auto Components. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry should take necessary steps 
for achieving better scheme output, including policy changes and 
financial outlay, for enhancement of manufacturing capabilities for 
Advanced Automotive Technology products thus creating an ecosystem 
to manufacture components of electric vehicles locally and promoting 
manufacturers as global Automotive Champions. 
(Para 47) 
 
10. Although the Ministry of Heavy Industries is striving hard 
towards Make in India and Atmanirbhar Bharat with the Schemes like 
PLI-Auto, PLI-ACC and Phased Manufacturing Programme under 
FAME-II Scheme, the Committee is of the view that to make India a 
Global EV Hub, the Ministry should have supportive, transparent, and 
consistent government frameworks at national, state, and local levels 
and also focus towards establishing dedicated Manufacturing Hubs and 
Industrial Parks for manufacturing of batteries, cells and Electric 
Vehicle auto components. The Committee believes that this would 
encourage and strengthen economic development of the country. 
(Para 56) 
 
11. The Committee notes that MoRTH has issued various guidelines 
and advisories to States and Union Territories so as to incentivize and 
bring down the initial cost of electric vehicles. Many States have 
complied with these guidelines and included the measures in their 
respective EV policy but, to increase the targeted penetration of electric 
vehicles by 2030, more needs to be done. Since 19 States/Union 
Territories are only providing exemptions and rebate in road tax, the 
Committee recommends that the MoRTH should take up the issue with 

46 
 
the remaining States/Union Territories in order to bring in all the States 
and Union Territories such as Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Haryana etc. on a 
common platform as well as make efforts to slash down the road tax 
further and provide other possible exemptions in respect of electric 
vehicles. MoRTH, in order to decarbonise the Automotive Sector, 
should also make electric vehicles mandatory for public transport in 
cities with high rate of air pollution. 
(Para 60) 
 
12. The Committee notes the efforts of the Ministry of Power towards 
augmentation of distribution network through Revamped Distribution 
Sector Scheme (RDSS). The Committee is of the view that with more 
penetration of electric vehicles, EV owners may prefer to charge their 
vehicles at home during non-solar hours which may lead to surge in 
electricity demand ultimately overloading the electrical systems. The 
Committee recommends that Ministry of Power should encourage solar 
hours charging of electric vehicles through advertisements, including 
regional languages, to minimize the load on electrical systems during 
non-solar hours and promote establishing charging stations/points at 
work locations/office buildings/premises with minimum parking facility 
to increase charging network as well as solar hours charging to 
minimize load on electric system. Ministry of Power should also 
encourage Solarization of EV Charging Stations, in coordination with 
the Ministry of Heavy Industries, by providing subsidy for installation 
of EV Charging Stations both under public as well as private sector.  
(Para 65) 
 
13. The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Power should 
popularize such Apps and recommends that the scope of the EV Yatra 
App should be enlarged to help even the potential electric vehicle buyers 
to know about the cost of the vehicle, cost of battery, insurance and 
comparison between EV and ICE vehicles as a single stop solution for 
all issues related to electric vehicles. 
(Para 66) 
 
14. The Committee appreciates such a move of the Ministry of Power 
and recommends that the benefits of the aforesaid Portal and Guidelines 
should be given wide publicity vigorously in all prominent languages 
through various modes of media, including social media. 
(Para 67) 
 
 

47 
 
15. Electric Vehicles have range constraints as its range depends on 
battery capacity and therefore, the vehicles need charging at frequent 
intervals, whereas ICE Vehicles have a fuel tank which gives them range 
advantage vis-a-vis electric vehicles. The Committee recommends that 
Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas should also consider including the 
sub-urban and rural areas under the target areas for establishing 
Charging Stations, as installations of charging stations only at retail outlets 
of Oil Marketing Companies would not be adequate due to range anxiety 
in case of electric vehicles. Further, in view of the targeted Electric 
Charging Stations of 22,000, the sanctioned Charging Stations of 7,432 for 
installation under FAME-II is way below the target and, therefore the 
Committee recommends that sincere efforts should be made for setting up 
of more Charging Stations to address the issue of range anxiety and boost 
the EV penetration in the automotive sector in the country. 
(Para 73) 
 
16. The Committee was informed by the Ministry of Heavy Industries 
that 520 Charging Stations had been sanctioned under the Phase-I of 
FAME India Scheme. Further, 2,877 charging stations in 68 cities across 
25 States/UTs and 1576 charging stations across 9 Expressways and 16 
Highways have been sanctioned under FAME-II India Scheme. The 
Committee recommends that other Ministries should be roped in along 
with charging infrastructure operators to put in place a comprehensive 
plan for establishment of a Charging Network in the country to address 
the issue of road anxiety of electric vehicle owners.  
(Para 74) 
 
17. The Committee is of the view that one of the biggest barriers to the 
widespread adoption of Electric Vehicles remains the lack of charging 
infrastructure and the overall time required to charge such batteries. With 
a Battery Swapping System, EV owners will save on the high cost of 
buying a new set of battery at periodic intervals as they can simply replace 
the exhausted batteries for fully charged ones at Battery Swapping 
Stations. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Heavy 
Industries should conduct a study regarding the feasibility of battery 
standardisation and formulate a stable Battery Swapping Policy with the 
highest levels of safety standards that can infuse confidence in consumer’s 
decision making thereby boosting demand whilst inducing infrastructure 
build-out by swapping operators, which has a huge potential to invite FDI 
into the battery swapping network creation in the country. 
(Para 77) 
 
 

48 
 
18. The Committee is of the view that one of the major challenges to 
make electric vehicles more affordable and economical to operate is 
their high ownership cost vis-a-vis ICE vehicles, as the electric vehicles 
include a battery pack that forms about 40-45 per cent of their 
ownership cost. Since the Lithium-ions Batteries (LIBs) for electric 
vehicles has a greater durability with relatively high energy and power 
density, the Committee recommends that Government should explore 
the possibility of shrinking further the GST on Lithium-ion batteries to 
bring down the ownership cost of electric vehicles. Further, there is a 
need to address the issue of GST for manufacturers as well in order to 
reduce the high cost of electric vehicles and consequently its 
affordability for the potential buyers to promote faster adoption of 
electric vehicles. 
(Para 83) 
19. Section 80EEB of the Income Tax Act 1961 allows an individual to 
claim tax savings of up to Rs. 1.5 lakh on interest paid on a loan made 
specifically to purchase an electric vehicle. Section 80EEB specifically 
states that the deduction benefits in case of purchase of electric vehicles 
are available only if the loan is approved by the Financial Institutions 
during the period 1st January 2019 to 31st March, 2023. The Committee 
is of the view that pollution is still a major concern and therefore, there 
is a need to work towards Green Grow. In order to facilitate faster 
adoption of electric vehicles, the Committee recommends that the 
provision under Section 80EEB may be considered for extension at least 
up to 31st March, 2025. 
(Para 84) 
20. The Committee is of the view that proper disposal and recycling 
of Lithium-ion Batteries (LIBs) are crucial to minimize the threat they 
pose to the environment as well as to the public health and therefore, 
there is a need for advanced battery recycling technologies and 
increased awareness of the importance of proper disposal of e-wastes. 
The Committee recommends that initiatives should be taken to 
encourage advanced R&D efforts for development of sustainable e-
waste recycling technologies and to develop Sodium-ion as an 
alternative to Lithium-ion in battery manufacturing in coordination 
with the OEMs and Channel Partners for a more sustainable future. 
Besides, training modules should be designed for proper training and 
skilling of recyclers and labourers engaged in the business for effective 
management and disposal of LIBs and e-wastes.  
(Para 90) 

49 
 
 
21. The Committee notes the efforts made by the Ministry of New and 
Renewable Energy for harnessing of renewable sources of energy such 
as wind and solar energy to supplement the generation of electricity. It 
is of the considered view that a pragmatic and earnest focus on 
generating renewable and non-fossil energy will go a long way in 
meeting the electricity demands of the society. Moreover, players in the 
automotive sector are moving the needle on renewable energy transition 
by leveraging cutting-edge auto electrification technologies. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry should make all out efforts to 
tap the maximum energy that can be harnessed from such renewable 
energy sources to supplement the current electricity demand arising 
from households and industries, including EV Charging Stations, to 
support the Electric Mobility in the country. EV-Ready India Dashboard 
should also be given wide publicity, especially in regional languages, to 
encourage electric vehicles as a cleaner and more efficient alternative to 
ICE vehicles.  
(Para 95) 
 
22. The Committee notes the initiatives undertaken by NITI Aayog 
such as e-AMRIT Portal and Shoonya Campaign and hopes that 
launching comprehensive nationwide awareness campaigns to educate 
the general public about the environmental and financial advantages of 
electric vehicles would help dispel the misconceptions and increase 
acceptance of the electric vehicles among the populace. The Committee 
is of the view that help of NGOs, social media and popular celebrities 
may also be considered for creating awareness and popularising electric 
vehicles (EVs).  Further, the Ministry of Heavy Industries, in 
coordination with the NITI Aayog, should take initiatives to encourage 
the Governments of States/UTs to develop their respective EV Portals, 
in line with the e-AMRIT Portal, to generate public awareness 
regarding the advantages of electric vehicles. 
(Para 99) 
 
23. The Committee is of the view that the States are drivers of electric 
mobility movement in the country and they need to be equipped with 
efficient tools and policies to make electric vehicle revolution a success 
and contribute towards net zero emission. The Committee recommends 
that a comparative analysis of the notified EV policies of States/UTs 
should be conducted and based on the analysis outcome, a 
comprehensive stable EV policy may be adopted to address the 
misconceptions regarding electric vehicles among the people and to 

50 
 
boost EV revolution in the country. Further, States/UTs, which are yet 
to notify their EV Policy, should be provided expert guidance and 
scientific assistance by NITI Aayog and other related organisations in 
formulation of their EV policy. 
(Para 101) 
 
24. The Committee notes the efforts made by some of the State/UT 
Governments in decarbonising their respective bus fleet and is of the view 
that, along with buses, the logistics sector also needs to be decarbonised as 
it is a major contributor to air pollution. Therefore, in order to 
decarbonise the Transport Sector, efforts should be made to set a deadline 
for making Transport Sector in the country mandatorily electric. 
(Para 102) 
 
25. The Committee notes the challenges associated with financing the 
Electric Vehicles and is hopeful that the efforts of NITI Aayog, World 
Bank and SIDBI will be helpful in addressing the issue of finance 
availability for the potential EV buyers. Taking into consideration the 
efforts of the Government for promoting Electric Vehicles and green asset 
creation, the Committee recommends that Electric Vehicles should be 
brought under the Priority Sector Lending (PSL) category until the 30 per 
cent penetration target fixed for 2030 is achieved, for accelerating India’s 
commitment towards net-zero emissions. Further, cooperation between EV 
Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) and lenders may be 
encouraged to improve EV buyers accessibility to finance. Ministry of 
Heavy Industries may also consider including private EV Four Wheelers 
in FAME-II so as to improve their share in the Electric Mobility Mission. 
(Para 108) 
 
26. Lithium is very critical for the development of EV industry. 
Consequently rise in demand for raw materials for batteries is expected 
with the progress of PLI-ACC scheme. Over two-third of World’s known 
lithium reserves are in the Lithium Triangle of Argentina, Bolivia and 
Chile. With the recent findings of reserves of Lithium in Jammu & 
Kashmir and Rajasthan, India could also become a game changer in the 
EV industry by boosting its domestic battery manufacturing industry. The 
Committee recommends that the Government should take initiatives such 
as framing of rules and guidelines to accelerate the process of lithium 
extraction so that India become Atmanirbhar in the field of Lithium-ion 
Battery manufacturing to facilitate transition to Electric Mobility. 
(Para 112) 
 
 

51 
 
27. The Committee notes the achievements of Schemes such as PLI-
Auto and National Programme on ACC, but until the benefits of these 
schemes spread across the country and self-sufficiency in 
manufacturing of batteries and auto components is achieved, the 
Government should ensure adequate supply of components, cells and 
batteries for growth of Electric Vehicles vis-à-vis ICE Vehicles. The 
Committee recommends the Ministry to foster international 
cooperation/partnership with global suppliers/countries to ensure and 
maintain the supply chain requirements of the domestic Electric Vehicle 
industry. Ministry of Heavy Industries should also work in coordination 
with the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises to help 
develop a Manufacturing Network for manufacture of Battery and EV 
components and progress in this regard may be shared with the 
Committee. 
(Para 114) 
 
28. For the promotion and penetration of Electric Vehicles, creating 
awareness regarding the environmental and economic benefits of 
adoption/migration to Electric Vehicles among the people is necessary. 
It's equally important to convey the initiatives taken by the Central & 
State governments to promote e-mobility in the country. The Committee 
recommends that awareness campaigns, events, etc. at the local level in 
coordination with urban local bodies/municipalities, etc. should be 
organised in the regional languages in the States to promote Electric 
Vehicles and their wide acceptance by general public. Print, Audio 
Video, Radio, and Social Media modes should also be utilised to enhance 
the outreach. 
 (Para 117) 
29. According to a report of NITI Aayog, Indian Gig force is expected 
to rise to 23.5 million by 2029-30, from the current workforce of 7.7 
million. Most of the delivery start-ups especially in food & grocery 
delivery employ gig force on a large scale, which could be a potential 
driving agent for increasing the Electric Vehicles penetration in the 
country, particularly in 2-Wheeler segment. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry should take steps in coordination with 
the stakeholders to make the vehicle fleet of 2-Wheelers in these start-
ups/companies mandatorily to be Electric Vehicles in order to achieve 
the 30 per cent target of EV penetration by the year 2030.   
(Para 118) 

52 
 
30. The Committee observes that in phase-2 of FAME Scheme, only 9 
major cities having population of over 4 million were targeted in 
aggregation model for e-buses and very few States have earlier 
participated in operational cost model. With the announcement of PM 
e-Bus Sewa, the Committee is hopeful that the Scheme will help 
transform urban mobility landscape in smaller cities also. The 
Committee recommends that the concerned Ministry(ies) should strive 
for the early implementation of the scheme so that the benefits of the 
scheme will proliferate in an efficient manner and timely. 
(Para 121) 
 
******** 
 
 
 
 
 
  

53

Action Taken Replies 
Ministry of Power amended its Consolidated Guidelines for Charging 
Infrastructure for EVs on 27.04.2023 vide which it included provisions to 
incentivize the charging of EVs at Public charging stations during the solar hour 
and discourage it in the non-solar hour. Details of these provisions are as follows:  
i. Cost of electricity supply by an Electricity Distribution Company 
(DISCOM) to a public electric vehicle charging station shall be 0.8 times of 
Average Cost of Supply (ACoS) during solar hours and 1.2 times Average Cost of 
Supply (ACoS) during non-solar hours. Solar hours mean 9:00 AM to 4:00 PM and 
non-solar hour mean the remaining period of the day. 
ii. Ceiling limits of service charges being levied by public electric vehicle 
charge point operators on  the EV customers to recover the cost of servicing the 
capital investments (excluding GST) made by it in setting up of public charging 
station has been specified as Rs.2.50 per unit and Rs.3.50 per unit of electricity 
used for slow AC charging of EVs at pu blic charging stations during the solar 
hours (9 AM to 4 PM) and non -solar hours (for remaining part of the day) 
respectively. Additionally, a ceiling limit of Rs.10.0 per unit and Rs.12.0 per unit 
of electricity used has also been specified for DC Fast ch arging of electric vehicles 
at public charging stations during the solar and non-solar hours respectively. 
Further, with the objective of accelerating use of renewable energy adoption, 
ensuring access to affordable, reliable, sustainable and green energy, “Green 
Energy Open Access Rules 2022” have been notified with Open Access 
Transaction limit reduced from 1 MW to 100 kW and appropriate provisions for 
cross-subsidy surcharge, additional surcharge, which will incentivize the common 
consumers to get Green P ower at reasonable rates. This is expected to encourage 
Public charge point operators to avail Green Energy through open access from 
Grid for charging of EVs. 
In addition to this, Ministry of Power notified the Electricity (Rights of 
Consumers) Amendment Rules, 2023 on 14.06.2023 wherein a clause on Time -of-
Day Tariff (TOD) has been included with a provision for promoting power 
consumption during solar hours. The clause is as re-produced below:

ELECTRIC VEHICLE (EV) SUBSIDIES AND INCENTIVES 
(Extension of Section 80EEB of the Income Tax Act) 
Recommendation/Observation 
13. Section 80EEB of the Income Tax Act 1961 allows an individual to claim tax 
savings of up to Rs.1.5 lakh on interest paid on a loan made specifically  to 
purchase an electric vehicle. Section 80EEB specifically states that the deduction 
benefits in case of purchase of electric vehicles are available only if the loan is 
approved by the Financial Institutions during the period 1 st January 2019 to 31st 
March, 2023. The Committee is of the view that pollution is still a major concern 
and therefore, there is a need to work towards Green Grow. In order to facilitate 
faster adoption of electric vehicles, the Committee recommends that the provision 
under Section 80EEB may be considered for extension at least up to 31st March, 
2025.  
(Para 84) 
Action Taken Replies 
As per the information received from Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance, 
Section 80EEB of the Income Tax Act 1961 allows an individual to claim tax 
savings of up to Rs.1.5 lakh on interest paid on a loan made specifically to 
purchase an electric vehicle. Section 80EEB specifically states that the deduction 
benefits in case of purchase of electric vehicles are available only if the loan is 
approved by the Financial Institutions during the period 01.01.2019 to 31.03.2023. 
The end date for taking loan for the purpose of purchasing an electric vehicle for 
claiming additional tax deduction of Rs.1.5 Lakh on the interest paid for such loan 
under Section 80EEB of the Act has not been extended beyond 31.03.2023, in 
view of the policy of the Govt. to move away from exemptions and deductions. 
Furthermore, due to the same reason, there is no proposal to make the same/similar 
clause/exemption available under the new tax regime. This is in line with the stated 
policy of the Government to phase out exemptions and deductions.

ENVIRONMENT & SUSTAINIBILITY 
(Disposal & Recycling of Lithium-Ion Batteries) 
Recommendation/Observation 
14. The Committee is of the view that proper disposal and recycling of Lithium -ion 
Batteries (LIBs) are crucial to minimize the threat they pose to the environment as 
well as to the public health and therefore, there is a need for advanced battery 
recycling te chnologies and increased awareness of the importance of proper 
disposal of e -wastes. The Committee recommends that initiatives should be taken 
to encourage advanced R&D efforts for development of sustainable e -waste 
recycling technologies and to develop So dium-ion as an alternative to Lithium -ion 
in battery manufacturing in coordination with the OEMs and Channel Partners for 
a more sustainable future. Besides, training modules should be designed for proper 
training and skilling of recyclers and labourers en gaged in the business for 
effective management and disposal of LIBs and e-wastes.            
(Para 90) 
Action Taken Replies 
As per information received from Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate 
Change (MoEFCC): 
To address the safe disposal of batteries including batteries generated from Electric 
Vehicles in environmentally sound manner, Ministry of Environment, Forest and 
Climate Change (MoEF&CC) has notified Battery Waste Management Rules, 
2022, as amended from time to time. Extended Producer Respon sibility (EPR) 
targets have been prescribed for Producers under the rules for collection and 
recycling or refurbishment of waste batteries.  
Under the Battery Waste Management Rules, 2022, as amended, the Extended 
Producer Responsibility certificate for recycler or for refurbisher shall be generated 
based on the weight of waste Battery processed or refurbished, as the case may be, 
and weight of Battery material produced as per guidelines of the Central Pollution 
Control Board and the Central Pollution Contr ol Board shall ensure that every 
certificate is issued based on the waste Battery processed or refurbished. 
Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has established 
Centre of Excellence on E -waste Management at Centre for Materials for 
Electronics Technology (C -MET) Hyderabad, with the basic objective to create 
physical infrastructure and cost-effective recycling technologies to manage India‟s 
e-waste and necessary processing equipment for the same are developed by the 
Centre at pilot plant scale. The developed technology envisages selective recovery 

15 
 
of Lithium (Li), Cobalt (Co), Manganese (Mn) and Nickel (Ni) values from 
assorted types of discarded lithium -ion batteries (LIBs). The technology has been 
transferred to 15 industries, so far, on non -exclusive basis for establishing 
recycling facilities on pan India basis. The major areas of R&D activities under the 
centre include:  
Recovery of valuable metal contents from discarded lithium -ion batteries (LIBs); 
Extraction of rare earth elements (REE) from spent permanent magnets;  
Recycling of spent Printed Circuit Boards (PCBs) for effective recovery of 
precious metals such as gold, silver, palladium, copper etc., and

Recommendation/Observation 
19. Lithium is very critical for the development of EV industry. Consequentl y,

19

(Para 112) 
Action Taken Replies 
Ministry of Mines has stated that in order to accelerate the process of lithium 
extraction, the following reforms have been implemented: 
i. The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 [MMDR 
Act, 1957] was amended through the MMDR Amendment Act, 2023 with effect 
from 17.08.2023. 
ii. Through the said amendment, Lithium -bearing minerals have been omitted 
from the list of atomic minerals specified in Part -B of the First Schedule to the 
MMDR Act. Consequent to removal of these minerals from the list of atomic 
minerals, mineral concessions  regarding these minerals can be granted to private 
sector companies through auction as being followed for other major minerals. 
iii. Further, the Central Government has been empowered to exclusively auction 
mining lease and composite licence for 24 critical minerals listed in the new Part-D 
of the First Schedule to the said Act which includes the mineral Lithium. 
iv. The objective of the said amendment is to increase exploration and mining of 
critical minerals including Lithium and ensure self -sufficiency in supply of critical 
minerals which are essential for the advancement of many sectors, including high - 
tech electronics, telecommunications, transport and defence. They are also vital to 
power the transition to a low -emission economy, and the renewable technologie s 
that will be required to meet the „Net Zero‟ commitment of India by 2070. 
v. The auction of critical and strategic minerals brings several key benefits, 
including bolstering domestic production, reducing import dependency, promoting 
sustainable resource man agement, attracting investments in the mining sector and 
the development of key industries crucial for India's industrial and technological 
advancement. This is a step towards creating a reliable supply chain of these 
mineral and making an „Atma  Nirbhar Bharat‟ and contribute towards increased 
economic growth. 
vi. The Central Government has launched the first tranche of e -auction of 20 
mineral blocks of critical and strategic minerals on 29.11.2023 which includes two 
blocks of Lithium and associated minerals for grant of composite licence which on 
completion of G2 level of exploration followed by production aims to ensure 
steady supply of these minerals, thus reducing our reliance on imports and ensuring 
a more secure and resilient supply chain. 

20 
 
vii. Besides auction of critical minerals by the Central Government, in order to 
further boost exploration of critical and deep -seated minerals, a new mineral 
concession namely, exploration licence has been introduced for 29 critical and 
deep-seated minerals. Critical and d eep-seated minerals such as Cobalt, Lithium, 
Nickel, Gold, Silver, and Copper are difficult to explore and mine as compared to 
surfacial or bulk minerals. The country is mostly dependent on imports of these 
minerals. The exploration licence granted through auction shall permit the licencee 
to undertake reconnaissance and prospecting operations for critical and deep-seated 
minerals mentioned in the newly inserted Seventh Schedule to the MMDR Act. 
viii. Exploration license aims to create an enabling mechanism where in the Junior 
Mining Companies will bring in expertise from across the world in acquisition, 
processing and interpretation of exploration data and leverage the risk -taking 
ability in discovery of deep -seated mineral deposits through adoption of expertise 
and latest technologies. 
ix. KABIL, a Joint venture between 3 central PSE of Ministry of Mines has 
signed a Moll with CAMYEN, Govt. Company in Catamarca province of 
Argentina on 29.12.2020 to explore sourcing of lithium and other mineral assets in 
Argentina. Subsequently, KABIL has entered into an agreement with CAMYEN 
on 15.01.2024 to start its first ever Exploration and Development project for 
Lithium exploration followed by exploitation of 5 lithium blocks covering an area 
of 15000 ha in Catamarca province of  Argentina. All the above measures are 
aimed to ensure that India will become Atma  Nirbhar in the field of Lithium -ion 
battery manufacturing to facilitate transition to Electric mobility.

CHAPTER 1 
INTRODUCTION 
 
The Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI)  is crucial in driving industrial growth, fostering 
technological advancements, and promoting self -reliance in the manufacturing sector. It 
formulates policies and implements schemes to strengthen key industries such as the automotive, 
heavy engineering equipment and machine tools, and heavy electrical industries.  
The automotive sector, a key pillar of the economy, contributes 6.8% to India’s GDP and 
accounts for 40% of the manufacturing GDP. The capital goods sector, comprising heavy 
engineering equipment and machine  tools, constitutes 12% of the total manufacturing output, 
translating to 1.8% of GDP. The heavy electrical industry further adds a 1% share to the GDP. 
Given their substantial contributions, these sectors play a vital role in India's economic growth 
and industrial development. 
 
Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) 
 
2. The Ministry administers three key industry sectors: the Automotive Industry, including 
Tractor and earth -moving equipment; the Heavy Engineering Equipment and Machine Tools 
Industry (HE&MT); a nd the Heavy Electrical Industry (HEI). It also administers 21 central 
public sector enterprises (CPSEs) and four autonomous bodies. Out of the 21 CPSEs, 16 are 
operational. The remaining 4 CPSEs are under closure, and one is non-operational. 
Budget Highlight (2025-26) 
3. The Union Budget 2025 -26 included 35 capital goods in the exemption notification for 
lithium-ion battery manufacturing for electric vehicles (EVs). Th e move is expected to 
significantly impact the automotive industry by promoting the adoption of indigenous advanced 
chemistry cells and strengthening the domestic EV ecosystem. 
4. After the Union Budget 2025 -26 presentation, the Detailed Demands for Grants (2025-
26) of the Ministry of Heavy Indust ries were referred to the Department -related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Industry for detailed examination and reporting. The Committee: 
i. Analysed background notes provided by the Ministry, budget documents from the 
Ministry of Finance, and other relevant materials to ensure a comprehensive assessment. 
ii. Examined various documents, including the Annual Report 2024 -25, budget documents 
such as the Details of Demands for Grants and the Output -Outcome Framework, and the 
Ministry’s replies to the questionnaires.  
iii. Deliberated on the Ministry's Demands for Grants in its meeting on 21st February, 2025, 
during which the Secretary, Ministry of Heavy Industries, and other senior officials  
provided a comprehensive PowerPoint presentation.

Overview of the Automotive Industry 
18. The Indian automotive industry is one of the fastest -growing sectors. Over the years, 
nearly all major global automobile manufacturers have established production facilities in India. 
As a result, vehicle production has surged from 2 million units in 1991 -92 to approximately 28 
million units in FY 2023 -24. India manufactures a wide range of vehicles, including two -
wheelers, three-wheelers, passenger cars, light commercial vehicles, trucks, buses, tractors, and 
heavy commercial vehicles. The production, sale s, and export figures for various vehicle 
categories during financial year 2023-24 are as follows:

contributing 6.8% to the country's GDP and 40% of manufacturing GDP.  The sector plays a 
crucial role in employment generation, providing direct employment to 42 lakh  individuals and 
indirect employment to approximately 265 lakh people. Regarding global trade, automobile 
exports stand at ₹2.9 lakh crore . Additionally, the industry is a significant contributor to the 
national exchequer, generating ₹2.93 lakh crore in GS T revenue, which accounts for 14% -15% 
of the total GST collection. 
 
20. The Committee observes that India holds a strong global position in automobile 
production, ranking 2 nd in 2-Wheelers, 1st in 3-Wheelers, 4th in Passenger Vehicles, and 5 th  
in Commercial Vehicles. However, despite high production volumes - 214.69 lakh 2 -
wheelers, 9.93 lakh 3 -wheelers, 49.02 lakh passenger vehicles, and 10.66 lakh commercial 
vehicles in FY 2023 -24, exports remain relatively low, particularly in passenger and  
commercial vehicles. 
 
21. The Committee recommends that the Ministry formulate targeted strategies to 
enhance global competitiveness, address export barriers, and strengthen trade agreements 
to boost international market penetration. Additionally, policy interventions should focus 
on improving domestic demand, incentivizing innovation, and ensuring the sustainable 
growth of all vehicle categories to reinforce India's leadership in the global automotive 
industry.

22. The MHI informed that the Government launched a new scheme titled "PM Electric 
Drive Revolution in Innovative Vehicle Enhancement (PM E-DRIVE)" from 1st October 2024 for 
two years. The earlier Electric Mobility Promotion Scheme (EMPS -2024), which was 
implemented from 1st April 2024 to 30 th September 2024, has been subsumed under the PM E -
DRIVE scheme. Consequently, the PM E-DRIVE scheme is effective from 1 st April 2024 to 31st 
March 2026 with a total outlay of  Rs. 10,900 crore. For the financial year  2025-26, a budgetary 
allocation of Rs. 4000 crore has been made for this scheme. 
23. The primary objective of the PM E-DRIVE scheme is to expedite the adoption of EVs by 
providing upfront incentives for their purchase  and by facilitating the establishment of essential 
charging infrastructure for EVs. The scheme also promotes mass mobility by supporting mean s 
of public transportation. The scheme aims to promote EVs to reduce the environmental impact of 
transportation, fuel security and improve air quality.

48. Electric vehicles run on batteries; currently, most of the batteries and associated raw 
materials are imported from China. As announced in the Union Budget 2025 -26, the 
Government's recent exemption of customs duties on 35 additional capital goods essential for 
lithium-ion battery manufacturing is poised to significantly impact the automotive industry 
regarding the use of indigenous advan ced chemistry cells.  As Lithium -Ion Cell manufacturing 
technology is a niche technology, currently not fully developed in India, the Cell manufacturers 
are required to invest heavily , including on import of the latest Capital Goods required for 
manufacturing of ACCs. Due to lack of indigenous sourcing of capital goods, only way to get a 
competitive edge is by exempting customs duties on such critical  Capital Goods. The duty 
exemptions complement the PLI ACC scheme by incentivising domestic manufacturing of ACC 
technologies. This synergy is anticipated to strengthen India's position in the global EV market, 
making the country's automotive sector more competitive internationally.  
 
49. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Heavy Industries implement the 
recent customs duty exemptions on 35 additional capital goods essential for lithium -ion 
battery manufacturing. Given India's reliance on battery imports, particularly from China, 
and the high investment required for ACC production, these exemptions wi ll provide a 
competitive edge to domestic manufacturers. Additionally, their alignment with the PLI 
ACC scheme is expected to boost indigenous manufacturing, reduce import dependence, 
and enhance India’s position in the global EV market.  
 
50. The Committee notes the significant changes in the Mines and Minerals (Regulation 
and Development) [MMRD] Amendment Act, 2023 *. The amendments to the Act enables 
participation of private companies in mining exploration by providing them with 
exploration license for reconnaissance and prospecting of critical minerals. The Committee 
is hopeful that the participation of private players will expedite the exploration and mining 
of critical minerals like lithium without technological constraints. This is expected to 
strengthen indigenous manufacturing of lithium -ion batteries for electric vehicles and 
reduce dependence on imports of critical minerals.

Autonomous Bodies 
 
60.    India has established a strong and diversified manufacturing base for the production of a wide 
variety of basic and capital goods to meet the requirements of various sectors including heavy 
electrical, power generation and transmission industries, process equipment, automobiles, ships, 
aircrafts, mining, chemicals, petroleum, etc. However, the share of the man ufacturing sector in 
India's economy is still quite low. There is a considerable potential for growth which, in a globalised 
world economy, has to be based on improving productivity and competitiveness. Innovation and 
adoption of new technologies are the k ey factors in competitiveness. In order to achieve these, the 
Secretary, MHI during the presentation on the Demands for Grants (202 5-26) informed the 
Committee that the following Autonomous Bodies under the purview of MHI are working in the field 
of R& D and technology upgradation:

(iii) National Automotive Board (NAB).

61. In the Budget Estimates 2025-26 for autonomous bodies, an amount of Rs 2 0.03 crore has 
been allocated to CMTI, Bengaluru.  An Autonomous R&D Institute under the MHI, CMTI primarily 
focuses on developing Science and Technology (S& T) driven solutions to address 4P (Product – 
Process – People – Production) related challenges in the manufacturing sector.  The Committee 
notes that among the 04 autonomous bodies under the Ministry, only the Central 
Manufacturing Technology Institute (CMT I) has been allocated funds in the BE for FY 2025 -

importance of R&D and technological upgradation in maintaining global competitiveness, it

receive adequate budgetary support for technological advancement. Furthermore, the budget 
allocated to CMTI, Bengaluru, should be utilised efficiently to achieve the intended outcomes.

the Payment Security Mechanism . The funds will be utilized by Convergence Energy 
Services Limited (CESL) to act as a payment security mechanism or a financial safeguard 
against the pa yments related to the 38,000 e -buses targeted under the scheme. It 
recommends that the Ministry ensure the efficient and timely utilization of these funds to 
support the successful implementation of the programme.  
71. The Committee observed that no budgetary allocation has bee n made under the 
Capital Section in BE 2025 -26 for skill development programs for locals in CPSEs under 
the Ministry. Emphasizing the need for a skilled workforce in the evolving industrial 
landscape, it recommends that sufficient funds be sought at the RE stage (2025 -26) in 
collaboration with the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship to impart 
vocational training to local for enhancing their employability and strengthen India's 
industrial competitiveness. 
  

24 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE AT A GLANCE 
 
1. The Committee observes with dismay  that the Ministry could not fully utilise its 
allocated budget for the previous two financial years i.e. 2022 -23 and 2023 -24. In 2022-23, 
the Ministry utilized only 84.23% of RE, while in 2023 -24, the utilization further declined 
to 76.87%. In the current financial year 2024-25, only Rs. 1,750.16 crore out of the Revised 
Estimate (RE) allocation of Rs. 4,560.69 crore has been utilised, accounting for just 38.37% 
(as on 31.01.2025).  It recommends that the Ministry ensure the entire RE is fully utilised 
within the financial year. For the next FY 2025 -26, it recommends that the Ministry 
adheres to the Monthly Expenditure Plan (MEP)  and Quarterly Expenditure Plan (QEP) 
to ensure proper and timely utilisation. 
(Para 8) 
2. The Committee observes that u nder the flagship scheme of the Ministry – PM E-
Drive, a sum of Rs. 1870.76 crore was allocated in RE 2024 -25 against which the Ministry 
has only utilised Rs. 366.83 crore ( *under EMPS- subsumed in PM E -Drive) till 31 st 
January, 2025. It expresses serious concern over the underutilisation of funds under PM E-
Drive and the non-utilization under the Payment Security Mechanism. It recommends that 
the Ministry may take necessary steps to ensure utilisation of funds allocated at the RE 
stage. Additionally, the Ministry should avoid accumulation of the unspent funds in the last 
quarter of the financial year and refrain from spending mo re than 33% of the allocated 
amount during the last quarter and 15% in the last month of the Financial Year, as per the 
directions of Ministry of Finance.  
(Para 10) 
 
3. The Committee observes that for the Financial Year 2025 -26, the Ministry of Heavy 
Industries has been allocated a BE of Rs. 7,680.23 crore by the Ministry of Finance, which 
constitutes 85.09% of its projected requirement of Rs. 9,025.83 crore. The Ministry of 
Heavy Industries has informed the Committee that the FAME -II Scheme ended on 31 st 
March 2024, and the budget proposal of Rs. 722.00 crore under BE 2025 -26 was intended 
to meet payments for ongoing committed liabilities. However, the request was not acceded 
to. Given the pending liabilities, the Committee recommends reconsidering the allocation 
for the FAME -II Scheme at the RE stage to ensure the settlement of outstanding 
commitments. It further recommends that the Ministry make every effort to strategize and 
utilise the significant part of the allocations in a timely manner. After tha t, more funds 
should be allocated at the RE stage to implement the key schemes effectively. 
(Para 12) 
 

25 
 
4. The Committee observes that significant funds have been surrendered in key 
schemes such as PLI Scheme for the Automobile and Auto Component Industry a nd the 
Enhancement of Competitiveness in the Indian Capital Goods Sector since FY 2022 -23 to 
2023-24. The Committee urges the Ministry to analyse the underlying reasons for the 
inadequate receipt of proposals under the key schemes. Additionally, the Minist ry should 
identify and address procedural bottlenecks, particularly PFMS validation checks,  to 
expedite fund disbursement. Furthermore, the Ministry should formulate a strategic plan 
to enhance awareness and outreach through targeted campaigns, ensuring optimal use and 
evenly distribution throughout the year  of allocated funds and effectively contributing  to 
the vision of Viksit Bharat @ 2047. 
(Para 16) 
5.  The Committee notes that the Budget 2024 -25 announced the establishment of a 
joint venture between NTPC and BHEL to set up an 800 MW commercial plant utilizing 
Advanced Ultra Super Critical (AUSC) technology, with the govern ment providing 
necessary fiscal support. The Committee is pleased to know  that the site for the 800 MW 
AUSC technology-based power plant has been finalized at Korba, Chhattisgarh, and that 
the technical specifications and supply chain have also been finalized.  
(Para 17) 
6. The Committee observes that India holds a strong global position in automobile 
production, ranking 2 nd in 2-Wheelers, 1st in 3-Wheelers, 4th in Passenger Vehicles, and 5 th  
in Commercial Vehicles. However, despite high production volumes - 214.69 lakh 2 -
wheelers, 9.93 lakh 3 -wheelers, 49.02 lakh passenger vehicles, and 10.66 lakh commercial 
vehicles in FY 2023 -24, exports remain relatively low, particularly in passenger and  
commercial vehicles. 
(Para 20) 
 
7. The Committee recommends that the Ministry formulate targeted strategies to 
enhance global competitiveness, address export barriers, and strengthen trade agreements 
to boost international market penetration. Additionally, policy interventions should focus 
on improving domestic demand, incentivizing innovation, and ensuring the sustainable 
growth of all vehicle categories to reinforce India's leadership in the global automotive 
industry. 
(Para 21) 
 
8. The Committee notes that the budget allocation at the RE stage, amounting to Rs. 
1,870.76 crore, has reached only 19.61% utilisation as o n 12.02.2025. It recommends 

26 
 
therefore t hat the Ministry accelerate the implementation process and take proactive 
measures to ensure optimal budget utilisation in strict adherence to Financial Rules. 
(Para 25) 
 
9. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Heavy Industries reconsider the 
reduction in incentives for registered e -2 wheelers, e -Rickshaws, e-Carts, and e -3 wheelers 
(L5) in FY 2025-26, as the lower subsidy may slow down EV adoption in the country. Given 
the significant increase in the indicative number of vehicles to be supported across these 
segments, maintaining higher incentives would ensure sustained mark et growth, 
affordability, and alignment with the Government's clean mobility goals.  
(Para 28) 
10. The Committee observed that 4,57,840 claims were submitted on the PM E-DRIVE 
Portal. Of these, 2,26,099 claims (49.4%) had been incentivised as of 30 th November 2024. 
The Committee  recommends that the Ministry of Heavy Industries expedite processing 
pending incentive claims. The Committee also observed that while the e -2W and e-3W (L5) 
categories have achiev ed 64.3% and 100.3% of their respective targets, the extremely low 
performance of e -rickshaws & e -carts, meeting only 2.99% of the target, necessitates 
urgent holistic intervention. It recommends that the Ministry implement targeted 
awareness campaigns, facil itate financial access, and enhance infrastructure support to 
improve uptake in these segments.  Additionally, it recommends the establishment of a 
robust monitoring mechanism and regular stakeholder consultations to track progress and 
ensure the timely dis bursement of incentives. These measures will help align the 
implementation of the scheme with the Government’s vision for accelerated adoption of 
electric mobility. 
(Para 30) 
 
11. The Committee also notes that e -4 wheeler passenger vehicles and hybrid vehi cles 
have not been included in the PM E -DRIVE Scheme. Since 4-wheeler passenger vehicles 
constitute a significant share of the vehicle population, particularly in major cities, the 
Committee believes that incentivizing these categories would further accele rate the 
adoption of electric mobility in the country. Therefore, it recommends incorporating these 
vehicle categories into the scheme.  Additionally, it suggests introducing a subsidy 
mechanism linked to the scrapping of old diesel vehicles to encourage th eir phased 
replacement with electric vehicles , thereby promoting cleaner and sustainable 
transportation and ensuring a healthy environment. 
(Para 31) 
 

27 
 
12. The Committee acknowledges the steady growth in electric vehicle (EV) adoption,  
with the overall EV s hare rising from 5.30% in 2022 -23 to 7.32% in 2024 -25 (as on 
February 10). The significant penetration of electric three -wheelers (e -3Ws), surpassing 
57%, reflects a strong shift towards electrification in this segment. However, the growth of 
electric two -wheelers (e-2Ws) and electric four -wheelers (e-4Ws) remain moderate, while 
the adoption of electric buses and electric trucks continues to be limited. To accelerate this 
transition and work towards the country’s ambitious goal of 35% of total vehicle sales  
being electric by 2030, it recommends that the Ministry enhance policy support through 
targeted financial incentives, expansion of charging infrastructure particularly for e -2Ws 
and e-4Ws and promotion of localized manufacturing of key EV components. Addi tionally, 
a strategic focus on high -utilization segments like e -buses and e -trucks is crucial to 
decarbonizing commercial transport. 
(Para 33) 
 
13. The Committee observes that, at the initial stage, the Scheme covers only major 
cities with populations exce eding 40 lakh. Given India’s vast geography and the pressing 
need to reduce fossil fuel imports and vehicular air pollution, limiting e -bus deployment to 
a few large cities will not be sufficient to address these challenges comprehensively. 
Therefore, it recommends that the Ministry expand the scope of the Scheme to include 
smaller cities. If necessary, the Ministry should seek additional budgetary allocations at the 
Revised Estimates (RE) stage from the Ministry of Finance to maximize the Scheme’s 
potential in promoting electric bus adoption and green energy transition.  
(Para 35) 
14.   The Committee emphasises that charging infrastructure is crucial for successfully 
transitioning to electric mobility. A meagre Rs. 180.00 crore was allocated  at the RE stage 
for 2024 -25 for installing EV public charging stations across the country, and the entire 
amount remains unutilised. It recommends that the Ministry proactively seek enhanced 
funding from the Ministry of Finance at the RE stage (2025 -26) to expedite the installation 
of charging infrastructure under the PM E -DRIVE, thereby providing a much -needed 
boost to electric mobility. 
(Para 38) 
15. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Heavy Industries finalize 
guidelines and SOPs to ensure the swift and effective implementation of the PM e-Bus Sewa 
Payment Security Mechanism (PSM) Scheme. It is crucial to expedite coordination with 
States to  facilitate the registration of Direct Debit Mandates (DDMs) with the RBI, 
ensuring wider participation beyond Karnataka and Telangana. Additionally, the Ministry 

28 
 
should establish a robust monitoring mechanism to track implementation progress and 
address any challenges stakeholders face to enhance the scheme’s effectiveness. 
(Para 40) 
 
16.  The Committee was informed that the Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme 
for Automobile and Auto Components is expected to attract an  investment of 
approximately Rs. 42,500 crore and generate around 1.48 lakh direct employment 
opportunities over five years. As on 19.02.2025, total 77 variants of Champion Original 
Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) and 39 variant of Component Champion OEMs, both 
overseas and Indian, have been approved under the components of this scheme.  As per 
data provided by the Ministry of Heavy Industries, the actual expenditure under the 
scheme for financial year 2024 -25 up to 31 st January 2025 stands at Rs. 246.21 cror e, 
representing approximately 70.98% of the allocated funds. Given the critical role of this 
scheme in strengthening domestic manufacturing under the Make in India  and 
Aatmanirbhar Bharat initiatives, the Committee recommends that the funds allocated at the 
Revised Estimate (RE) stage be fully utilized by the end of the current financial year.  
(Para 43) 
 
17.  The scheme's budget rose sharply in 2024 -25, but actual expenditure remains below 
RE, highlighting utilisation challenges. For 2025-26, a budget allo cation of ₹155.76 crore 
has been proposed.  The Committee believes this scheme facilitates realising  the goal of 
Make in India and Atmnirbhar Bharat by promoting newer and niche technologies . It needs 
to be implemented promptly and effectively with robust zeal. Therefore, it is recommended 
that the scheme's implementation be streamlined to ensure efficient fund utilisation, timely 
disbursement, and alignment with industry demand to maximize its impact on domestic 
battery manufacturing.  
(Para 47) 
18. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Heavy Industries implement the 
recent customs duty exemptions on 35 additional capital goods essential for lithium -ion 
battery manufacturing. Given India's reliance on battery imports, particularly from China, 
and th e high investment required for ACC production, these exemptions will provide a 
competitive edge to domestic manufacturers. Additionally, their alignment with the PLI 
ACC scheme is expected to boost indigenous manufacturing, reduce import dependence, 
and enhance India’s position in the global EV market.  
(Para 49) 
 
 

29 
 
19. The Committee notes the significant changes in the Mines and Minerals (Regulation 
and Development) [MMRD] Amendment Act, 2023 *. The amendments to the Act enables 
participation of private companies in mining exploration by providing them with 
exploration license for reconnaissance and p rospecting of critical minerals. The Committee 
is hopeful that the participation of private players will expedite the exploration and mining 
of critical mine rals like lithium without technological constraints. This is expected to 
strengthen indigenous manufacturing of lithium -ion batteries for electric vehicles and 
reduce dependence on imports of critical minerals. 
(Para 50) 
 
20. The Committee recommends regular assessment and monitoring of Phase II of the 
Scheme for Enhancement of Competitiveness in the Indian Capital Goods Sector  to ensure 
its effective implementation, with a focus on strengthening domestic manufacturing 
capabilities and reducing reliance on imported high -end machines. This will help foster a 
globally competitive and self-reliant capital goods industry.  
(Para 57) 
 
21. The Committee notes with concern the drastic reduction in Budget Estimates (BE) 
for 2025 -26 to Rs. 120.00 crore from Rs. 250.00 crore in previous two financial years, 
raising questions about the Ministry’s ability to implement key initiatives effectively. The 
shortage of funds poses a significant challenge to the execution of schemes. It recommends 
that the Ministry address funding shortfalls at the Revised Estimates (RE) stage to prevent 
underutilisation. Furthermore, the Committee observes that no allocations have been made 
for industry associations and public sector undertakings (PSUs) to support the capital 
goods sector. Given the crucial role of these entities in promoting Government schemes and 
raising stakeholder awareness, the Committee urges the Min istry to engage with the 
Ministry of Finance to reassess and enhance budgetary provisions for these essential 
activities. 
(Para 59) 
 
22. The Committee notes that among the 04 autonomous bodies under the Ministry, only 
the Central Manufacturing Technology I nstitute (CMTI) has been allocated funds in the BE 
for FY 2025 -26, while no provision has been made for the other 03 autonomous bodies. Given 
the critical importance of R&D and technological upgradation in maintaining global 
competitiveness, it recommends that the Ministry extend its focus to other R&D institutions 
and ensure they receive adequate budgetary support for technological advancement. 
Furthermore, the budget allocated to CMTI, Bengaluru, should be utilised efficiently to achieve 
the intended outcomes. The Ministry may consider seeking an enhancement at the RE stage if 
additional funds are required. 
(Para 61)

administrative control of the Ministry of Heavy Industries, 6 2 CPSEs are loss making

The Chairman welcomed the Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) officials to discuss the 2025 -26 
Budget. He highlighted/ stated/ asked for 
(i) MHI's role is to develop capital goods, automobile, and heavy electrical equipment sectors 
while overseeing CPSEs and autonomous organisations.  
(ii) MHI's budget allocation for 2025-26 is about 85% of the proposed ₹9,025.83 crores. 
(iii) Action plan for optimally utilising the enhanced budgetary allocation for 2025-26, focusing 
on the PM E-Drive Scheme, which has been allocated more than 50% of the total budget.  
(iv) Information on schemes’ progress, strategies planned for the year, and the targets set.  
(v) Data on performance of CPSEs, steps taken to improve output and productivity, and any 
restructuring or revival plans for sick or loss-making CPSEs.  
2. After the Chair’s permission, through a presentation, the Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI)  
(i) outlined their budget performance from 2020-21 to 2024-25,  
(ii) focused on schemes like the PLI -Automobile Scheme, with an outlay of ₹25,938 crore, 
aimed at boosting the electric vehicle sector,  
(iii) Shared the technological advancements and significant growth of the Heavy Electrical 
Industry and 
(iv) Highlighted the importance of developing Advanced Chemistry Cells to accelerate the 
production of electric vehicles (EVs).  
(v) Provided an overview of the automotive industry, highlighting India’s global position in the 
sector, and discussed the awareness programs launched by the Ministry to educate the 
public about electric vehicles (EVs).  
(vi) Stressed the need to scale up manufacturing capabilities, create jobs, and improve India's 
position in the global automotive market.  
3. The CMDs briefed the Committee about BHEL, Bridge and Roof Company Ltd, and 
Braithwaite Burn and Joseph Construction Co. Ltd.  
4. After the presentation, the Chairman and Committee Members  
(i) Raised underutilisation of the budget in previous years, ranging from 2022-23 to 2024-25 
(ii) Pointed out the reduced allocation under capital heads vis a vis the total allocation; 
(iii) Sought reasons for continuing the legacy name of Braithwaite Burn and Jessop. 
(iv) Inquired about the steps taken to protect domestic players given global players like Tesla 
entering the Indian market 
(v) Sought replies on points like job work, underground coal gasification, coll aboration with 
J&T, Hyderabad for skill development, gravitational storage for large-scale solutions.

(vi) Highlighted that a key challenge is the customs duty on scrap material. When specialized 
material is imported for manufacturing, such as a one -tonne valve, the duty is charged on 
the full weight, including scrap, which adds unnecessary costs. The committee recommends 
addressing this issue with the Ministry of Finance or Commerce. Additionally, large 
companies like BHEL, with their technological capabilities, should focus more on job work 
opportunities. 
(vii) Reminded CMD HEC for the background note, as the Committee intends to recommend 
steps to revive the organisation 
5. The Committee directed that the following be recommended in their DFG report: 
(i) Passenger vehicles (four wheelers) and hybrid vehicles may also be incentivised under the

25, compared to 175 in FY 2020-21

CHAPTER-1 
INTRODUCTION 
 
Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises 
 
Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) envisions a progressive 
MSME sector by promoting growth and development of small business, including khadi, village 
and coir industries, in cooperation with Ministries/Departments, State Governments and other 
stakeholders, by providing support to existing enterprises, adopting cutting edge technologies 
and encouraging creation of new enterprises. The Ministry is dedicated to fostering inclusive 
growth by ensuring geographic inclusivity of rural and urban areas, demographic inclusivity of 
socially and economically weaker sections such as Scheduled Castes (SCs) / Scheduled Tribes 
(STs)  communities, and promoting women entrepreneurship to boost gender parity. 
 
2. To promote and develop the MSME sector in the country, the Ministry is supported by 
various statutory and non-statutory bodies, including the Khadi and Village Industries 
Commission (KVIC), the Coir Board, National Small Industries Corporation (NSIC), National 
Institute for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (ni-MSME), and the Mahatma Gandhi 
Institute for Rural Industrialization (MGIRI). These organizations play a crucial role in fostering 
growth and providing support to the MSME sector 
 
3. The Ministry of MSME implements more than 25 schemes for credit support, 
technological assistance, infrastructure development, skill development, and training, enhancing 
competitiveness and market assistance to MSME, and creating self-employment opportunities. 
 
4. The Parliamentary Standing Committee, per its mandate, undertook a comprehensive 
assessment of the Ministry's detailed Demand for Grants. The Committee  
i. Reviewed various documents, including the Annual Report (2024-25), Economic Survey, 
Budget documents such as the Details of Demand for Grants, Output-Outcome 
Framework; 
ii. Examined the background note and the answers to the questionnaires; 
iii. Solicited evidence, interacted with and obtained replies from the Ministry. 
iv. Desktop research on Global Data related to MSMEs Sector. 
Public Procurement Policy for Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs ) 
5. The Ministry of MSME implemented the Public Procurement Policy for Micro and Small 
Enterprises (MSEs) under the MSMED Act, 2006, which became mandatory in 2015. The policy 
mandates that Public Sector companies procure 25% of their total purchases from MSEs, with 
4% reserved for SC/ST-owned MSEs and 3% for women-owned MSEs. The Ministry reduced 
the requirements from seven to four in August 2021 to ease compliance. 
6. Additionally, the MSME Sambandh Portal, launched in 2017, tracks procurement data, 
with 40.77% of total procurement reported from MSEs, benefiting over 161,000 MSEs. 
However, the participation of women and SC/ST-owned MSEs remains low at 2.32% and 
1.33%, respectively. The Ministry also encourages MSEs to join the Government e-Marketplace 
(GeM) Portal, with a simplified registration process integrated into the Udyam Registration 
online form. 

2 
 
7. While reviewing the performance of several CPSEs under the central Government, the 
National Hydro Power Corporation (NHPC) has displayed a strong example of successful policy 
implementation. It was observed that the NHPC has effectively engaged vendors, especially from 
remote areas by organizing vendor meetings at the project level to educate them on registration, 
obtaining Udyam certificates, and participating in the tendering process. Further, by uploading 
its annual procurement plan on a web portal, NHPC has ensured vendors have advance 
knowledge of requirements, thereby increasing eligible MSE participation in tenders. 
Recommendations 
8. The Committee, notes that despite efforts to implement sub-quotas within the Public 
Procurement Policy (PPP) for women and SC/ST-owned MSEs, significant gaps remain in 
achieving the quotas, with some regions reporting as low as 70% fulfillment. 
(i) In light of the success of the NHPC, the Committee recommends the MSME 
Ministry to take immediate and decisive action to eliminate barriers preventing the 
fulfillment of sub-quotas. The Ministry must prioritize the implementation of targeted 
measures to ensure full compliance and equitable distribution without delay.  
(ii) Additionally, it is suggested that the Ministry consider including Other Backward 
Classes (OBC)-owned MSEs within the overall PPP quotas, which could enhance their 
participation and further strengthen the policy's inclusivity and effectiveness. 
Budget Speech/Budget Highlights 
9. The Union Budget 2025-26 focuses on strengthening the MSME sector, recognizing it 
as second engine of India’s economic growth alongside agriculture, investment, and exports. 
With 6 crore registered MSMEs employing over 25 crore people and contributing 30% to the 
GDP, 36% to the manufacturing output, 45.73% to India’s total exports in 2023-24, and ₹5 lakh 
crore to GST, the sector plays a crucial role in manufacturing, exports, and employment. The 
new budget introduces a series of measures designed to foster innovation, improve 
competitiveness, and equip MSMEs to expand their reach and boost India’s economic 
development. Following are the highlights of the Union Budget 2025-26 for the MSME Sector:

Credit Cards for Micro Enterprises 
10. A new initiative will be introduced to empower micro enterprises registered on the 
Udyam portal by offering personalized credit cards with a ₹5 lakh limit. This initiative will 

3 
 
provide financial support to help these businesses grow, with 10 lakh cards set to be issued in the 
first year. 
Fund of Funds for Startups 
11. The Alternate Investment Funds (AIFs) for startups have secured commitments exceeding 
₹91,000 crore, supported by a Fund of Funds with a government contribution of ₹10,000 crore. A 
new Fund of Funds, with an expanded scope and an additional ₹10,000 crore contribution, will 
now be established to further support startups. 
Scheme for First-time Entrepreneurs  
12. A new scheme will be launched to support 5 lakh first-time women, Scheduled Castes, 
and Scheduled Tribes entrepreneurs by providing term loans of up to ₹2 crore over the next 5 
years. Drawing from the successful Stand-Up India scheme, it will also include online capacity 
building for entrepreneurship and managerial skills to empower these entrepreneurs. 
Focus Product Scheme for Footwear & Leather Sectors 
13. A focus product scheme will be implemented to enhance India's footwear and leather 
sectors’ productivity, quality, and competitiveness. The scheme will support design capacity, 
component manufacturing, and the necessary machinery for producing non-leather quality 
footwear, along with leather footwear and products. It is expected to generate employment for 22 
lakh people, achieve a turnover of ₹4 lakh crore, and drive exports exceeding ₹1.1 lakh crore..  
Measures for the Toy Sector 
14. Building on the National Action Plan for Toys, a new scheme will be implemented to 
make India a global toy hub. The scheme will focus on developing clusters, enhancing skills, and 
creating a robust manufacturing ecosystem. This will enable the production of high-quality, 
innovative, and sustainable toys that reflect the 'Made in India' brand, boosting India's presence in 
the global toy market. The global toy market is projected to experience significant growth in the 
coming years. Valued at approximately* ₹94,952 crore in 2024, the market is expected to 
generate revenues of around ₹1,10,273.8 crore in 2025. Looking further ahead, forecasts indicate 
the market will expand from US Dollar ₹1,00,015 crore to ₹1,68,573 crore by 2034, reflecting a 
compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 6%. This growth highlights the increasing demand and 
evolving trends within the global toy industry. 
Support for Food Processing 
15. In line with the commitment towards 'Purvodaya,' a National Institute of Food 
Technology, Entrepreneurship, and Management will be established in Bihar. This institute aims 
to boost food processing activities in the Eastern region, leading to enhanced income for farmers 
through value addition to their produce. It will also create skilling, entrepreneurship, and 
employment opportunities for the youth, fostering economic growth in the area. 
Manufacturing Mission - Furthering “Make in India” 
16. The Government will establish a National Manufacturing Mission to advance "Make in 
India" by offering policy support, execution roadmaps, and a governance and monitoring 
framework for both central ministries and states, covering small, medium, and large industries. 
 
 
*amount is converted from US Dollar to Rupees

Export Promotion Mission  
17. An Export Promotion Mission will be established with sectoral and ministerial targets, 
led jointly by the Ministries of Commerce, MSME, and Finance. This mission will provide easy 
access to export credit, cross-border factoring support, and assist MSMEs in overcoming non-
tariff barriers in international markets. 
Global Scenario in MSMEs’ Classification 
18. The International Finance Corporation MSME definition* classifies enterprises as micro, 
small, or medium based on two of three criteria: employees, assets, or sales, or by the MSME 
loan size proxy. Micro enterprises have under 10 employees, assets, and sales below $100,000, 
with loans under $10,000, while small and medium enterprises have higher thresholds. 
Recommendations 
19. The Committee notes that, as of December 31, 2024, out of the 5.77 crore total 
MSMEs, 5.69 crore are micro, 7.3 lakh are small, and 69,000 are medium. Despite this, the 
new revised investment and turnover limits could potentially undermine the purpose of 
MSMEs by elevating micro-enterprises beyond their original scope. It is recommended that 
the Government revise the definition of Micro, Small, and Medium enterprises and create a 
new category –nano with the lowest financial criteria around ₹10 lakh. This would ensure 
that businesses with a turnover above ₹2.5 crore do not deviate from the core purpose of 
MSMEs—driving employment generation and supporting smaller enterprises. 
20. The Committee appreciates the new initiative to issue customized credit cards with a 
₹5 lakh limit for micro enterprises. It recommends that the Ministry expedite the 
distribution of these cards, focusing on micro enterprises that are not entirely digitised. 
Financial literacy programs should also be provided to help these businesses effectively 
utilize the cards, improving access to working capital and financial services.
