Recommendations 
24. On Budget Utilization:-  
(i) The Committee recommends that the Ministry prioritize the optimal 
utilization of the allocated ₹23,168.15 crore by focusing on high-impact schemes, 
particularly those supporting technological upgradation, market access, and employment 
generation. To address the ₹2,439.08 crore shortfall, the Ministry may seek additional 
funds at the Revised Estimates (RE) stage or explore alternative funding sources, such as 
public-private partnerships (PPP) and collaborations with financial institutions, to ensure 
the uninterrupted implementation of critical programs. 
 (ii)  The Committee committee observes with concern that there is a significant 
gap between the Revised Estimate and actual expenditure, and a clear under achievement 
in the QEP, with only 41.74% of the allocated budget utilised as of January 20, 2025. This 
shortfall is attributed to challenges posed by the Model Code of Conduct during the general 
elections. The Committee recommends that the Ministry must adopt a more flexible and 
efficient planning approach to mitigate such disruptions in the future. Additionally, it 
should explore methods to accelerate fund utilization in the remaining months of the fiscal 
year to minimize any long-term impact on program outcomes. 
25. With regard to QEP targets set for the Financial Year 2025-26, the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry apply lessons learned from the previous year by 
implementing a clear Quarterly and Monthly Expenditure Plan to ensure efficient fund 
utilization. Additionally, the Ministry should focus on strengthening initiative planning, 
execution, and budget absorption capacity to guarantee that allocated funds are utilized 
effectively, driving tangible outcomes in MSME initiatives. 
26. The Committee notes that 96.9% of the Ministry's budget allocation is allocated to 
revenue expenditure, with only 3.1% earmarked for capital expenditure. To drive 
substantial growth and achieve encouraging outcomes, the Ministry should prioritize 
increasing capital expenditure, as this will give an impetus to infrastructure and 
developmental initiatives. 
27. The Committee acknowledges that most schemes are demand-driven, but it 
recommends that the Ministry set clear, predefined targets for these schemes. IT 
recommends utilizing behavioural science tools to nudge, encourage, and motivate 
organisations, leading to better stakeholder outcomes. 
28. The Committee has observed the following in the explanatory note submitted by the 
Ministry on the proposed Revenue and Capial Outlays – 
i. High Savings in Non-Functional Heads: A large portion of savings was seen in non-
functional heads under the revenue section. Although funds were re-appropriated to 
functional heads for specific regions like the North East and Sikkim, the non-functional 
heads remained underutilized. 
ii. Delayed Scheme Approvals: Several schemes, including MSME Champions and MSME 
Innovative Scheme, were delayed in approval and launch, resulting in zero or minimal 
expenditure since funds couldn’t be utilized until later in the fiscal year. 

8 
 
iii. Lack of Proposals for Demand-Driven Schemes: Demand-driven schemes like Prime 
Minister’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP) and Entrepreneur Skill 
Development Programme (ESDP) experienced savings due to the lack of viable 
proposals. Insufficient participation and low proposal submissions led to funds not being 
fully utilized. 
iv. Delayed Sanctioning Process for Infrastructure Development: Infrastructure 
development schemes saw savings due to delays in the sanctioning process and the low 
number of project proposals received, leading to underutilization of allocated funds. 
v. Zero Expenditure under PMEGP and other Credit Schemes & Self Reliant 
Initiative (SRI) Fund Schemes: The SRI Fund of Fund schemes had no expenditure, as 
the funds were dependent on daughter funds raising their own resources, which caused 
delays in deploying the allocated funds. 
vi. Underutilization of Infrastructure Establishment Funds: The infrastructure 
establishment fund also saw savings due to the non-receipt of viable project proposals, 
leading to unspent funds being surrendered. 
vii. High Percentage of Unutilized Funds: Many schemes, such as the Infrastructure 
Development Programme and Research and Evaluation Studies, saw high savings, mainly 
due to delayed approvals and insufficient demand for the schemes. 
And based on these observations the Committee recommends that  
29. The Ministry should establish a structured timeline for the approval and launch of 
schemes to ensure timely operationalization and prevent delays, as seen with the MSME 
Champions and MSME Innovative Schemes. Allocating funds to functional heads at the 
start of the fiscal year will reduce re-appropriations and streamline project 
implementation. To tackle underutilization due to insufficient proposals, the Ministry 
should enhance efforts to engage potential proposers, especially for demand-driven 
schemes like PMEGP, ESDP, and the Infrastructure Development Programme, through 
more targeted awareness campaigns, workshops, webinars, and networking events. A 
robust monitoring system may also be implemented to track proposal submissions, 
ensuring timely follow-ups and support. 
 
30.  The Ministry should prioritize the prompt deployment of capital funds, particularly 
for the SRI Fund of Fund & PMEGP and other credit schemes by collaborating with 
daughter funds to mobilize resources quickly and establishing follow-up mechanisms for 
fund deployment. To improve utilization of infrastructure-related funds, the sanctioning 
process may be expedited, and project proposals should be regularly solicited. An effective 
real-time monitoring system should track fund utilization, enabling quick identification of 
underutilization and corrective actions. Periodic reviews of fund allocation will ensure 
alignment with actual needs. Ministry may focus more towards strengthening coordination 
with implementing agencies and introducing flexibility in fund reallocation will help 
optimize resource usage, reduce savings, and address delays. Additionally, enhancing the 
Ministry's financial management and forecasting capacity may improve fund allocation 
and utilization.

MAJOR SCHEMES AND PROGRAMMES 
33. The Ministry of MSME has introduced various dynamic and comprehensive schemes to 
promote the growth and development of Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises across India. 
These initiatives focus on key areas such as finance, technology, infrastructure, employment 
generation, entrepreneurship, and marketing. Most of these schemes are managed under three 
divisions of the ministry: the Small and Medium Enterprises (SME) Division, the Agro and 
Rural Industry (ARI) Division, along with the Office of the Development Commissioner (DC, 
MSME), an attached office. The major schemes covering 80% of their budgetary allocation of 
the Ministry and their budget analysis are as below:- 
GUARANTEED EMERGENCY CREDIT LINE (GECL) 
34. The Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS), launched on 23rd May 2020 as 
part of the Atmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyaan, aimed to support MSMEs and other businesses 
impacted by the COVID-19 crisis. The scheme provided a 100% guarantee to Member Lending 
Institutions (MLIs) on credit extended to eligible borrowers, enabling businesses to meet 
operational liabilities and resume activities. Implemented by the Department of Financial 
Services (DFS) under the Ministry of Finance, the scheme was operational until 31st March 
2023. According to a research report by SBI dated 23rd January 2023, the scheme protected 
nearly 14.6 lakh MSME accounts, with 98.3% of these being from the micro and small enterprise 
categories, and helped prevent about 12% of outstanding MSME credit from being classified as 
non-performing assets (NPAs). 
35. The allocation for the ECLGS is determined based on the demand raised by the DFS and 
the National Credit Guarantee Trustee Company (NCGTC). While the scheme was designed to 
act as a safeguard fund in case of NPAs arising from loans extended during the pandemic, there 
has been no shortage of funds for credit guarantee coverage. In fact, Rs. 5 lakh crore worth of 
credit guarantees have been provided over the last two years. As NPAs within MSMEs have 
been declining, the budgetary allocations for the GECL scheme are no longer required to be fully 
utilized. Similarly, for other smaller schemes, the allocations have either remained consistent or 
increased, demonstrating the continued need for support without concerns of unutilized funds.

CREDIT SUPPORT/GUARANTEE SCHEMES 
37. The Credit Guarantee Scheme for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE) offers 
collateral-free credit to MSEs through banks, financial institutions, and NBFCs. The scheme's 
loan ceiling was increased from ₹2 crore to ₹5 crore per borrowing unit as of April 1, 2023, with 
up to 90% guarantee coverage. The scheme supports women-led enterprises with enhanced 
coverage and charges a nominal Annual Guarantee Fee (AGF). As of December 2024, the 
scheme has approved 1.01 crore proposals totalling ₹8.07 lakh crore, benefiting MSEs across 
more than 100 sectors, with a significant focus on underserved regions. 
38. In FY 2023-24, the government infused ₹9,000 crore into the CGTMSE corpus, which 
includes ₹8,500 crore from GoI and ₹500 crore from SIDBI (Small Industries Development 
Bank of India). Revamped measures, such as a 50% reduction in guarantee fees and simplified 
claims processing for loans up to ₹10 lakh, are designed to reduce credit costs for MSEs and 
enhance their growth potential. These changes aim to boost credit access and foster the 
development of small businesses, particularly in rural and regional areas. 
39. CGTMSE has leveraged digital platforms to streamline the application process for 
guarantee coverage, with automated approvals and API integration with 13 major banks for 
seamless data flow. These digital advancements led to a significant rise in guarantee approvals, 
reaching ₹2.04 lakh crore by January 31, 2025, surpassing the previous year's record of ₹2.02 
lakh crore. In the upcoming financial year, CGTMSE plans further digital enhancements, 
including complete end-to-end API (Application Programming Interface) integration with MLIs 
(Member Lending Institutions) and improvements to user interfaces and experiences.

RAISING AND ACCELERATING MSME PERFORMANCE (RAMP) 
58. The RAMP (Raising and Accelerating MSME Performance) scheme is a World Bank-
assisted Central Sector initiative to boost MSME performance by promoting innovation, 
digitisation, technology upgradation, market access, credit, and sustainability initiatives. With a 
total outlay of ₹6062.45 crore from FY 2022-23 to FY 2026-27, the World Bank provides ₹3750 
crore (USD 500 million) in support. 
59. Besides providing gap funding to States under Strategic Investment Plans (SIPs), RAMP 
supports various MSME schemes, including the MSME Champions Scheme, Procurement and 
Marketing Support, and International Cooperation. It also introduces four new sub-schemes: the 
MSE Green Investment and Financing for Transformation (MSE GIFT Scheme), MSE Scheme 
for Circular Economy Promotion (MSE SPICE Scheme), MSE Online Dispute Resolution 
(ODR) for Delayed Payments, and MSME Trade Enablement & Marketing (MSME TEAM) 
Initiative. The programme is expected to benefit over 5.5 lakh MSMEs during its five-year 
duration. 
60. Besides, it is informed that all 36 States and Union Territories (UTs) are participating in 
the RAMP Scheme, with each receiving a grant of ₹5 crore to prepare a Strategic Investment 
Plan (SIP) for the development and promotion of the MSME sector. 34 States/UTs have 
submitted SIPs, and a total of ₹2966.144 crore has been approved for selected projects within 
these plans. The first instalment of grants has been released to these States/UTs to implement the 
approved projects.

of ₹ 50,000 Crore has a provision of ₹10,000 Crore from Government of India and ₹40,000

growth capital to the deserving and eligible units of MSME sector. As of Now, Ministry of

As of 06.02.2025, ₹1,641.78 crore has been sanctioned and released to the implementing agency. 
Additionally, in the last three years, approximately 100% of the allocated funds have been 
utilized. To ensure the continued infusion of the ₹10,000 crore, it is essential to increase the 
budget provision. Therefore, the proposed Budget Estimate (BE) for the year 2025-26 is ₹700 
crore.

RECOMMENDATIONS AT GLANCE 
 
1. The Committee, notes that despite efforts to implement sub-quotas within the Public 
Procurement Policy (PPP) for women and SC/ST-owned MSEs, significant gaps remain in 
achieving the quotas, with some regions reporting as low as 70% fulfillment. 
(i) In light of the success of the NHPC, the Committee recommends the MSME 
Ministry to take immediate and decisive action to eliminate barriers preventing the 
fulfillment of sub-quotas. The Ministry must prioritize the implementation of targeted 
measures to ensure full compliance and equitable distribution without delay.  
(ii) Additionally, it is suggested that the Ministry consider including Other Backward 
Classes (OBC)-owned MSEs within the overall PPP quotas, which could enhance their 
participation and further strengthen the policy's inclusivity and effectiveness. 
(Para-8) 
2. The Committee notes that, as of December 31, 2024, out of the 5.77 crore total 
MSMEs, 5.69 crore are micro, 7.3 lakh are small, and 69,000 are medium. Despite this, the 
new revised investment and turnover limits could potentially undermine the purpose of 
MSMEs by elevating micro-enterprises beyond their original scope. It is recommended that 
the Government revise the definition of Micro, Small, and Medium enterprises and create a 
new category –nano with the lowest financial criteria around ₹10 lakh. This would ensure 
that businesses with a turnover above ₹2.5 crore do not deviate from the core purpose of 
MSMEs—driving employment generation and supporting smaller enterprises. 
(Para-19) 
3. The Committee appreciates the new initiative to issue customized credit cards with a 
₹5 lakh limit for micro enterprises. It recommends that the Ministry expedite the 
distribution of these cards, focusing on micro enterprises that are not entirely digitised. 
Financial literacy programs should also be provided to help these businesses effectively 
utilize the cards, improving access to working capital and financial services. 
(Para-20) 
4. On Budget Utilization:-  
(i) The Committee recommends that the Ministry prioritize the optimal 
utilization of the allocated ₹23,168.15 crore by focusing on high-impact schemes, 
particularly those supporting technological upgradation, market access, and employment 
generation. To address the ₹2,439.08 crore shortfall, the Ministry may seek additional 
funds at the Revised Estimates (RE) stage or explore alternative funding sources, such as 
public-private partnerships (PPP) and collaborations with financial institutions, to ensure 
the uninterrupted implementation of critical programs. 
 (ii)  The Committee committee observes with concern that there is a significant 
gap between the Revised Estimate and actual expenditure, and a clear under achievement 
in the QEP, with only 41.74% of the allocated budget utilised as of January 20, 2025. This 

42 
 
shortfall is attributed to challenges posed by the Model Code of Conduct during the general 
elections. The Committee recommends that the Ministry must adopt a more flexible and 
efficient planning approach to mitigate such disruptions in the future. Additionally, it 
should explore methods to accelerate fund utilization in the remaining months of the fiscal 
year to minimize any long-term impact on program outcomes. 
 (Para-24) 
5. With regard to QEP targets set for the Financial Year 2025-26, the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry apply lessons learned from the previous year by 
implementing a clear Quarterly and Monthly Expenditure Plan to ensure efficient fund 
utilization. Additionally, the Ministry should focus on strengthening initiative planning, 
execution, and budget absorption capacity to guarantee that allocated funds are utilized 
effectively, driving tangible outcomes in MSME initiatives. 
(Para-25) 
6. The Committee notes that 96.9% of the Ministry's budget allocation is allocated to 
revenue expenditure, with only 3.1% earmarked for capital expenditure. To drive 
substantial growth and achieve encouraging outcomes, the Ministry should prioritize 
increasing capital expenditure, as this will give an impetus to infrastructure and 
developmental initiatives. 
(Para-26) 
7. The Committee acknowledges that most schemes are demand-driven, but it 
recommends that the Ministry set clear, predefined targets for these schemes. IT 
recommends utilizing behavioural science tools to nudge, encourage, and motivate 
organisations, leading to better stakeholder outcomes. 
(Para-27) 
8. The Ministry should establish a structured timeline for the approval and launch of 
schemes to ensure timely operationalization and prevent delays, as seen with the MSME 
Champions and MSME Innovative Schemes. Allocating funds to functional heads at the 
start of the fiscal year will reduce re-appropriations and streamline project 
implementation. To tackle underutilization due to insufficient proposals, the Ministry 
should enhance efforts to engage potential proposers, especially for demand-driven 
schemes like PMEGP, ESDP, and the Infrastructure Development Programme, through 
more targeted awareness campaigns, workshops, webinars, and networking events. A 
robust monitoring system may also be implemented to track proposal submissions, 
ensuring timely follow-ups and support. 
(Para-29) 
 
9. The Ministry should prioritize the prompt deployment of capital funds, particularly 
for the SRI Fund of Fund & PMEGP and other credit schemes by collaborating with 
daughter funds to mobilize resources quickly and establishing follow-up mechanisms for 
fund deployment. To improve utilization of infrastructure-related funds, the sanctioning 

43 
 
process may be expedited, and project proposals should be regularly solicited. An effective 
real-time monitoring system should track fund utilization, enabling quick identification of 
underutilization and corrective actions. Periodic reviews of fund allocation will ensure 
alignment with actual needs. Ministry may focus more towards strengthening 
coordination with implementing agencies and introducing flexibility in fund reallocation 
will help optimize resource usage, reduce savings, and address delays. Additionally, 
enhancing the Ministry's financial management and forecasting capacity may improve 
fund allocation and utilization. 
(Para-30) 
10. The Committee appreciates Ministry’s efforts to support MSMEs through various 
initiatives, including the Credit Guarantee Schemes, TReDS on boarding, establishing 50 
food irradiation units and 100 NABL-accredited food testing labs, expansion of SIDBI 
branches, etc. To further strengthen these initiatives, Government must implement the 
announcements made a soon as possible specifically: 
(i)  To strengthen the Credit Guarantee Scheme for MSMEs in Special Mention 
Accounts (CGS-MSMA), it is recommended to integrate an automated monitoring 
system within the dashboard. This system should flag potential MSME accounts at risk 
of entering the SMA stage well in advance, allowing for timely intervention. The 
mechanism should include backward and forward linkages to track financial stress 
indicators, ensure proactive support, and facilitate real-time reporting to relevant 
stakeholders.  
(ii)  It is recommended that the establishment of 50 food irradiation units and 
100 NABL-accredited food testing labs must be approved as soon as possible to ensure 
timely financial support, strengthen food safety infrastructure, and enhance MSME 
participation in the food processing sector. 
(Para-32) 
11. The Committee appreciates that while the digital initiatives, such as API 
integrations with 13 major banks, have led to a significant rise in guarantee approvals, the 
committee recommends that the scheme can further streamline and simplify the user 
experience. CGTMSE should continue improving its digital interface to make the 
application process more user-friendly and ensure full end-to-end integration with all 
lending institutions, thereby reducing application processing time and enhancing overall 
efficiency. 
(Para-41) 
12. The Committee is of the view that given the significant increase in guarantee 
approvals, particularly in the manufacturing sector, it is recommended that CGTMSE 
focus on continuing to strengthen and incentivize the manufacturing sector through 
enhanced guarantee coverage and tailored support. This could include providing additional 
benefits or financial incentives for MSEs in manufacturing, which could help boost 
industrial output and employment, particularly in key sectors driving economic growth. 
(Para-42) 

44 
 
13. The Committee acknowledges the remarkable progress made under the PM 
Vishwakarma Scheme, with 2.66 crore applications received and over 27.49 lakh 
beneficiaries registered within just 16 months, already exceeding the 5-year target. 
However, it urges the Ministry to build on this success by further expanding the scheme's 
outreach, ensuring the timely and efficient disbursement of loans, and strengthening the 
marketing and digital support provided to artisans. 
(Para-46) 
14. The Committee also appreciates the allocation of ₹5,100 crore for FY 2025-26 to PM 
Vishwakarma Scheme and recommends that the Ministry focus on optimizing the 
utilization of these funds to maximize the scheme’s impact and further benefit artisans. 
(Para-47) 
15. The Committee commends the success of PMEGP in fostering self-employment 
and micro-enterprises, creating over 9.87 lakh businesses. The Committee also 
recommends scaling up the program, focusing on rural and Aspirational Districts, while 
expanding support for women, SCs, and STs.  
(Para-55) 
16. The Committee appreciates the successful implementation of the PMEGP, noting 
its steady allocation and expenditure in recent years. To enhance supporting micro-
enterprises, the Ministry is encouraged to increase the 2025-26 allocation to meet growing 
demand, especially in underserved areas. Additionally, the Ministry should streamline fund 
disbursement processes to sustain employment and entrepreneurship growth momentum. 
(Para-56) 
17. The Committee acknowledges the steady progress in supporting a significant 
number of micro units and generating employment in PMEGP. However, the decline in 
margin money disbursed and the number of micro-units assisted in 2024-25 raises 
concerns. The Committee recommends that the Ministry, in collaboration with the RBI, 
establish a uniform and streamlined interest/margin rate for MSMEs across all banks. 
Furthermore, the Ministry should focus on increasing allocations and enhancing outreach 
efforts to ensure the scheme reaches its full potential. 
(Para-57) 
18. The Committee appreciates that the actual expenditure in FY 2023-24 was quite 
close to the budget estimate (₹1319.41 crore against ₹1320.77 crore) in RAMP, indicating 
efficient fund utilisation. However, for FY 2024-25, the revised estimate (₹750 crore) was 
significantly lower than the budget estimate (₹1170 crore), with actual spending recorded 
at ₹504.48 crore. The Committee suggests that the remaining allocation should be utilised 
within the specified period inconsonance with the Financial Rules. As Rs. 1500 crore has 
been proposed under this scheme for the FY2025-26, the Committee hopes that the focus be 
shifted towards ensuring timely and complete utilisation of funds so that the RAMP scheme 
can achieve its objectives. 
(Para-62) 

45 
 
19. The Committee appreciates a steady increase in the budgetary allocation for KGVY, 
the Committee recommends the Ministry to continue optimizing the utilization of funds. 
The Ministry should closely monitor the progress of the schemes, especially in areas such as 
awareness building, skill enhancement, and infrastructure support, to ensure that the full 
potential of these allocations is realized for sustainable growth in the Khadi and village 
industries. 
(Para-66) 
20. The Committee appreciates the increased allocations for the Khadi Vikas Yojana 
(KVY) in the upcoming financial year. Given the positive trajectory of the scheme, the 
Ministry is encouraged to continue this momentum and ensure full utilization of allocated 
funds. Furthermore, it is recommended that efforts be made to enhance outreach and 
support for Khadi artisans, especially in rural areas, through targeted marketing and 
technology adoption initiatives. 
(Para-67) 
21. The Committee acknowledges the upward trend in the allocations for Gramodyog 
Vikas Yojana (GVY) in FY 2024-25 and FY 2025-26. This increase is a positive sign for the 
promotion of village industries and the modernization of traditional sectors. The 
Committee recommends the Ministry focus on expanding skill development programs and 
modernizing infrastructure to ensure the competitiveness of village industries in global 
markets, particularly in agro-based and wellness industries, to maximize the impact. 
(Para-68) 
22. The Committee appreciates the effective utilization of allocated funds in SRI Fund 
of Funds in the last three years. The Committee recommends that the Ministry continue to 
focus on enhancing the fund's reach and impact by ensuring the full utilization of the 
proposed ₹700 crore allocations for FY 2025-26. The Ministry should ensure timely and 
efficient deployment of funds to maximize the scheme's benefits for the MSME sector. 
(Para-71) 
23. The Committee observes the previous years' under-utilization of allocated funds, in 
TCSP, and it is recommended that the Ministry of MSME focus on timely execution of 
contracts and procurement processes to ensure optimal utilization of the ₹400 crore budget 
for FY 2024-25. The Ministry should streamline processes, set clear timelines, and closely 
monitor progress to avoid delays and ensure full fund utilization, maximizing the impact of 
the Technology Centre Systems Programme. 
(Para-76) 
24. The Committee notes that the Revised Estimate (RE) for the establishment of new 
Technology Centres/Extension Centres has been significantly reduced over the last three 
years, although the full utilization of the RE is appreciated. The Committee recommends 
the adoption of more effective budgeting methods to minimize changes at the RE stage. It is 
hoped that this year's allocation of ₹591 crore will be fully utilized, ensuring proper 
budgeting for the successful implementation of the scheme. 

46 
 
(Para-77) 
 
25. The Committee observed that the BE allocation of ₹400 crore for FY 2024-25 was 
revised to ₹300 crore, with actual expenditure at ₹136.38 crore (45.5% of RE) in MSE-
CDP. The Committee recommends the Ministry to create a plan for optimal fund 
utilisation and ensure the remaining 54.5% of the RE is effectively used in compliance with 
Financial Rules for the rest of FY 2024-25. Further, given the higher funds allocated for FY 
2025-26, the Ministry needs to be equipped with a viable implementation year-plan and 
avoid expenditure push in the year end.  
(Para-80) 
 
26. The Committee notes a significant discrepancy between the Budget Estimates 
(BE) and actual expenditure for SFURTI, with a drastic shortfall in the last three years, 
particularly in 2024-25, where actual expenditure was only 0.01% of the RE. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry strengthen the monitoring and implementation 
framework for SFURTI to improve fund utilization. If expenditure continues to fall short 
of BE, the Ministry may adjust future allocations to better align with actual needs and 
execution capacity, ensuring that resources are effectively targeted and fully utilized to 
maximize the scheme’s impact. 
(Para-84) 
 
27. The Committee appreciates the allocation of ₹362.00 crore for the SFURTI 
Scheme for FY 2025-26 and recommends that the Ministry ensure optimal utilization of 
these funds for employment generation and the benefit of artisans. 
(Para-85) 
 
28. The Committee acknowledges out of the 513 approved clusters, only 376 have 
become operational so far. The Committee recommends that the Ministry expedite the 
process of setting up the remaining clusters and ensure that all approved clusters become 
functional particularly in disadvantaged sections of society within the stipulated timeframe. 
This will further benefit artisans and strengthen the impact of the scheme. 
(Para-86) 
 
29. The Committee appreciates that the financial allocations being generally aligned 
with actual expenditure and it notes that there is consistent shortfall in meeting annual 
targets under the NSSH scheme (85-67% achievement in the last three years), it 
recommends that the Ministry should revise outreach strategies such as targeted awareness 
campaigns, expanding regional offices, and providing more accessible channels for SC/ST 
entrepreneurs to engage with the scheme, which will help increase participation and 
achieve targets. 
(Para-91) 
30. The Committee notes that for FY 2024-25, the Ministry has maximized the 
utilization of allocations at the RE stage in Coir Vikas Yojana. Similarly, it recommends 

47 
 
that for FY 2025-26, the allocated amount of Rs. 104.39 crore be utilized optimally and 
efficiently. If required, the Ministry should request an enhanced allocation at the RE stage, 
considering the scheme’s significance in supporting employment, particularly for women 
artisans in rural areas. 
(Para-94) 
31. The Committee further observes that the coir industry, being traditional, holds 
substantial potential for skill development. To drive growth and expand into non-
traditional areas, the Ministry should prioritize regular training and skill development 
programs, including those focused on technological innovations, to enhance the capabilities 
of artisans and foster overall development in the coir sector. 
(Para-95) 
32. The Committee notes the steady increase in the budget allocations for the 
Entrepreneurship and Skill Development Programme (ESDP), reflecting the importance of 
promoting self-employment and entrepreneurship, particularly among marginalised 
groups. However, to ensure that the scheme's full potential is realized, the Ministry is 
recommended to focus on improving the utilization of allocated funds, especially in the 
later years of the scheme.  
(Para-98) 
33. The Committee observes variations in the BE and AE of the Scheme over the past 
two years. Given the underutilization of funds in FY 2024-25 and the BE of ₹65 crore for 
FY 2025-26, Committee recommends to focus on timely fund disbursement, enhanced 
outreach to MSMEs, and targeted capacity-building initiatives to improve fund utilization 
and align with actual absorption capacity. 
(Para-101) 
34. The Committee notes the variation in RE and AE for the Financial Year 2024-25. 
Accordingly, it is recommended that a mid-year review process be implemented for the 
MSME Champion Schemes to improve the effective utilisation of the allocated budget and 
to identify and address the reasons for the significant underutilisation (AE of Rs 25.5 Cr 
versus BE of Rs 54.72 Cr). This review may focus on streamlining implementation, 
enhancing outreach to MSMEs, and ensuring that funds are used efficiently. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry demand more funds at the RE stage as 
innovation and manufacturing techniques are critical for the MSME sector to remain 
competitive. 
(Para-104) 
35. The Committee notes the significant underutilization in FY 2024-25, with the actual 
expenditure being considerably lower than the revised estimate it recommends that the 
Ministry focus on optimizing the utilization of allocated funds for the SPIC scheme in FY 
2025-26. The proposed Budget Estimate for FY 2025-26 should be used efficiently to 
maximize the scheme's impact, particularly in enhancing MSME exports and international 
cooperation. 
(Para-108) 

48 
 
36. The Committee also recommends the enhancement in the utilization of allocated 
funds under the International Cooperation (IC) Scheme, particularly for the year 2025-26. 
While there has been a good level of participation in international exhibitions and 
conferences, the actual expenditure in 2024-25 (₹10.82 crore) was significantly lower than 
the revised estimate of ₹18 crore, indicating underutilization. The Ministry should focus on 
increasing MSME engagement in global markets, ensuring timely execution of activities, 
and streamlining the reimbursement processes. 
(Para-109) 
37. The Committee notes the underutilisation of allocated funds in the North Eastern 
Region (NER) in multiple financial years, particularly in 2024-25, and consistent 
underperformance in expenditure across various schemes. It  recommends that the 
Ministry of MSME adopt a proactive approach to improve fund utilization in the North 
Eastern Region (NER), This may include strengthening monitoring and evaluation 
frameworks with quarterly reviews, ensuring timely fund release to avoid delays, and 
providing additional support to local stakeholders for better project implementation. 
Furthermore, targeted awareness campaigns should be conducted to enhance awareness of 
available schemes and processes, particularly in regions with low participation, to foster 
greater engagement and effective utilization of allocated funds. 
(Para-114) 
39. The Committee observes a decline in the number of micro enterprises supported 
under the PMEGP scheme and significant disparities in production, sales, and employment 
across NER states. To boost entrepreneurship and create sustainable micro enterprises, it 
recommends that the Ministry of MSME focus on boosting entrepreneurship and micro 
enterprise growth in the North Eastern Region (NER) by targeting underperforming states 
with specialized support, training, and mentorship.  
(Para-115) 
40. The Committee observes a significant decrease in the number of women 
beneficiaries under the PMEGP scheme, with only 11,415 women entrepreneurs assisted in 
2024-25 (up to December), marking a nearly 69% reduction compared to the previous 
year. To reverse this decline, it recommends that the Ministry of MSME launch targeted 
outreach and awareness campaigns, particularly in areas with low participation, to 
encourage more women to take advantage of the scheme’s benefits. 
(Para-117) 
41. The Committee notes the decline in differently-abled beneficiaries under the 
PMEGP scheme, particularly in 2024-25. It recommends that the Ministry of MSME 
enhance outreach and awareness about PMEGP and related schemes, simplify the 
application process, and provide additional incentives to boost beneficiary numbers and 
encourage entrepreneurship among differently-abled individuals. 
(Para-120) 
 
42. The Khadi sector has demonstrated steady growth in production and sales, with 
encouraging projections for 2024-25. It is recommended that the Ministry continue to 
support this growth by ensuring supply of quality raw materials, enhancing marketing 
strategies, and expanding Khadi's reach through diverse sales channels. Furthermore, 

49 
 
additional funds may be considered at the Revised Estimate (RE) stage to accelerate the 
sector's growth. 
(Para-124) 
43. The Committee acknowledges the efforts of the Coir Board in supporting 
production, export promotion, and research. Women's continued involvement in fibre 
extraction and spinning is also a positive development. However, considering the slight 
decline in the production of coir and coir products in the current year (2024-25), it is 
recommended that MSME provide additional support to the Coir Board to enhance 
technological innovation, improve production efficiency, and explore new export markets. 
Further investment in value addition and product diversification could lead to significant 
growth in domestic and international markets. 
(Para-129) 
44. The Committee recommends that the Ministry allocate additional resources to 
expand the credit support facilities, which have shown a steady rise, from ₹7,221 crore in 
2022-23 to a projected ₹9,450 crore in 2024-25. This growth underscores the increasing 
demand for financial assistance among MSMEs. Moreover, given the growth in the number 
of trainees (from 61,090 in 2022-23 to a projected 79,200 in 2024-25), the committee urges 
the Ministry to further invest in skill development programs, ensuring that MSMEs are 
equipped with the necessary technical expertise to thrive in the evolving market. 
(Para-132) 
45. The Committee observes a decline in new member registrations under the Single 
Point Registration Scheme (SPRS), despite an overall increase in units served. To address 
this, it recommends that the Ministry intensify efforts to encourage MSMEs, particularly in 
high-potential sectors, to register under the SPRS. Additionally, given the projected rise in 
agency sales to ₹4,500 crore in 2024-25, the Ministry may enhance market access for 
MSME products, ensuring a robust and expanding customer base. 
(Para-133) 
46. The Committee acknowledges MGIRI’s vital role in promoting rural 
industrialization and advancing the KVI and to sustain and scale the achievements, it 
recommends that the Ministry of MSME may increase budgetary support to MGIRI, 
especially for R&D, technology development, and capacity building. The decrease in funds 
for 2024-25 highlights the need for adequate financial resources to support MGIRI's 
mission and drive further growth in rural industries. 
(Para-137) 
47. The Committee observes that there has been a notable increase in the success rate of 
wage and self-employment among trainees over the past years. To sustain and enhance the 
effectiveness of the scheme, it is recommended that the Ministry may increase its support 
for monitoring and evaluation mechanisms. The Ministry may also consider strengthening 
collaboration with industry partners to increase the employment outcomes for trainees in 
future programs. 
(Para-140)

Discussion with Representatives of the Ministry of Heavy Industries 
The Chairman welcomed the Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) officials to discuss the 2025-
26 Budget. He highlighted/ stated/ asked for 
(i) MHI's role is to develop capital goods, automobile, and heavy electrical equipment 
sectors while overseeing CPSEs and autonomous organisations.  
(ii) MHI's budget allocation for 2025-26 is about 85% of the proposed ₹9,025.83 crores. 
(iii) Action plan for optimally utilising the enhanced budgetary allocation for 2025-26, 
focusing on the PM E-Drive Scheme, which has been allocated more than 50% of the 
total budget.  
(iv) Information on schemes’ progress, strategies planned for the year, and the targets set.  
(v) Data on performance of CPSEs, steps taken to improve output and productivity, and 
any restructuring or revival plans for sick or loss-making CPSEs.  
2. After the Chair’s permission, through a presentation, the Ministry of Heavy Industries 
(MHI)  
(i) outlined their budget performance from 2020-21 to 2024-25,  
(ii) focused on schemes like the PLI-Automobile Scheme, with an outlay of ₹25,938 crore, 
aimed at boosting the electric vehicle sector,  
(iii) Shared the technological advancements and significant growth of the Heavy Electrical 
Industry and 
(iv) Highlighted the importance of developing Advanced Chemistry Cells to accelerate the 
production of electric vehicles (EVs).  
(v) Provided an overview of the automotive industry, highlighting India’s global position 
in the sector, and discussed the awareness programs launched by the Ministry to 
educate the public about electric vehicles (EVs).  
(vi) Stressed the need to scale up manufacturing capabilities, create jobs, and improve 
India's position in the global automotive market.  
3. The CMDs briefed the Committee about BHEL, Bridge and Roof Company Ltd, and 
Braithwaite Burn and Joseph Construction Co. Ltd.  
4. After the presentation, the Chairman and Committee Members  
(i) Raised underutilisation of the budget in previous years, ranging from 2022-23 to 2024-
25 
(ii) Pointed out the reduced allocation under capital heads vis a vis the total allocation; 
(iii) Sought reasons for continuing the legacy name of Braithwaite Burn and Jessop. 
(iv) Inquired about the steps taken to protect domestic players given global players like 
Tesla entering the Indian market 

58 
 
(v) Sought replies on points like job work, underground coal gasification, collaboration 
with J&T, Hyderabad for skill development, gravitational storage for large-scale 
solutions. 
(vi) Highlighted that a key challenge is the customs duty on scrap material. When 
specialized material is imported for manufacturing, such as a one-tonne valve, the duty 
is charged on the full weight, including scrap, which adds unnecessary costs. The 
committee recommends addressing this issue with the Ministry of Finance or 
Commerce. Additionally, large companies like BHEL, with their technological 
capabilities, should focus more on job work opportunities. 
(vii) Reminded CMD HEC for the background note, as the Committee intends to 
recommend steps to revive the organisation 
5. The Committee directed that the following be recommended in their DFG report: 
(i) Passenger vehicles (four wheelers) and hybrid vehicles may also be incentivised under 
the PM E-Drive Scheme,  
(ii) Disbursement of incentives under PM E-Drive be streamlined and expedited,  
(iii) Additional funds be allocated to CPSEs, in collaboration with Ministry of Skill 
Development and Entrepreneurship to impart vocational training to locals for 
enhancing their employability 
(iv) Subsidies be offered for scrapping diesel vehicles when purchasing electric vehicles. 
6. The Chairman thanked the Secretary and other Officers for their input and requested that 
they provide written replies to the queries of Hon’ble MP to the Secretariat within 3 days.  
II Discussion with Representatives of Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises 
(MSME) 
7. The Chairman welcomed the Secretary and Officers of the Ministry of MSME and its 
allied agencies to the meeting to discuss the Ministry’s budgetary allocations for FY 2025-26, 
and he 
(i) Acknowledged the increase in the MSME sector's budget allocation for 2025-26 to 
₹23,168 crore, up from ₹22,137.95 crore in the previous financial year,  
(ii) Inquired about the impact of less-allocation(by ₹2,439.08 crore) from the Ministry's 
projected ₹25,607.23 croreon the operation of various schemes, 
(iii) Expressed concern about the capital expenditure allocation, only 3% of the total budget, 
(iv) Sought the strategies for optimal budget utilisation, employment generation for micro 
and small enterprises, technological upgradation and enhanced R&D investment in the 
sector, 
(v) Asked for the reasons for rise in MSME closures, with 32,000 shutting down in FY 
2024-25, compared to 175 in FY 2020-21  
(vi) Sought sector-wise breakdown of NPAs from RBI; 
(vii) Expressed concern on underutilisation of funds allocated to KVIC. 
8. After the Chair’s permission, the Secretary, M/o MSME apprised the Committee on the 
2025-26 budget highlights, including  

59 
 
(i) Key measures to strengthen the sector, including increased investment and turnover 
limits, doubling of credit guarantee cover, a ₹5 lakh credit scheme for Udyam-
registered micro-enterprises, and a ₹10,000 crore Fund of Funds for startups. 
(ii) Focus and sectoral growth in footwear, leather, toys, and clean tech, with MSMEs 
contributing 30.1% of India’s GDP and ₹12.39 lakh crore in exports.  
(iii) Continued support of artisans and MSMEs through schemes like PM Vishwakarma and 
PMEGP, with 25% of public procurement reserved for MSMEs. 
(iv) Reclassification of MSMEs and showcasing significant growth in the MSME sector, 
with registered MSMEs set to rise from 1.65 crore in 2023 to 6 crore by 2025 
(v) Increased (21X) procurement from SC-ST MSEs over the past decade under the 
National SC-ST Hub (NSSH).  
(vi) Emphasizing sustainable development, the Ministry aims to improve access to credit, 
market opportunities, technological support, and infrastructure, ultimately driving the 
MSME sector’s growth as a key engine of the Indian economy, 
(vii) Introducing customised credit cards for micro-enterprises to address the credit gap. 
(viii) Lays a target of supporting 5.55 lakh MSMEs between 2022 and 2027, with 
partnerships across 34 states.  
(ix) Significant increase in registered MSMEs, projected to reach 6 crore, with continued 
efforts to reduce credit gaps, enhance scalability, and drive investment.  
 
9. The Committee directed that the following be recommended in their DFG report: 
(i) The Government may revise the definition of Micro, Small, and Medium and if 
required, create a new category (nano or any other name) with lowest financial criteria 
(say, around Rs. 10 Lakh) arguing that businesses with a turnover above ₹2.5 crore 
might not align with the core purpose of MSMEs1 
(ii) RBI may regulate a uniform and streamlined interest/ margin rate for MSMEs across 
banks.  
(iii) The Government may remove the entry barrier of class 8 qualifications in PMEGP and 
focus on talent and skill instead of the current support for artisans and handicrafts, 
which often perpetuates family-based traditions and reinforces caste-based systems. 
(iv) The Ministry may improve awareness of UMANG and other MSME IT platforms. 
10. The Chairman thanked the Secretary and other Officers for their input and asked them to 
furnish the written replies to the queries raised by the Hon’ble MPs to the Secretariat within three 
days.  
11. A verbatim record of the proceedings of the meeting was kept. 
The Committee adjourned at 2.10 pm.

CHAPTER 1 
INTRODUCTION 
1.1 The Prime Minister’s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP) is a credit-linked 
subsidy scheme launched in August 2008 by merging the Prime Minister’s Rojgar Yojana (PMRY) 
and Rural Employment Generation Programme (REGP).  
1.2 Legal and Policy Framework 
1.2.1 PMEGP operates under guidelines issued by the Ministry of MSME. The scheme aligns with 
national policies aimed at promoting entrepreneurship, reducing unemployment, and fostering 
inclusive economic growth. 
1.3 The Parliamentary Standing Committee, as per its mandate, aimed to assess the effectiveness 
of the PMEGP scheme in fostering growth in the MSME sector. As part of the process, the 
Committee- 
i. Reviewed background data and annual reports of the ministry, its official website to identify 
challenges or areas for improvement 
ii. Interacted with officials from the Ministry, key stakeholders like KVIC, public sector banks, 
and beneficiaries 
iii. Circulated detailed questions. 
iv. Conducted study visits to Udaipur (Rajasthan), Mumbai (Maharashtra), Goa, 
Vishakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh), Kolkata (West Bengal), Srinagar (Jammu &Kashmir), 
Varanasi (Uttar Pradesh), Kochi (Kerala), Chennai (Tamil Nadu), & Chandigarh (Haryana- 
Punjab) ,and 
v. Field visits to identify challenges and areas for improvement. 
vi. Desktop research on Global Data related to MSMEs Sector. 
1.4 Objectives of the Scheme:- 
 
Generate employment opportunities in rural as well as urban areas of the country through setting up of new self-employment ventures/projects/micro enterprisesBring together widely dispersed traditional artisans/ rural and urban unemployed youth and give them self-employment opportunities to the extent possible, at their place;Provide continuous andsustainable employmentto traditional andprospective artisans, aswell as rural and urbanunemployed youth. Thiswill help arrestmigration of rural youthto urban areasIncrease the wage-earning capacity of artisans and contribute to an increase in the growth rate of rural and urban employment.

2 
 
1.5 Union budget 2025-26 announcements related to MSMEs impacting PMEGP: 
1.5.1 The Union Budget 2025-26 emphasises strengthening the MSME sector, recognizing it as the 
second engine of India’s economic growth alongside agriculture, investment, and exports. Notably, it 
revises the MSME classification by increasing the investment and turnover limits:

1.5.2 The Committee observes that the revised MSME classification under the Union Budget 
2025-26 has modified the Investment and Turnover limits for MSMEs. The new revised investment 
and turnover limits could potentially undermine the purpose of MSMEs by elevating micro-
enterprises beyond their original scope and further noting the increase in margin money 
disbursement, the number of assisted units has declined due to higher per-unit costs.  
1.5.3 The Committee, in its 327th Demand for Grant Report (2025-26) for the Ministry of 
MSME, has recommended the creation of a "nano" category within the MSME framework, 
with a financial limit of Rs. 10 lakh. The Committee recommends the Ministry to provide 
additional benefits and focused support under the PEMGP Scheme. This initiative aims to 
enhance access to credit and subsidies for micro-entrepreneurs, rural artisans, and street 
vendors, fostering financial inclusion in rural and semi-urban areas.

2.4 Eligibility Criteria:- 
2.4.1 For PMEGP new enterprises (Units):- 
i. Any individual, above 18 years of age 
ii. There will be no income ceiling for assistance. 
iii. Beneficiaries must have at least VIII standard education for projects costing over 
Rs.10lakh (Manufacturing) or Rs.5 lakh (Business/Service). Assistance under the 
scheme is available only for new projects. 
iv. Self Help Groups (SHGs) : including those belonging to BPL if they have not availed 
benefits under any other scheme, Institutions registered under the Societies 
Registration Act,1860, 
v. Production Co-operative Societies registered under relevant cooperative acts and 
Charitable Trusts. 
vi. There will be no income ceiling to assist in setting up projects under PMEGP. 
vii. Existing units or those with prior government (Central or State) subsidy schemes are 
ineligible. 
 
Note:-Only one person from one family is eligible to obtain financial assistance for 
setting up projects under PMEGP. The 'family’ includes self and spouse. 
2.4.2 For up-gradation of existing PMEGP units: 
i. Margin Money (subsidy) claimed under PMEGP must be successfully adjusted after 
the completion of the 3-year lock-in period. 
ii. The First loan under PMEGP/REGP/MUDRA must be repaid within the stipulated 
time. 
iii. The unit is profit-making, and the potential for further growth with

4.1 Various changes and modifications have been incorporated, and activities are being carried 
out for the effective implementation of the PMEGP Scheme: -

Expanded list of permitted activities. 
ii. Implementing Agencies can process applications in all areas (rural/urban). 
iii. Weekly webinars for youth and entrepreneurs. 
iv. The list of activities permitted under the scheme has been expanded. 
v. 1.3lakh units geo-tagged for verification and real-time data. 
vi. Technical, Marketing, and retired bank officials have been hired at state offices to support 
PMEGP beneficiaries. Additionally, 1,056 model Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) for 
various industries are available on the PMEGP portal. 
vii. KVIC introduced a call centre linked to the EDP portal. 
viii. Awareness camps, workshops, and exhibitions held to promote PMEGP. 
ix. Rejection rate dropped by 10% from 2020 to 2023.

2022-23 from 28% in FY2019-20.

impact, credit adequacy, and challenges, with interim findings by December2024. 
xiii. India Post was engaged in conducting physical verification of PMEGP units. 
xiv. Applicants from aspirational districts and transgenders are included in Special Category for 
higher subsidy. 
xv. Modified Negative List to allow more activities under Animal Husbandry.

xvii. New PMEGP units must be registered under the Udyam Portal before physical verification. 
xviii. District Level Task Force Committee has been discontinued. 
 
4.2 The Committee observes that the current loan application process under PMEGP involves 
extensive scrutiny, leading to delays, especially for small-value loans. The Committee 
recommends Ministry must implement a self-certification mechanism for loan applications up 
to loan amount of Rs 10 Lakh to streamline the process and reduce delays. Applicants would 
submit a self-certified declaration of compliance with eligibility and documentation, with 
random sample testing conducted periodically for transparency.  
4.3 The Committee appreciates the Ministry's involvement of technical/marketing experts and 
ex-bankers in guiding applicants. It recommends establishing a dedicated help desk to provide 
real-time assistance and offer continuous hand-holding support throughout the application 
process till the final loan disbursement.

entrepreneurs and strengthen PMEGP promotion.

4.12 The Committee noted that banks charge interest rates ranging from 9.5% to 12.5% on 
PMEGP loans, while the guidelines suggest a normal interest rate and a repayment schedule of 3 to 7 
years. Furthermore, during its interaction with entrepreneurs with PMEGP loans, the Committee 
came across several beneficiaries who were required to make collateral bonds for loans of even less 
than Rs. 10 lakhs.  
4.13 The Committee notes that high interest rates and inconsistencies across banks are 
challenging for PMEGP loan applicants, particularly given their lack of regular income. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry, in collaboration with the RBI, must establish a 
uniform and streamlined interest/margin rate for MSMEs across all banks. Furthermore, the 
Ministry should focus on increasing allocations and enhancing outreach efforts to ensure the 
scheme reaches its full potential.

4.14 The Committee observes that while PMEGP includes capacity-building measures such as 
Entrepreneurship Development Programmes (EDPs) to equip beneficiaries with the necessary skills 
and knowledge to establish and manage their businesses, there is a need to improve the quality of 
training, extend outreach in rural areas, and provide sector-specific skills to align with evolving 
market demands. 
4.15 The Committee recommends that the Ministry must strengthen capacity-building 
initiatives by updating training modules, increasing collaboration with industry experts, and 
expanding outreach in rural areas. It also suggests introducing digital skills programmes and 
providing continuous post-training support to enhance project sustainability and 
entrepreneurial success. 
4.16 The Committee further observes that Artificial Intelligence (AI) can significantly improve 
the efficiency and accessibility of the scheme. AI-driven analytics could facilitate real-time project 
monitoring, identify emerging business trends, and support evidence-based policy decisions. 
However, the Committee notes that inadequate digital infrastructure and limited technological 
awareness, particularly in rural and semi-urban areas, may hinder the effective implementation of AI 
solutions. 
4.17 In view of the impact of AI in the Scheme, the Committee recommends that the 
Ministry integrate AI technology across PMEGP operations and portal to improve service 
delivery and promote financial inclusion. This includes adopting AI tools for faster application 
processing, automated project monitoring feedback, address the gaps continuously and 
predictive analytics to identify sector-specific opportunities. Additionally, the Committee 
advises the Ministry to collaborate with technology experts and research institutions to develop 
AI solutions tailored for MSMEs.

CHAPTER 7 
 CONCLUSION 
In conclusion, the Committee recognises that the PMEGP scheme, designed to promote 
entrepreneurship and employment generation among MSMEs, has demonstrated its capacity to drive 
economic growth and empower a diverse range of beneficiaries across the country. By providing 
financial support and fostering a conducive environment for innovation, the scheme has successfully 
reached multiple sectors and regions, thereby contributing to the broader development agenda of the 
Ministry of MSME. 
7.1 At the same time, the Committee’s in-depth analysis has revealed persistent challenges 
related to policy structures, administrative bottlenecks, and gaps in outreach, particularly in rural 
areas. The integrated recommendations underscore the need for digital enhancements, streamlined 
processes, and better synergy with other government initiatives. Addressing these issues will not 
only reinforce the strengths of PMEGP but also pave the way for a more inclusive and sustainable 
economic future.

MSME, has recommended the creation of a "nano" category within the MSME framework, 
with a financial limit of Rs. 10 lakh. The Committee recommends the Ministry to provide 
additional benefits and focused support under the PEMGP Scheme. This initiative aims to 
enhance access to credit and subsidies for micro-entrepreneurs, rural artisans, and street 
vendors, fostering financial inclusion in rural and semi-urban areas. 
(para-1.5.3) 
2. The Committee acknowledges PMEGP as a skill-based program preserving traditional 
artisanship and It recommends the ministry that it must remove the VIII standard education 
requirement under PMEGP, recognizing that many artisans acquire skills through family 
traditions and mentorship rather than formal education.  
(para-2.7) 
3. The Committee recommends the Ministry/KVIC to accept the application forms both 
online and offline in all 22 scheduled languages and further expanding awareness through 
multilingual training, particularly in rural and semi-urban areas. It suggests creating and 
distributing concise video clips in regional languages to promote PMEGP in remote areas.  
(para-2.8) 
4. The Committee recommends that the Ministry must set up a single-window clearance 
system to facilitate faster approvals and reduce procedural delays, improving the overall 
effectiveness of the scheme. 
(para-2.9) 
5. The Committee observes that delays and lack of real-time communication in the 
PMEGP application process leave applicants unaware of their status of application. It 
recommends that the Ministry must implement a mobile-based notification system to provide 
real-time updates on PMEGP applications in that single window clearance system. This system 
must inform applicants at each stage, notify them of any delays, apprise about the reasons of 
rejection of their applications both by banks and nodal agencies, and offer updates via SMS 
and additionally a mobile app to give feedback mechanism.  
(para-2.10) 
6. The Committee recommends that instead of the existing input based EDP training the 
Ministry must implement an output-based training and eligibility system under the PMEGP 
scheme. The system is to link the approval of loans or subsidies to measurable outcomes, such 

23 
 
as business readiness, skill proficiency, and a viable business plan. This approach would 
enhance accountability, support capable applicants, and improve the scheme’s effectiveness.  
(para-2.11) 
7.  The Committee commends the Ministry for exceeding PMEGP targets since FY2021-
22 and extending the scheme until 2025-26 with increased funding. However, it reiterates that 
the scheme’s success should be measured by employment generated, not by Margin Money 
utilized (as stated in the Committee's 251st Report). The Committee recommends to proper 
fund usage and job creation, expecting the increased budget to increase youth employment 
opportunities. 
(para-3.7) 
8. The Committee appreciates the Ministry's efforts to fully utilize the PMEGP budget 
and seek additional funds. It recommends that the Ministry and DFS focus on generating self-
employment through micro-enterprises. The Committee urges IAs and banks to adopt the best 
practices and suggestions from the meetings. It also suggests holding conferences and seminars 
to share experiences and best practices, helping achieve targets. 
(para-3.8) 
9. The Committee observes that the current loan application process under PMEGP 
involves extensive scrutiny, leading to delays, especially for small-value loans. The Committee 
recommends Ministry must implement a self-certification mechanism for loan applications up 
to loan amount of Rs 10 Lakh to streamline the process and reduce delays. Applicants would 
submit a self-certified declaration of compliance with eligibility and documentation, with 
random sample testing conducted periodically for transparency.  
(para-4.2) 
10.  The Committee appreciates the Ministry's involvement of technical/marketing experts 
and ex-bankers in guiding applicants. It recommends establishing a dedicated help desk to 
provide real-time assistance and offer continuous hand-holding support throughout the 
application process till the final loan disbursement.  
(para-4.3) 
11. To improve outreach, the Committee urges the Ministry and banks to enhance publicity 
through media, workshops, awareness camps, and social media, with a special focus on youth 
and women artisans for employment generation. Additionally, the Ministry is encouraged to 
collaborate with RBI and Rural Self-Employment Training Institutes (RSETI) to educate 
entrepreneurs and strengthen PMEGP promotion. 

24 
 
(para-4.4) 
12. The Committee appreciates the inclusion of aspirational districts and transgender 
applicants. However, it emphasizes the importance of upskilling, reskilling and unlearning. It 
recommends developing training modules on digital literacy, financial management, and 
entrepreneurship in collaboration with the Ministry of Skill Development and 
Entrepreneurship.  
(para-4.5) 
13.  The Committee further recommends monitoring the impact of increased project costs 
and relaxing the negative list for animal husbandry activities. The Ministry should implement 
a quarterly review system to assess the uptake of these changes and ensure that they effectively 
address entrepreneurs' capital needs. 
(para-4.6) 
14.  The Committee notes the discontinuation of the District Level Task Force Committees 
(DLFTC) due to the online portal. It recommends that state and district-level bodies continue 
monitoring to maximize PMEGP’s impact. These bodies should address applicant issues, 
improve processes, and encourage local participation. They should conduct regular reviews, 
guide applicants, and track progress. A feedback loop with central offices should inform policy 
adjustments and improve the scheme’s effectiveness. 
(para-4.7) 
15. The Committee notes that high interest rates and inconsistencies across banks are 
challenging for PMEGP loan applicants, particularly given their lack of regular income. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry, in collaboration with the RBI, must establish a 
uniform and streamlined interest/margin rate for MSMEs across all banks. Furthermore, the 
Ministry should focus on increasing allocations and enhancing outreach efforts to ensure the 
scheme reaches its full potential. 
(para-4.12) 
16. The Committee recommends that the Ministry must strengthen capacity-building 
initiatives by updating training modules, increasing collaboration with industry experts, and 
expanding outreach in rural areas. It also suggests introducing digital skills programmes and 
providing continuous post-training support to enhance project sustainability and 
entrepreneurial success. 
(para-4.14) 
17. In view of the impact of AI in the Scheme, the Committee recommends that the 
Ministry integrate AI technology across PMEGP operations and portal to improve service 

25 
 
delivery and promote financial inclusion. This includes adopting AI tools for faster application 
processing, automated project monitoring feedback, address the gaps continuously and 
predictive analytics to identify sector-specific opportunities. Additionally, the Committee 
advises the Ministry to collaborate with technology experts and research institutions to develop 
AI solutions tailored for MSMEs. 
(para-4.16) 
18. The data shows uneven utilization of margin money in the Northeast, with states like 
Arunachal Pradesh and Sikkim over using funds while Meghalaya and Manipur. The 
Committee recommends a data-driven formula for margin money allocation in Northeast 
states, based on eligible population, unemployment rate, and artisan share. It also recommends 
performance-based incentives—increasing funds for high-demand states with effective 
utilization and providing support to underutilizing states to improve access and capacity. 
(para-5.3) 
19. The Committee appreciates KVIC's efforts to provide employment in NER under 
PMEGP. However, there has been a decline in project support from FY 2021-22, especially in 
Assam, Nagaland, Manipur, and Mizoram. The Committee recommends enhancing support 
through targeted outreach, simplifying the application process, and making region-specific 
modifications. Additionally, the Committee suggests prioritizing additional financial assistance 
for successful units to support scalability, create jobs, and improve economic resilience. 
(para-5.4) 
20. The Committee notes that while margin money disbursement has increased, the 
number of assisted units has declined due to higher per-unit costs. It believes this trend 
contradicts PMEGP’s goal of maximizing employment and stresses that without a budget 
increase, fewer beneficiaries will be supported. The Committee strongly recommends 
providing smaller loans to more beneficiaries to ensure the scheme’s success. 
(para-6.4) 
21. The Committee appreciates the efforts of State Governments and banks in promoting 
PMEGP. It recommends that banks should take more responsibility in providing financial 
literacy, forwarding applications, and assessing project viability. The Ministry of MSME 
should streamline the process and continue offline applications for less educated applicants. 
The Committee recommends reviewing State schemes and improving PMEGP. It also urges 
KVIC to be more proactive in recovering dues from beneficiaries. 
(para-6.5) 
22. To improve PMEGP’s accessibility, success rate, and participation, the Committee 
recommend that the Ministry must collaborate with Department of Finances (DFS) to include 

26 
 
more number of private banks to promote PMEG. Scheme State-level PMEGP bodies should 
be empowered to identify and prioritize key sectors specific to their regions, with a reduced 
beneficiary contribution requirement for economically weaker sections in these sectors. 
(para-6.7) 
23. The Committee, concerned about the high rejection rate of applications, it recommends 
that the Ministry must implement an automated, menu-driven application form to screen out 
ineligible applicants. It also recommends forming committees with key stakeholders to reduce 
bank branch-level rejections and ensure applications are not rejected without valid reasons. 
(para-6.10) 
24. The Committee also found that there is a lack of clarity on project details and funding 
among applicants. The Committee recommends that the Ministry and banks provide detailed 
educational materials and training to help applicants prepare project reports and manage 
funds effectively. 
(para-6.11) 
25. The Committee endorses the suggestions from stakeholders and witnesses, urging the 
Ministry of MSME and the Department of Financial Services to address the concerns within 
their mandates and provide an action-taken report. 
(para-6.13)

ANNEXURE VI 
MEASURES TAKEN BY RBI FOR IMPROVING FLOW OF CREDIT TO MSME SECTOR 
i). Priority Sector Lending Guidelines: In terms of Master Direction on ‘Priority Sector 
Lending (PSL) – Targets and Classification’ dated September 4, 2020, all bank loans to 
MSMEs conforming to the conditions prescribed therein qualify for classification under 
priority sector lending. A target of 7.5 percent of ANBC or Credit Equivalent Amount of 
Off- Balance Sheet Exposure, whichever is higher, has been prescribed for SCBs for lending 
to Micro Enterprises. Further, loans sanctioned by banks to NBFC-MFIs and other MFIs 
(Societies, trusts, etc.) which are members of RBI recognized SRO for the sector for on-
lending to MSME sector, loans to registered NBFCs (other than MFIs) for on-lending to 
Micro & Small Enterprises and bank finance to start-ups up to ₹50 crore, as per definition of 
Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Govt. of India will be considered part of priority sector 
lending. 
ii). Collateral requirements of MSME units: SCBs have been mandated not to accept 
collateral security in the case of loans up to ₹10 lakh extended to units in the MSE sector. 
Banks have also been advised to strongly encourage their branch level functionaries to avail 
themselves of the Credit Guarantee cover, including making performance in this regard a 
criterion in the evaluation of their field staff.  
iii). Working Capital Computation: Computation of working capital requirements of MSE 
units to be done by banks on the basis of simplified method of minimum 20% of the 
projected annual turnover of the unit for borrowal limits up to ₹5 crore. 
iv). Streamlining flow of credit to Micro and Small Enterprises for facilitating timely and 
adequate credit flow during their ‘Life Cycle’: In terms of our circular FIDD.MSME & 
NFS.BC.No.60/06.02.31/2015-16 dated August 27, 2015 on ‘Streamlining flow of credit to 
Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs) for facilitating timely and adequate credit flow during 
their ‘Life Cycle’, banks have been advised to tune their policies for lending to MSME sector 
by incorporating therein the provisions for sanctioning of, inter alia, Additional Working 
Capital Limits, Mid Term Review of Regular Working Capital Limits, Timelines for Credit 
Decisions, so as to facilitate timely and adequate availability of credit to viable MSE 
borrowers especially during the need of funds in unforeseen circumstances. 
v). Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS):In order to solve the problem of delayed 
payment to MSMEs, RBI has issued guidelines for setting up and operating the TReDS.  The 
scheme facilitates the financing of trade receivables of MSMEs from corporate and other 
buyers, including government departments and public sector undertakings (PSUs) through 
multiple financiers electronically. Three entities viz. Receivables Exchange of India Limited 
(RXIL), Mynd Solutions Private Limited and A. TREDS have started operating TReDS. 
vi). Priority Sector Lending status for Factoring Transactions: In terms of our circular 
FIDD.CO.Plan.BC.10/04.09.01/2016-17 dated August 11, 2016 ‘with recourse’ factoring 
transactions by banks which carry out the business of factoring departmentally wherever the 
‘assignor’ is a Micro, Small or Medium Enterprise are eligible for priority sector 

37 
 
classification under MSME category.  The factoring transactions taking place through 
TReDS are also eligible for classification under priority sector. 
vii). Interest rates on loans to MSMEs: With a view to improve monetary policy transmission, 
banks have been advised to link loans to Micro and Small Enterprises to an external 
benchmark from October 01, 2019 in terms of circular DBR.DIR.BC.No.14/13.03.00/2019-
20 dated September 04, 2019.To further improve the transmission of monetary policy rates, 
the Reserve Bank vide circular dated February 26, 2020, stipulated that w.e.f April 01, 2020 
loans to Medium Enterprises shall also be linked to external benchmark. The reset clause for 
loans has also been reduced to three months under the external benchmark system. Further, to 
make the benefit of the external benchmark-based interest regime available to the existing 
borrowers, banks have been advised to provide a switchover option as per mutually agreed 
terms. 
viii). Regulatory Retail Portfolio: The Regulatory Retail Portfolio threshold to a single 
counterparty was increased from ₹5 crore to ₹7.5 crore in respect of all fresh as well as 
incremental qualifying exposures vide circular DOR.No.BP.BC.23/21.06.201/2020-21 dated 
October 12, 2020. Accordingly, banks may assign a lower risk weight of 75% to exposure to 
MSME entities with counterparty exposure up to ₹7.50 crore as against ₹5 crore earlier. 
ix). Co-Lending by Banks and NBFCs to Priority Sector: The “Co-Lending Model” (CLM) 
under ‘Priority Sector Lending’ envisages to better leverage respective comparative 
advantages of the banks and NBFCs in a collaborative effort and to improve the flow of 
credit to the unserved and underserved sectors of the economy (including the MSME 
Enterprises). The scheme is applicable to all registered NBFCs (including Housing Finance 
Companies). In terms of the CLM, banks are permitted to co-lend with all registered NBFCs 
(including HFCs) based on a prior agreement. The co-lending banks will take their share of 
the individual loans on a back-to-back basis in their books. However, NBFCs shall be 
required to retain a minimum of 20 per cent share of the individual loans on their books. 
x). Lending by Small Finance Banks (SFBs) to NBFC-MFIs, for the purpose of on-lending 
to priority sectors: With effect from May 5, 2021, fresh credit extended by SFBs to 
registered NBFC-MFIs and other MFIs (Societies, Trusts etc.) which are members of RBI 
recognized ‘Self-Regulatory Organization’ of the sector, and which have a ‘gross loan 
portfolio’ of up to ₹500 crore as on March 31 of the previous financial year, for the purpose 
of on-lending to individuals, is permitted to be classified as Priority Sector Lending. To 
ensure continuation of the synergies that have been developed between banks and NBFCs in 
delivering credit to the specified priority sectors, it has been decided to allow the above 
facility on an ongoing basis. 
xi). Regulatory Sandbox (RS): The Reserve Bank had opened the Third Cohort under RS for 
MSME Lending and eight entities were shortlisted for the Test Phase. Products of the entities 
which completed the ‘Test Phase’ were evaluated and five products have been found viable. 
This cohort is expected to spur innovations that can fill the lending gap for MSMEs through 
the use of technology and data analytics. 
xii). Account Aggregator (AA) Framework: As a regulator, the Reserve Bank has created an 
enabling environment for growth of digital technology for new financial products and 

38 
 
services. RBI has facilitated the AA framework under which information related to financial 
assets of a customer is collected from the holders of such information (Financial Information 
Providers) and is presented to the customers or specified users (Financial Information Users). 
Further, it has been decided to include GSTN on board the AA ecosystem as an FIP for 
MSME lending. The approach is to make sharing and aggregation of financial data possible 
in a secure, transparent, and efficient manner by setting up an intermediary which will also 
be responsible for the customers' consent management.

BUDGET ALLOCATIONS 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.  The Committee notes that the Budget 2024 -25 announced the establishment of a joint

Ultra Super Critical (AUSC) technology, with the government providing necessary fiscal 
support. The Committee is pleased to know that the site for the 800 MW AUSC technology -based 
power plant has been finalized at Korba, Chhattisgarh, and that the technical specifications and 
supply chain have also been finalized.  
(Para 17)

Noted.

Recommendation/Observation 
 
2. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Heavy Industries finalize guidelines and 
SOPs to ensure the swift and effective implementation of the PM e -Bus Sewa Payment Security 
Mechanism (PSM) Scheme. It is crucial to expedite coordination with States to facilitate the 
registration of Direct Debit Mandates (DDMs) with the RBI, ensuring wider participation

 The Steering Committee, headed by MHI, is formed to monitor the implementation and progress 
of the Scheme. Two Steering Committee meetings are held as on 30th May, 2025. 
 
CAPITAL GOODS SECTOR (HEAVY ENGINEERING AND MACHINE TOOLS) 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
3. The Committee notes that among the 04 autonomous bodies under the Ministry, only the 
Central Manufacturing Technology Institute (CMTI) has been allocated funds in the BE for FY 
2025-26, while no provision has been made for the other 03 autonomous bodies. G iven the 
critical importance of R&D and technological upgradation in maintaining global 
competitiveness, it recommends that the Ministry extend its focus to other R&D institutions and 
ensure they receive adequate budgetary support for technological advance ment. Furthermore, 
the budget allocated to CMTI, Bengaluru, should be utilised efficiently to achieve the intended 
outcomes. The Ministry may consider seeking an enhancement at the RE stage if additional funds 
are required. 
(Para 61) 
 
Action Taken Replies 
 
The Central Manufacturing Technology Institute (CMTI) received Rs.18.89 Cr. in FY 2024 -25. 
This is the partial support towards meeting expenditure of salary and administrative expenses. 
CMTI fully utilized this amount for the said purpose.   The total expe nditure towards Salaries & 
Welfare and other Administrative Overheads for the FY 2024-25 (unaudited) = Rs.43.42 Cr.   
 
CMTI Challenges and the need for financial support  
 
The Central Manufacturing Technology Institute (CMTI) faces several challenges as a Research 
and Development (R&D) institute dedicated to designing and developing cutting-edge machinery 
that is new to India. These challenges highlight the need for financial support to ensure the 
Institute's continued success. 
 
CMTI's expertise in designin g and developing pioneering machines and process technologies 
makes a significant contribution to nationally essential programs. For instance, CMTI has 
designed and manufactured various new machines for the Indian Space Program and defence 
missions, with i nstitutions such as ISRO, BARC, and DRDO as they relying on CMTI's 
expertise. Additionally, CMTI supports Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) by 
providing specialized testing, inspection, and calibration services. It also plays a crucial role in 
training the workforce to enhance the country's manufacturing capabilities.
