course of the next Finance Commission cyc le, the Ministry, in consultation with the 
Ministry of Finance, gradually rebalance its portfolio so that the share of pure 
guarantee-style interventions is reduced relative to deeper, capacity -building 
investments in productivity, competitiveness and resilience of MSMEs. (Para-2.42) 
 
17. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry institute a mandatory 
mid-year expenditure review mechanism for all schemes that have witnessed a BE -to-
RE reduction exceeding 30% in any of the preceding three financial years. Such 
schemes — particularly SFURTI, TCSP and New TC/ECs — should be required to 
furnish scheme -specific implementation roadmaps with quarterly milestones, and 
Budget Estimates for subsequent years should be calibrated against demonstrated 

71 
 
absorptive capacity rather than aspirational targets. The Committee is of the view that 
credible budgeting, anchored in realistic assessment of implementation readiness, is a 
prerequisite for restoring parliamentary confidence in the Ministry's expenditure 
planning. (Para-2.43) 
PUBLIC PROCUREMENT POLICY FOR MSMEs 
18. In the light of the information gathered by the Committee, it strongly 
recommends that the Ministry, in coordination with the Department of Public 
Enterprises and procuring CPSEs, put in place a time-bound and enforceable 
mechanism to achieve the mandated sub -targets for SC/ST -owned and women -owned 
MSEs. This should include CPSE -wise annual sub -targets, mandatory disclosure of 
shortfalls with reasons, and strengthening of MoU -linked penalties so t hat non -
compliance results in tangible managerial consequences rather than mere mark 
deductions. The Committee further recommends targeted vendor development drives 
exclusively for SC/ST and women -owned MSEs in technical and high -value sectors, 
with mandat ory handholding for GeM onboarding and tender participation, and 
institutionalised post-VDP mentoring with structured vendor -to-buyer matching. Time-
bound integration of the MSME Sambandh Portal with GeM and creation of a 
centralised national vendor direct ory should be completed within a defined timeline to 
enable real-time accountability and evidence-based procurement planning. (Para-2.49) 
19. The Committee notes the Ministry‘s submission that there is presently no 
provision for monitoring procurement from  MSEs owned by Other Backward Classes 
(OBCs) on the MSME Sambandh portal and that introducing an additional sub -target 
category may increase compliance burden and create overlaps with existing SC/ST and 
women sub-targets. The Committee, while conscious of these constraints, recommends 
that the Government examine the legal and administrative feasibility of tracking, and 
where appropriate incentivising, procurement from OBC -owned MSEs, without 
diluting the focus on achieving the existing sub -targets for SC/ST - and women-owned 
MSEs. (Para-2.50) 
DELAYED  PAYMENTS: A STRUCTURAL CHALLENGE 
20. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Ministry strengthen the 
Samadhaan and ODR ecosystem through mandatory buyer compliance, integration 
with GeM for automatic flagging of delayed payments, and time -bound resolution 
mandates backed by penal provisions under the MSMED Act, 2006. (Para-2.53) 
QUALITY OF OUTPUT-OUTCOME FRAMEWORK AND DATA GOVERNANCE 
21. The Committee recommends that the Ministry undertake a comprehensive OOF 
redesign in consultation with NITI Aayog and CGA, ensuring SMART indicators with 
balanced output, outcome and impact metrics, clear baselines and verification 
protocols. All OOF data sho uld be subjected to annual third -party audits, and future 

72 
 
DFGs should include a performance scorecard highlighting schemes with consistent 
over/under-achievement and corrective actions taken. (Para-2.56) 
NITI AAYOG'S REPORT ON ENHANCING COMPETITIVENESS OF MSMES 
22. Taking the Report of NITI Aayog on ‗Enhancing MSMEs' Competitiveness in 
India‘ forward, the Committee recommends that the Ministry formally adopt a 
competitiveness framework aligned with NITI Aayog's recommendations, mapping 
each major scheme to the specific pillars of financing, skills, technology adoption and 
market access. In view of the structural ―missing middle‖, wherein medium enterprises 
account for only a small share of MSME units but contribute a disproportionately high 
share of MSME exp orts, a dedicated Medium Enterprise Window within RAMP and 
the SRI Fund should be designed and operationalised for Industry 4.0 adoption, R&D 
collaboration and deeper integration into global value chains. Cluster -based testing and 
certification facilities under MSE-CDP and Technology Centres should be accelerated 
through a time -bound action plan, prioritising sectors and clusters with high export 
potential identified in the NITI Aayog report. (Para-2.59) 
 
CHAPTER 3: SCHEME-WISE ANALYSIS 
GUARANTEED EMERGENCY CREDIT LINE (GECL) 
23. Considering a scenario as discussed above, the Committee is of the firm view that 
unutilised guarantee allocations should not be surrendered mechanically. Instead, given 
that these funds are already reflected under the MSME head, the Committee strongly 
recommends that the Ministry pursue the matter with the Ministry of Finance to retain 
and repurpose the available fiscal space for MSME priorities. (Para-3.4) 
 
24. The Committee further recommends that such funds be strategically redeployed 
to strengthen credit support, skill development, technology upgradation and 
region‑specific interventions, particularly for the North‑Eastern Region, aspirational 
districts and other under‑serv ed areas, as well as for MSME schemes demonstrating 
higher absorption capacity and developmental impact. The Committee underscores that 
retaining this buffer is fiscally prudent, as it provides policy flexibility to respond swiftly 
to future unpredictable shocks, rather than re‑mobilising resources afresh at a later 
stage. (Para-3.5) 
 
CREDIT GUARANTEE SUPPORT: CGTMSE 
25. In view of the above, the Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry 
urgently shift the assessment of the Credit Guarantee Scheme from a mere approval‑ 
and disbursement‑driven framework to a results‑ and impact‑b ased monitoring system. 
The Ministry should mandatorily track and place before the Committee 
beneficiary‑level outcomes, including enterprise survival beyond one and three years, 
employment generated or sustained, turnover growth, repayment and NPA trends,  and 

73 
 
graduation of units from micro to small categories, with disaggregation by social 
category and region. (Para-3.10) 
 
26. The Committee further recommends strict enforcement of collateral‑free lending 
norms under CGTMSE. Banks must not dilute the intent  of the scheme by demanding 
collateral or third‑party guarantees. Any deviation from scheme guidelines should 
require mandatory written justification, and repeated violations at the branch level 
should attract deterrent penalties. The Committee also recomm ends rationalisation of 
guarantee fees, bank charges and insurance practices, including limiting insurance 
coverage strictly to the outstanding loan balance, in order to reduce the effective cost of 
borrowing for micro and small enterprises. (Para-3.11) 
 
27. The Committee also recommends comprehensive reform of credit appraisal 
practices under CGTMSE. Excessive reliance on CIBIL scores should be curtailed, 
particularly for first‑generation entrepreneurs and youth, and alternative assessment 
parameters based on business viability, cash flow and local economic conditions should 
be institutionalised. To address persistent awareness gaps, the Committee recommends 
mandatory outreach targets for banks in rural and semi‑urban areas, supported by 
structured handhold ing through MSME Development Institutes and State‑level 
agencies. (Para-3.12) 
 
28. The Committee further recommends strengthening transparency, monitoring 
and institutional coordination. A comprehensive public dashboard for CGTMSE should 
be created, providing scheme‑wise data on applications, sanctions, rejections, sectoral 
coverage and employment outcomes. Successful State‑level MSME convergence models 
should be replicated nationwide, and structured coordination among Central 
Ministries, State Governments, banks and MSME support institutions should be 
institutionalised to ensure uniform imp lementation and long‑term resilience of the 
MSME credit ecosystem. (Para-3.13) 
PRIME MINISTER‘S EMPLOYMENT GENERATION PROGRAMME (PMEGP) 
29. In light of the above, the Committee recommends expeditious rollout of the 
PMEGP 2.0 single‑window portal within a defined timeline, followed by outcome‑based 
monitoring of key indicators such as application‑to‑disbursement time, 
grievance‑redressal timelines and bank/State‑wise performance. Periodic analytical 
reports should be placed before the Committee to ensure im proved efficiency, 
transparency and accountability. (Para-3.17) 
 
30. The Committee is also of the concerted view that the low uptake and lower 
sanction rates of offline applications reflect inadequate awareness, insufficient 
handholding by implementing agencies and weak facilitation at the grassroots level. The 
Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry devise a targeted outreach and 
capacity‑building strategy for offline applicants, particularly in rural areas, aspirational 

74 
 
districts and among women,  SC and ST beneficiaries, including mandatory facilitation 
counters at KVIC/KVIB/DIC offices, involvement of CSCs, SHGs and NGOs as 
application‑support partners, periodic awareness drives in local languages and 
structured training of field officials to ens ure parity in appraisal quality and sanction 
outcomes between offline and online applications. (Para-3.18) 
 
31. The Committee, in view of these structural and implementation deficiencies, 
recommends a comprehensive recalibration of PMEGP to restore its relevance, 
inclusiveness and employment‑generating potential. The Committee strongly 
recommends that the Ministry revi se the project‑cost ceiling for manufacturing units 
upward from the existing ₹50 lakh, with periodic indexation to inflation, and expand 
eligibility beyond proprietary enterprises to include partnerships and other suitable 
business forms, so as to enable s cale, formalisation and higher‑quality employment.  
(Para-3.21) 
 
32. The Committee further recommends time‑bound and accountable release of 
margin‑money subsidy, with clearly prescribed stage‑wise timelines, automatic 
escalation in cases of delay and robust  offline fallback mechanisms to address portal 
downtime, particularly in rural, hilly and North‑Eastern regions. To address 
persistently high bank rejection rates, the Committee urges the Ministry to issue 
binding advisories to banks for uniform applicatio n of collateral‑free norms, moderated 
use of CIBIL scores for first‑generation entrepreneurs and introduction of risk‑sharing 
or partial credit‑guarantee mechanisms to realign lending behaviour with the scheme‘s 
social objectives. (Para-3.22) 
 
33. The Comm ittee also recommends revamping Entrepreneurship Development 
Programmes by restoring adequate duration, strengthening physical training 
components and linking EDP completion with structured post‑sanction handholding, 
mentoring and market‑linkage support. I n parallel, the Committee calls for urgent 
augmentation of manpower and field capacity in KVIC, DICs and implementing offices 
to ensure effective outreach, appraisal and monitoring. Finally, the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry adopt a region‑ and se ctor‑specific facilitation approach, 
with dedicated support for high‑potential activities such as oil and gas services in Assam 
and agarwood‑based enterprises in the North‑East, through coordinated policy backing, 
technical assistance and market linkage, t o maximise PMEGP‘s developmental impact.  
(Para-3.23) 
 
34. Further, in view of high demand, strong historical utilisation (around 98 per cent 
of the approved outlay under the current EFC cycle in the case of PMEGP) and the 
critical role of these schemes in supporting first -generation and vulnerable 
entrepreneurs, the Committee recommends that, subject to the overall fiscal 
consolidation path and resource availability, the Government consider higher 
allocations for PMEGP and PM Vishwakarma in forthcoming Budget exercises. Within 
the envelope approved, the Committee further urges the Ministry to give clear 

75 
 
operational priority to women, SC/ST and aspirational -district beneficiaries by 
tightening monitoring and handholding mechanisms. (Para-3.24) 
PM VISHWAKARMA SCHEME 
35. The Committee accordingly, recommends that the Government undertake an 
immediate structural rationalisation of the PM Vishwakarma Scheme by addressing 
systemic bottlenecks across the beneficiary pipeline. This should include strict 
time‑binding and simplification of Gram Panchayat and Urban Local Body verification 
through automated escalation and independent audits, transparent communication 
regarding the registration cap and pending applications and strengthened district‑level 
oversight to eliminate delays, subjectivity and beneficiary uncertainty. (Para-3.30) 
 
36. The Committee further recommends that the scheme be reoriented from a static, 
trade‑bound framework to a dynamic, market‑responsive livelihood programme. This 
would require periodic expansion and up dating of the eligible trade list, flexibility for 
beneficiaries to switch or upgrade trades, modernisation of training curricula with 
active industry participation and strengthening of the Guru –Shishya model through 
improved incentives to ensure relevance , quality and continuity of skill development.  
(Para-3.31) 
 
37. The Committee also recommends a decisive shift from input‑driven 
implementation to outcome‑based delivery. This should include strengthening credit 
linkage through greater branch‑level account ability and more flexible norms for 
first‑time and small‑ticket borrowers, enhanced beneficiary awareness on loan terms 
and the introduction of robust outcome indicators such as post‑training income 
enhancement, productivity gains, enterprise sustainabilit y and market access, to ensure 
that scheme interventions translate into durable and measurable livelihood 
improvements. (Para-3.32) 
 
38. The Committee further notes that the Budget Estimate for the PM Vishwakarma 
Scheme has been reduced to ₹3,860.89 crore in FY 2026‑27 from ₹5,100 crore in FY 
2025‑26 despite full utilisation of the registration cap and pending liabilities towards 
training, toolkit delivery and interest subvention.This budget compression, despite high 
demand and pending liabilities, warrants  urgent review of allocation adequacy in light 
of scheme scale and first-generation entrepreneur support. (Para-3.33) 
39. In addition, the Committee notes heavy trade‑wise concentration in occupations 
whose nomenclature is commonly perceived as caste‑linked in several regions, and finds 
that this undermines the inclusiveness and pan‑India acceptability of the scheme. (Para-
3.34) 
 
40. The Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry urgently rationalise 
trade nomenclature under the PM Vishwakarma Scheme by replacing caste‑ or 
region‑associated terms with profession‑neutral, function‑based names (for example, 

76 
 
―Footwear Artisan‖ instead of ―Cobbler‖, ―Ceramic and Clay Product Maker‖ instead 
of ―Potter‖ and ―Personal Grooming Service Provider‖ instead of ―Barber‖), in 
consultation with States and social experts, and notify a revised, standardised trade list 
applicable uniformly across the country. (Para-3.35) 
INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT: RAMP, MSE‑CDP, NEW TECHNOLOGY 
CENTRES AND TCSP 
41. The Committee accordingly recommends that the Ministry further sharpen the 
results‑based financing framework under RAMP by sequencing annual budgetary 
allocations strictly against the maturity of State‑level reforms and readiness of 
approved projects under Strategic Investment Plans. The Committee also recommends 
closer handholding of States with weaker institutional capaci ty to accelerate milestone 
achievement so that the remaining period of the programme is utilised to consolidate 
reforms on credit flow, market access, green transition and delayed payments and 
ensure full and timely utilisation of the approved outlay. (Para-3.39) 
 
42. In view of the above, the Committee recommends that the Ministry recalibrate 
conscious annual budgetary allocations under MSE‑CDP on the basis of committed 
liabilities and project‑wise implementation readiness, rather than uniform year‑on‑ year 
allocations. The Committee also recommends stricter milestone‑linked fund release 
mechanisms, improved handholding of State Governments and SPVs in project 
execution and time‑bound completion of CFCs and industrial‑estate projects to prevent 
cost over runs and idle infrastructure. Given the scheme‘s higher assistance for NER, 
aspirational districts, LWE‑affected areas and clusters dominated by micro, women and 
SC/ST‑owned units, the Committee recommends that such priority clusters be accorded 
first charge on available funds so that the equity and regional development objectives of 
the scheme are fully realised. (Para-3.43) 
 
43. The Committee recommends that the Ministry institutionalise a pre‑commitment 
framework under which approvals and budget provisio ning for new Technology 
Centres and Extension Centres are linked to upfront, time‑bound commitments from 
State Governments for land and built‑up space. The Committee further recommends 
prioritisation of funds for locations where land is already in possession and tenders have 
been finalised under the Autonomous/EPC mode, and early operationalisation of 
additional Extension Centres in aspirational districts and the NER, supported by 
PMIS‑based monitoring, so that revised allocations translate into tangible tr aining and 
technology services for MSMEs rather than recurring under‑expenditure. (Para-3.47) 
44. In this context, The  Committee recommends that the Ministry adopt a holistic 
phase‑wise, completion‑linked planning and budgeting approach for TCSP, aligning 
annual physical targets and financial allocations strictly with the commissioning status 
of individual centres and rea diness of procurement packages. The Committee also 
recommends tighter contractual safeguards and performance‑based monitoring of 
contractors and procurement agencies, alongside enhanced coordination with CPWD 

77 
 
and State authorities, to avoid time and cost o verruns. Given the strong outcomes 
already delivered by operational centres, the Committee recommends prioritising 
completion and full operationalisation of the remaining Technology Centres before 
expanding targets so that the proposed allocation for FY 20 26‑27 results in optimal 
utilisation of funds and durable strengthening of MSME competitiveness. (Para-3.50) 
EQUITY, ENTREPRENEURSHIP AND TRAINING 
45. The Committee appreciates the commitment shown by the Ministry to support 
MSMEs and recommends that the enhanced allocation under the SRI Fund be deployed 
in a targeted, outcome‑oriented manner, prioritising MSMEs with high growth and 
export potential and those affected by external trade disruptions, with a focus on 
technology upgradation, product diversifica tion and quality certification. The 
Committee further recommends strengthening the pipeline of investible MSMEs from 
Tier‑II and Tier‑III regions through structured handholding, incubation support and 
convergence with other MSME schemes, and instituting a robust monitoring 
framework with measurable indicators such as enterprise scale expansion, employment 
generation, export growth and private‑capital mobilisation to guide future allocations 
under the Fund. (Para-3.52) 
 
46. As it acknowledges the enhanced allocation for ATI, the Committee recommends 
that the enhanced allocation for ATI be utilised in a timely and optimal manner by 
aligning training and institutional‑support activities with emerging industry 
requirements, export‑market standards and technology‑upgradation needs of MSMEs. 
The Committee further recommends strengthening partnerships between training 
institutions, industry bodies, exporters and technology providers so that trainees 
acquire upskilling, market‑relevant  competencies, and instituting an outcome‑tracking 
framework covering enterprise creation, employment generation, export‑readiness and  
technology adoption to maximise the impact of this investment. (Para-3.54) 
KHADI, VILLAGE INDUSTRIES, COIR AND MARKET PROMOTION – KEY 
ISSUES 
47. The Committee therefore recommends just rationalization of establishment 
expenditure under Khadi Grant and systematic redirection of savings to field -level 
interventions that directly benefit artisans and rural enterprises. The Committee also 
recommends linking support such as Modified Market Development Assistance and 
marketing‑infrastructure assistance to measurable improvements in sales turnover, 
artisan incomes and institutional viability, so that financial assistance leads t o sustained 
competitiveness rather than continued reliance on subsidies. (Para-3.56) 
 
48.     The Committee notes that the Ministry has drawn up a milestone -based quarterly 
plan (20 –30–30–20) for utilisation of the ₹196 crore allocation  in 2026 –27. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry strictly adhere to its own milestone -linked 
phasing, with particular focus on expediting civil works, machinery installation and 

78 
 
commissioning, so that all sanctioned clusters reach functional status by the end of FY 
2026–27. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry furnish to it, by a 
specified date, a detailed status note on cluster -wise physical progress, fund releases and 
bottlenecks, along with corrective measures taken. (Para-3.58) 
 
49.     The Committee fails to comprehend the delays which it is of the firm believe 
should have been circumvented and recommends strict adherence to the 
milestone-linked plan for settlement of committed liabilities under SFURTI, with 
priority accorded to fun ctionalisation and operational readiness of clusters rather than 
mere financial closure. The Committee further recommends fixing accountability on 
Nodal and Implementing Agencies for avoidable delays in procurement and clearances, 
and systematic incorporat ion of lessons learnt from SFURTI into the design and 
execution of future cluster -based schemes such as MSE -CDP, particularly for 
traditional and artisan-based industries. (Para-3.59) 
 
50. The Committee expresses disappointment on the neglect to indigenous  section 
such as Coir and recommends that the Coir Board improve utilisation of funds through 
advance planning and timely execution of activities, expand outreach in non‑traditional 
coir‑producing States to achieve more balanced regional coverage and accel erate 
commercial‑scale adoption of research outputs through structured industry linkages 
and incubation support, so that S&T investments yield tangible gains in productivity, 
diversification and incomes for coir workers and entrepreneurs. (Para-3.61) 
 
51. The Committee recommends that PMS and IC be deployed more strategically as 
market-promotion and resilience instruments by adopting a flexible, shock -responsive 
funding approach—especially during periods of global trade stress—and by redesigning 
these schem es with clear, outcome -linked objectives related to export diversification, 
domestic-market substitution and sustained buyer linkages. The Committee further 
recommends closer integration of PMS and IC activities into a unified market -resilience 
framework s o that MSMEs receive coordinated support across domestic and 
international markets in response to evolving global trade uncertainties. (Para-3.64) 
 
CHAPTER 4: TARGETED SCHEMES / PROGRAMMES FOR VULNERABLE 
GROUPS 
NORTH EAST REGION 
52. In view of the persistent under -utilisation of funds despite adequate allocations, 
the Committee recommends that the Ministry put in place a mandatory time -bound 
execution framework for all NER projects, with clearly defined quarterly physical and 
financial milestones and release of funds strictly linked to their achievement. The 
Ministry should also conduct quarterly project -wise reviews and ensure reallocation of 
funds from delayed or non -performing projects to ready -to-execute projects within the 

79 
 
same financial year, so that enhanced allocations result in actual expenditure and visible 
outcomes in the NER. (Para-4.7) 
 
53. The Committee notes wide inter -State variation in PMEGP -supported micro 
enterprises across the North Eastern States. While Assam continues to account for the 
highest number of assisted units, several States such as Manipur, Mizoram, Meghalaya 
and Sikkim show fluctuating or declining trends in recent years, particularly in 2022 -23 
and 2023 -24, with partial recovery in 2024 -25. The Co mmittee is of the view that the 
uneven distribution of benefits, coupled with declining expenditure utilisation, suggests 
that existing institutional and delivery mechanisms require closer monitoring and more 
focused implementation to ensure that allocated  resources translate into actual project 
grounding and enterprise creation across all North Eastern States in an equitable and 
timely manner.  (Para-4.11) 
 
54. In view of the wide inter -State variation in PMEGP performance in the North 
Eastern Region, the Committee recommends that the Ministry fix State -wise PMEGP 
targets linked to past performance and absorptive capacity, provide focused 
handholding through KVIC/KVIB and District Industries Centres in consistently low -
performing States, and conduct quarter ly State -specific reviews to ensure timely 
grounding of projects and equitable distribution of benefits across all North Eastern 
States.  (Para-4.12) 
 
WOMEN 
 
55. The Committee therefore, recommends that the Ministry consider earmarking a 
minimum assured allocation for women entrepreneurs under PMEGP to safeguard 
their participation during periods of budgetary constraint. It further recommends that 
the Ministry explore  differential or graded subsidy support for women -led micro 
enterprises, especially in low-capital and service sectors, to mitigate the impact of rising 
project costs. The Committee also suggests strengthening convergence with skill 
development, market lin kage and mentoring initiatives to enhance the viability of 
women-led units, and instituting periodic monitoring of gender -disaggregated outcomes 
to ensure that the objective of inclusive and equitable entrepreneurship promotion 
under PMEGP is consistently achieved.  (Para-4.17) 
 
SCHEDULED CASTES/ SCHEDULED TRIBES 
 
56. The Committee recommends that the Ministry reassess the budgetary allocation 
for NSSH in light of the demonstrated demand and the strategic importance of inclusive 
entrepreneurship in the MSME ecosystem. Adequate and stable funding should be 
ensured to strengthen credit facilitation, procurement readiness and enterprise capacity 
building, particularly to accelerate progress towards the 4% procurement mandate. 
The Ministry should also improve fund utilisation efficiency through better planning, 

80 
 
monitoring an d convergence with other MSME schemes to maximise the impact of 
available resources.  (Para-4.22) 
 
SPECIALLY – ABLED PERSONS 
 
57. The Committee observes that despite preferential provisions, the number of 
beneficiaries has shown a consistent decline over the last five years, falling from 484 in 
2021-22 to 213 in 2024 -25 and further to 199 in the current year up to 31 December 
2025. This  downward trend suggests gaps in outreach, accessibility and effective 
utilisation of the scheme by differently-abled entrepreneurs. (Para-4.25) 
58. The Committee recommends that the Ministry earmark a minimum annual sub -
target under PMEGP exclusively for differently-abled beneficiaries, ensure district-wise 
identification of eligible cases through District Industries Centres, provide structured 
handholding support by KVIC/KVIB officials from application filing to loan 
disbursement, and undertake quarterly reviews of performance indicating applications 
mobilised, sanctioned and units operationalised for differently -abled persons.  (Para-
4.26) 
CHAPTER 5: AUTONOMOUS BODIES 
KHADI AND VILLAGE INDUSTRIES COMMISSION (KVIC) 
 
59. Therefore, the Committee recommends that KVIC formulate a comprehensive 
medium-term strategy to substantially expand artisan coverage and employment 
generation, with clearly defined annual physical and financial targets. 
Capacity-building initiatives under CoEK should be significantly scaled  up in coverage 
and geographical outreach, with measurable outcome indicators linked to productivity, 
quality improvement and income enhancement. KVIC should also strengthen 
institutional capacity by ensuring availability of adequate technical expertise an d 
reducing excessive reliance on short -term contractual arrangements. Focused efforts 
are further recommended to enhance branding, product diversification, e -commerce 
integration and export promotion. (Para-5.10) 
 
COIR BOARD 
 
60. The Committee therefore, r ecommends that the Ministry strengthen value 
addition, product diversification, and branding to improve export realisation. Skill 
development and technology transfer initiatives should be substantially scaled up with 
measurable outcomes linked to productiv ity and artisan incomes, particularly for 
women workers. The Ministry should also ensure timely release and efficient utilisation 
of funds to support effective implementation of programmes and sustained sectoral 
growth. (Para-5.18) 
 

81 
 
61. The Committee there fore, recommends that the Ministry formulate a targeted 
export resilience strategy for the coir sector, including market diversification beyond 
traditional destinations, support for compliance with international standards, and 
financial risk -mitigation mea sures for MSME exporters. The Ministry may also 
coordinate with the Ministry of Commerce to proactively address tariff -related 
challenges through trade negotiations and export incentive frameworks. (Para-5.20) 
NATIONAL SMALL INDUSTRIES CORPORATION (NSIC) 
62.     The Committee notes that NSIC has demonstrated strong institutional capacity 
and operational performance through its nationwide network, integrated service 
delivery model and consistent financial results. However, the Committee is of the 
considered view that the scale of financing and growth capital required by the MSME 
sector—particularly for first -generation entrepreneurs, technology -intensive 
enterprises, export-oriented units and enterprises located in aspirational or underserved 
regions—far exce eds the present resource envelope available with NSIC. The 
Committee observes that the absence of a dedicated, large -scale growth financing 
mechanism significantly constrains the Corporation‘s ability to catalyse private 
investment and support MSMEs in sca ling up operations, thereby limiting its potential 
developmental impact. (Para-5.25) 
 
63. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry of MSME, in 
consultation with the Ministry of Finance, operationalise the proposed ₹10,000 crore 
SME Growth Fund under NSIC in a phased, multi‑year manner, with a clearly defined 
implementation framework, timelines and measurable outcome parameters. The 
Committee emphasises that the proposed Growth Fund should be structured as a 
professionally managed veh icle, distinct from existing credit and guarantee schemes, 
and should focus on providing growth‑stage financing through blended‑finance, 
risk‑sharing and co‑lending models in partnership with financial institutions. Priority 
should be accorded to MSMEs eng aged in technology upgradation, export‑oriented 
activities and enterprises operating in underserved and aspirational regions. (Para-5.26) 
 
64.     The Committee further recommends that robust governance mechanisms be 
institutionalised for the proposed Grow th Fund, including the establishment of an 
independent investment committee, transparent eligibility criteria, periodic public 
disclosure of fund utilisation and outcome‑based monitoring linked to employment 
generation, enterprise growth and market access.  A mid‑term evaluation framework 
should also be incorporated to enable timely course correction and ensure that the Fund 
contributes meaningfully to scaling MSME competitiveness and long‑term 
sustainability, while remaining consistent with the overall fisc al consolidation path.  
(Para-5.27) 
 
65.     The Committee also observes that despite NSIC‘s expanded mandate, upgraded 
Schedule ‗A‘ status and commendable financial performance, its existing equity base of 

82 
 
approximately ₹532 crore remains modest relative t o the scale of operations and 
financial support expected from the Corporation. The Committee notes that this limited 
capital base constrains NSIC‘s leverage capacity and necessitates greater reliance on 
borrowings from banks and financial institutions, oft en at higher costs, which 
ultimately affects the affordability of assistance extended to MSMEs. (Para-5.28) 
 
66.     Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the Ministry consider substantial 
equity infusion into NSIC  at the earliest to strengthen its capital base in line with its 
strategic importance and enhanced responsibilities. The Committee is of the view that 
enhanced equity support would reduce dependence on high -cost borrowings, improve 
internal resource generation, and enable NSIC to offer more competitive interest rates, 
lower service charges and affordable support to MSMEs. (Para-5.29) 
 
67.     The Committee further recommends that any equity infusion into NSIC be 
explicitly linked to measurable expansion in MSME coverage, particularly in priority 
sectors and underserved regions, so that the intervention directly translates into lower 
cost of finance, improved credit accessibility and sustainable scaling of NSIC 
operations, in alignment with national objective s such as Atmanirbhar Bharat and 
Viksit Bharat. (Para-5.30) 
MAHATMA GANDHI INSTITUTE FOR RURAL INDUSTRIALISATION (MGIRI) 
68. In view of the enhanced financial support and MGIRI‘s expanding portfolio of 
technology development, quality assurance and capacity-building activities, the 
Committee recommends that the Ministry put in place a clearly articulated medium -
term outcomes framework for MGIRI, with defined milestones for technology 
dissemination, field -level adoption by Khadi and Village Industries , and measurable 
improvements in artisan incomes and rural enterprise productivity. The Committee 
further emphasises that future budgetary support should be closely aligned with 
MGIRI‘s role as a national resource centre, ensuring that increased allocation s 
translate into scalable, replicable and impact-oriented interventions across States. (Para-
5.33)

(iii) Expressed concern over the relatively low proportion of capital expenditure;

(i) Key budgetary highlights and major policy initiatives introduced to strengthen the 
MSME ecosystem, with particular emphasis on enhancing competitiveness, 
technology adoption and market integration. 

86 
 
(ii) Measures undertaken to facilit ate access to credit, including expansion of credit 
guarantee schemes, interest subvention support and development of customised 
financial products tailored to the needs of micro and small enterprises. 
(iii) Priority sectoral interventions focusing on industries  such as footwear, leather, 
toys, clean technology and startups, aimed at promoting innovation, employment 
generation and export potential. 
(iv) Implementation of Public Procurement Policy provisions, including targeted 
support and capacity -building measures fo r SC/ST and women entrepreneurs to 
improve their participation in government procurement. 
(v) Steps taken to promote formalisation of enterprises, bridge existing credit gaps 
and enhance domestic and global market access through digital platforms, cluster 
development and institutional support mechanisms. 
11. The Chairman and Members of the Committee raised a wide range of issues, inter 
alia, the following: 
(i) Absence of clear implementation roadmaps, timelines and accountability 
mechanisms for major Budget announcements such as the SME Growth Fund, 
TReDS integration and Corporate Mitra programme; 
(ii) Disproportionate emphasis on equity financing vis -à-vis skill development and

(iii) Pendency, verification delays and rejection trends under P M Vishwakarma

(iv) Need for collateral-free, cash-flow-based lending and concerns regarding ground -
level banking practices; 
(v) Impact of global trade developments, including tariff-related issues, on MSMEs; 
(vi) Flat allocations for procurement and marketing support despite emerging export 
challenges; 
(vii) Performance and revival of SFURTI clusters, including concerns regarding stalled 
and non-operational clusters; 
(viii) Variations in utilisation figures between Budget Estimates, Revised Estimates and 
Actual Expenditure, particularly with respect to GECL provisions; 
(ix) Outreach, awareness and district -level engagement to improve MSME 
registrations, skilling and institutional coordination, especially in rural areas; 
(x) Mandate, performance and outcomes of technology centres and institutions under 
the Ministry, including MGIRI.

The Ministry of Steel was requested to furnish detailed background note on problems being faced by Steel Industry. The Ministry in the background note have inter-alia stated that sluggish Steel demand, rising cost of inputs, high power tariff, lack of infrastructural facilities,
lack of fund flow, dumping of steel by CIS and South East Asian Countries. import of Sub-Standard Steel materials ore are the general problems of Steel Industry.
The Ministry of Steel, while stating the specific problems faced by SAIL, informed the Sub-Committee that the growth of steel consumption has come down from 22% in 1994-95 to about 1% in 1997-98. A general recession in the economy, like decline in GDP growth rate
and industrial growth has affected the prospects of SAIL. It was further informed that while there is a reduction in the international price of coal, there is an abnormal increase in coking coal prices in India (8% in 1994-95; 12% in 1995-96, 28% in 1996-97, 12% in 1997-98 )
impacting an additional burden of Rs.200 crore to SAIL. Moreover, SAIL has incurred capital expenditure of Rs. 16, 200 core on modernization and other addition & modification schemes and had to borrow7l%ofthe amount.
The Ministry of Steel apprised that the current manpower in SAIL is 1,77.000. consequently labour cost became substantially higher compared to domestic and international competitors. (SAIL has to incur 18% as labour cost in comparison to TISCO's 14.9%, RINL - 4.5%
Essar Steel -10.3%, Jindal's -2.1%, Lloyd Steel - 1.2% Moreover Labour cost is rising faster then any other element of cost and has increased from 14. 1 % to 16.5% of SAIL's turnover during last five years. Not only this, SAIL has about 28,000 contract labour and expenditure on
contractual labour stood about Rs.340 crore in 1997- 98 (3% of total cost).
The Ministry of Steel further stated that all the subsidiaries of SAIL like TISCO, VISL, MEL etc. are permanently dependent on SAIL and SAIL has extended about Rs.3000 crore in these subsidiaries in the form of equity investment, loans, and advances and waiver of interest
on loans given up to 3 1 "March, 1998.
As regards the tax-structure, the Ministry of Steel opined that Excise Duty -on Iron & Steel has increased over the year and at present, excise duty on steel is 15% ad-valorem as against 12.5% on :flat products and 1000 per tonne on long products before 1994-95. Project
increase in import duty on coking coal result in a substantial increase in the cost of production.  Similarly frequent increase in railway freight affected the competitiveness of SAIL. The Ministry of Steel suggested that there is a need to consider reduction in freight specifically for the
management of basic raw material like Iron Ore and coking coal, classification of steel may also be reduced 210 to 290 (T/L) and 230 to 210 9 (W/L) to reduce the freight on transportation of finished steel.

for the first time in an integrated steel plant. At present the plant is equipped to produce annually 31,53000 tonne of saleable steel comprising  of 5,00,000 tonne -of rails; 2,50,000 tonne of heavy structural; 5,00,000 tonne of merchant products such as bars, rods medium beams, angles
etc. and 4,00,000 tonne of wire rods; 9,50,000 tonne of plates and 5,53,000    tonne of semis for sale to be used by the re-rolling industry.

Meeting with workers of BSP
 
The Sub-Committee met the representatives of workers and came across the problems being faced by Steel Industry in general and the Bhilai Steel Plant in particular. Some specific problems of the workers were also discussed. The workers representatives expressed their
pleasure for being associated with BSP and the Sub-Committee noticed deeply rooted sense of belongingness of workers toward BSP as an Organisation.
            Workers representative viewed that recent recession in steel industry has marred the prospect of steel industry as a whole as it is difficult to sale the steel products, resulting in amassing of inventories. Workers requested for grants to steel Industry in such adverse situation. The
workers argued that as the global recession has crippled the sale of BSP 's products so the necessity is to sketch new marketing strategy. Dumping of steel products by international players in the domestic market is adding problems to the domestic market scenario hence there is need
to pass some anti-dumping law in order to protect the domestic market. Moreover workers representatives expressed concern over  “increasing operating cost" which pose as one of the major problems of BSP. They hoped that if some sort of financial motivation is provided to the
plant in terms of tax-relief, freight charge consideration etc the said problem should be solved to some extent. When the Sub- Committee asked whether the measure of financial autonomy' will smoothen the functioning of the plant, the workers representative argued that there is no
point in giving fillip to the policy of isolation.
            Workers representatives pointed out that demand is sluggish in almost all products due to overall adverse economic scenario. Moreover, BSP is facing tough competition from secondary sector and cheaper import. Demand from infrastructure, construction and capital goods
sector is very low so the immediate requirement is to boost the consumption of steel by promoting development works consuming steel; applying steel products in communication network; putting condition of consuming indigenous steel by MNCs while doing business in India:
encouragement to consumption of steel in agro-products- replacement of wooden by steel in construction of building which is eco-friendly: encouraging use of steel     sheet in house- construction in place of asbestos which is cheap in long run and health-server.
            The worker's representative informed the Sub-Committee that the issue of pension to workers as third wage is pending in the Supreme Court and expects the early disposal of case in the better interest of workers. The general issue of welfare measures in BSP also cropped up
during the meeting with workers representatives.
            The issue of the marginal efficiency of labour having a direct bearing on the performance of BSP was discussed. The Committee was apprised of the fact that the efficiency of labour is directly related to the performance of a steel plant and labour productivity is the Key index
of labour efficiency & performance. It was informed that in the steel industry, the standard unit of labour productivity in terms of crude steel production per man/year is denoted by :-
LP = Production of crude steel +1/4 production of pig iron

certain  arising  also  take place.  As  the supplies are  made  against  foreign specification,  these  arising are clarified as "Export surplus Plates". As the demand for plates in domestic the accumulation of arising, both for domestic as well as export, was on increase and was becoming
an operation limitation for plate Mill for smooth finishing & shipping operations. To liquidate these stocks, it was decided by SAIL-CMO that the Export surplus plates may be sold both by SAIL-CMO as well as SAEL-BSP w.e.f. April 98. Accordingly, the sale by SAIL- BSP also

FERRO SCRAP NIGAM LIMITED
 
            The Sub-Committee met Ferro Scrap Nigam Limited (FSNL) management on 149.98 who informed that FSNL was incorporated as a joint Sector Company on 28.3.79 with a paid-up capital of Rs.200 lakhs of which 60% Equity share are held by MSTC Ltd. and the remaining
40% are held by HARS Co. Corporation Besides its registered office at Bhilai, Madhya Pradesh, FSNL has its six operating units at Rourkela, Boars, Bhilai, Burnpur, Vizag & Durgapur.
            The management informed the Sub-Committee about the short-term objectives of FSNL which inter-alia include to maximise recovery of scrap; to ensure fair return on Capital employed, to meet the capital expenditure out of internal resources generation while long term
objectives includes Modernisation and up gradation of technology, taking over complete scrap recovery and handling job of the Steel plants of public and private sectors; undertaking R & D activity and thereby converting the slag, flyash and other industrial wastes into cost effective

            The Sub-Committee met the officials of Diamond Mines on the 14th September 1998 and came across the exploration and mining process of diamond. Interestingly, the word diamond has been derived from Greek word 'admas' meaning "the evincible" and denoting the quality
of exceptional hardness. With the passage of time the word ‘admas' slowly got converted into ademant, diamant and finally to diamond "a precious stone composed of crystallised carbon, usually colourless and of great brilliance hard substance known. Diamond is considered to be
found at a great depth in the mantle of earth under high temperature and pressure and is believed to be carried up to the surface and is believed to be carried up to the surface of earth magma, what is known as 'kimberlite'.
The Sub-Committee was informed that diamond are mainly divided into three categories as per their uses viz-gem. semi-gem and industrial diamond. Although there are more than 5000 thousand categories of diamond but from valuation point of view, it is mainly classified on
the basis of four Cs i.e. Cartage (weight); clarity, colour and cutting. The world famous diamonds like Kohimoor, Pitt or Regent, Orloff, Great Mogul, Akbar Shah, Mahan Patz, Nizam, Nasik, Pigot & Hope, having the best of all four C's are the bench mark in the sparkling diamond
heritage of India. The Dawn of 20
th Century brought in focus the kimberlitie deposit in Vindhvas and mining activities of diamonds started in the first quarter of this century in Panna areas of Madhya Pradesh. Initially, mining was carried out by private companies but in early sixties,
these mines were taken over by NMDC. The production in this area, though meagre but has distinction of producing some important gem quality diamonds viz, Giri, Girija, Uma, Subhadra. Vasundhara, Vajralaxmi, Urvashi.

occurrences are reported from Satna and Chhattarpur districts. The diamondiferous area of Panna district runs in the form of a belt for about 70 kms. In ENE-WSW trend and the belt extends from Palanikakhera in the ENE to Majhgawan in the WSW direction. The diamondiferous

DURGAPUR STEEL PLANT
 
            The Sub-Committee visited the plant-site on 20 th September, 1998. The Plant was set-up with British assistance in LATE 50s with an initial capacity of I million tome of ingots per annum and was commissioned in stages between December, 1959 & January 1962. The plant
launched expansion programme during 1967 to 1969 to 1.6 mt and the various units under its expansion were commissioned between June 1966 and August 1971 but actual performance remained low due to various problems being faced by the plant. The plant achieved its highest
production of 1.092 mt. during only in 1977-78 and later performance became inconsistent and continued to decline in the 80s and early 90s due to obsolete and unreliable health of technology and equipments.
 
            Henceforth, the modernisation plan was taken up in the year 1989 by the Government at an estimated cost of Rs.2668 crore against the sanctioned completion schedule of March, 1993 with the objectives of replacing old and obsolete equipment & technology, improve
productivity of various units and quality of products, to improve yield, to conserve energy, to reduce the cost of production and to abate environmental pollution. Against the sanctioned completion of March, 1993, all production units were completed by April, 1996. Other facilities

DEVELOPMENT COMMISSIONER FOR IRON AND STEEL CALCUTTA
 
The Sub-Committee met the officials of Development Commission for Iron and Steel (DCI & S) on 21st September 1998, which through its Regional offices Continued to perform its advisory, developmental and regulatory functions. The Sub-Committee was informed of the
organisational structure and detailed functions of the Office of DCI & S. As a part of the economic liberalisation process, the pricing mechanism of Joint Plant Committee (JPC) operating from 1964 was abolished with effect from 16th January, 1992 and pricing of Iron and Steel are
now governed by market forces of demand and supply.
 
With the deregulation of distribution and pricing of Iron & Steel, the DC (I&S) with the aid of its six regional offices located at Calcutta, Mumbai, New Delhi, Kanpur (under New Delhi), Chennai and Hyderabad (under Chennai) performs the following functions: -
 
a.       Collection, processing and dissemination of basic information relating to the Iron & Steel industry and to act as the data bank of the Department of Steel;
b.      Monitoring of regional price and supply trends suggesting to the Department remedial measures for correcting the imbalances, if any;
c.       Monitoring of import and export of Iron and Steel materials;
d.      Advice on matters relating to import and export policies of Iron and Steel;
e.       Management of distribution of Iron and Steel materials to the designated priority sectors such as Defence, Railway State Small Industries Corporation, Engineering Goods Exporters and North Eastern States;
f.        Allocation of materials to the state small scale Industry corporation;
g.       Allocation of materials to remote areas like North Eastern States;
h.       Assistance to Engineering Goods exports Units through priority allocation and monitoring thereof,
i.         Survey of various segments of Steel Industry;
j.        Rendering assistance to the EAF Units and secondary sector, by way of rapacity assessment, assistance in procurement of indigenous/imported raw-materials and import substitution measures aimed at overall development of the sector;
k.      Interface between the Government and different consumer groups to facilitate consumer-producer interaction.
l.         Co-ordination for movement of raw-materials to Steel plants; and
m.     Vigilance functions to prevent misuse of steel obtained from regulated sources.
 
The Sub-Committee was informed that DCI &. S continues to make allocation of pig Iron to the designated consumers and the main producers supply the material on the basis of such allocation. The DC also continues to issue Release Orders for supplies to exporters of
engineering goods and make annual supply plans for the North Eastern Region.
As regards the DCI &. S's roles in monitoring the price and supply trends in the changed market scenario, i.e. deregulation of distribution and pricing; transformation from a sellers to a buyer's market; the Sub-Committee was informed that DCI&S collects the open market
price of Iron and Steel from various region and apprise the same to the Ministry of Steel on weekly/fortnightly basis. DCI&S monitors supply trend of five designated sectors by holding meeting with different agencies. This office also makes supply plant for the Nodal Authority of

METAL SCRAP TRADE CORPORATION LIMITED
 
 
Meeting with Management of MSTC
 
            The Sub-Committee met the management of Metal Scrap Trade Corporation Limited on 21 st September, 1998, which was incorporated as a Public Limited company under the companies Act 1956 in the year 1964. The status of the company underwent change in February,
1974 to that of a subsidiary of SAIL and in 1982-83 the corporation was converted into a Government of India company transferring the shares of SAIL to President of India. Presently, the company has an authorised Capital of Rs.5.00 crore and paid up capital of Rs.2.20 crore, of
which 901/o is held by the President of India and the balance I0%  by the members  of Steel Furnaces  Association of India and Iron & Steel Scrap Association of India and others. Initially, the role of the company was essentially to determine the exportable surplus scrap availability
in the country after meeting the requirement of the indigenous industries, sign protocol with scrap importing countries and allow exporters to export scrap at prices above the floor price.    When the secondary Steel Sector comprising of Induction Furnaces, electronic arc Furnaces, Re-
rolling Mills grew, MSTC became the canalising agency for import of Carbon Steel Melting Scrap. Stainless Steel Melting Scrap. Re-roll able Scrap in the shape of old vessels for demolition, etc. Immediately after decanalisation, MSTC continued to import the erstwhile canalised
item viz. Carbon Steel Melting Scrap. During the period from 1992-93 to 1994-95, MSTC continued to retain the market share of more than 30% even though the total volume of import in the country dwindled and hence imports by MSTC in absolute terms started coming down.
            MSTC faced a serious crisis from 1995-96 in the shape of fluctuating International Prices and falling value of rupee vis-a-vis US dollar. Although materials imported were during 1995-96 and 1996-97 MSTC found difficulty in selling imported scrap. Ultimately, a crisis point
was reached in 1997-98 when the accumulated stock had to be sold at negative margin. During the year 1997-98 no further import was made.
With the depression in the Steel market and with 124 out of 184 EAF unit having closed their operation, the demand pattern of auto scrap changed except for major Steel producers in the Secondary Sector like Eastern Steel, Mukund, MVSCO and Jindal Strip, there is hardly
any demand for Shredded Scrap (auto scrap) being used by these plants.
Because of the size problem and the low value of the cargo, MSTC doesn't find it economical to import small quantities of H.M.S. as done by small consumers. Consequently, in 1997- 98 the volume of imports was zero.
            As import have been the main stay of the corporation and the company have found it very difficult to maintain traditional imports in Foreign trade so it was decided in 1989-99 to import slab and cuttings and petroleum products worth about Rs.27 crore.

PHASE-II
 
REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT COMMISSIONER (RDC), CHENNAI
 
            The Sub-Committee-I met RDC, Chennai and representatives of Private Entrepreneurs on 6th October, 1998 to discuss the problems being faced by Steel Industry (both in Public and Private Sector).
            The meeting started with the presentation by Shri M.S. Ramanujan, Regional Development Commissioner, Chennai, whose, initial, presentation banked on the formal functions of RDC, which interalia includes regulatory developmental and advisory to promote the Steel
Industry.
            The Office of RDC Chennai, monitors the regional price and supply trends and recommends to the Ministry the required remedial guidelines. RDC advises the Government with regard to exports & import policies of Iron and Steel.
            It looks after private Entrepreneurs and proved instrumental to the development of what is called Mini Steel Plant. It plays pivotal role in the allocation of materials to the small scale entrepreneurs.
            RDC office acts as data-bank' and is an important organ of the Ministry of Steel as the office collects, processes and disseminates the basic data relating to Iron & Steel Industry.
            RDC- Chennai has from time to time held discussion with users industry or groups in order to have consumer- producer interaction. The interaction process includes seminars, group discussion product exhibitions etc. and is responsible for enlarging the scope of consumption
of Steel. The Sub-Committee was informed that RDC-Chennai had accordingly, organised Automobile Exhibition as an attempt to promote steel industry. It also manages to distribute Iron & Steel materials to priority sectors such as Defence, Railway etc and proved determining in
creating the demands of Steel.
            In order to give 'a Kick start' to the Steel-Industry, RDC-Chennai have acted as surveyor of technical aspects of Steel Industry and contributed to the growth of Steel Industry,
            After giving details of traditional functions of RDC, Shri M.S. Ramanujan, shifted the focus of presentation on the problematic aspects of Steel Industry:-
            Starting with the problems of Pig Iron, it was brought forth to the notice of the Sub- Committee that South-Asian crisis has hit the Pig Iron-Industry, tremendously. South Asian countries China & Australia are dumping the Pig-Iron in India creating a mammoth problem for the
domestic market due to unviable competitive strength of indigenous producers as comparative cost of Pig-Iron production is higher in India in comparison to these countries. In order to inject the competitive advantages in indigenous producing it is expected from the Government to
waive anti-dumping duty on imported coke as indigenous coke is not suitable for mini-blast furnaces. It is expected that if duty on imported coke is reverted from 19.6% to 15%, there is every likelihood for a progressive and prospective trend of pig iron Industry.
As regards the Sponge Iron Industry, the Sub-Committee was informed that the major threat to indigenous Sponge industry is import of Scrap at lower price than the production cost of the Sponge Iron in India. According to the calculation of RDC-Chennai the difference between the
selling price of indigenous Sponge and the landed selling price of imported Sponge is Rs.600 per tonne pulling the indigenous Sponge Industry to a disadvantageous stage. The Sub-Committee
 
was requested to recommend to the Government to undertake suitable measures to safeguard the interest of the Industry and to inject the new life to the deadening domestic industry.
            The states of affairs with Electric Arc Furnace were reported not to be in a better condition. Out of 29 EAF Units in the Southern region four units have been converted into induction furnaces while 23 have been closed and only two units are in working condition. The major
reasons for the unviable operation of EAF are high power tariff and power shortage. Moreover production cost for the EAF route is more than that of the induction furnaces route due to low power consumption and investment in Induction Furnaces. 'Mere is a necessity of making the
commercial viability of Induction furnace, as out of 123 Induction Furnace only 74 units are in working conditions. The prospective overhauling of Induction Furnace Industry is possible by removing anomalies of compound excise levy system and by increasing the custom duty on
imported scrap.
            The Steel Re-rolling Industry is reeling under doldrums due to economic slowdown in general and indigenous competitions and improper & inappropriate taxation system in particular., The State of  Tamil  Nadu has about 250 steel re-rolling mills and most of them were set-up
in the post liberalisation phase i.e. 1991, attracted by the concessional tariff for new industries under the New Industrial Policy. Being a metallurgical industry the rolling mills are power intensive. But the irony of the fact is that the rolling mills, besides being subjected to the annual
rituals of increase in energy charges, are the victims of  differential cost of power tariff i.e. Rs.4.03 per unit in Tamil  Nadu compared to Rs. 1.25 in Goa and Rs.2.20 in Punjab. The sordid plight of rolling mills does not stop here at because of the refusal of Commercial tax
Departments to recognise genuine consignments transferred, the State levy 4% Central Sales Tax (CST) even on consignments transfers and if the sale is without the form  'C' a tax of 8% is leviable , besides a penalty of 150%. Adding to the ills of the Steel Rolling Mills Industry is
the system of assessing Central Excise Duty on the basis of the installed capacity and not on actual production, though unique system for encouraging higher capacity utilisation and avoidance of excise-tax evasion, but considering the fact of recession and loss of competitive edge the
manufactures are compelled to reduce production well below their capacity but have to pay duty based on the full capacity- thus even meritorious system of taxation is proving a last nail in the coffin of Steel Industry, as exemplified with "State Rolling Mills at Arakkonam"; despite
the budgetary support and better infrastructure available to the unit, it had to be closed down.
            The Sub-Committee was made to understand that the Rolling Mills Industry has to come out of vicious circle through 'realistic and rational taxation system' commercially viable to Steel Industry with propelling forces of industrial survival and sustainability otherwise a sinking
steel industry may not be a prospective means of State revenue collections, for a longer period. In order to simplify the excise structure all anomalies in the compound excise levy should be removed and the Government may think reduce excise duty from 15% ad-valorem to 10% ad-
valorem. The Government should also undertake the, measures to revive deemed credit available to re-rollers on Government and re-rollable scrap.
            The Sub-Committee was made aware of the fact of state of discouragement to steel manufacturer to produce the captive power and compelling them to purchase the power from State Electricity Board. It was further requested that Government should make a high level
immediate & impartial inquiry into the matters. It was further required that the Government may        cross - examine the commercial viability of setting up of National Power Grid for centrally distribution of power for continued and rational supply of power from the surplus power
States to the state with power shortage at uniform tariff rates to put the steel industry in all states on equal footing.

Representation from Madras Steel Re-Rollers Association
            The Sub-Committee received representation from Madras Steel Re-Rollers Association which highlighted the pathetic scenario of secondary Steel Units in India in general and Tamil Nadu in particular as Central Government decided to withdraw a number of existing facilities
in a phased manner and imposed excise duty on a fixed basis.
            The representations highlighted the wide variation in electricity tariff structure among neighbouring states  and pleaded for Tariff Regulatory Committee to achieve uniform tariff rates.  Association also pleaded for a Technical Committee to calculate excise duty arrived at as
per the formula and fix actual production as basis of taxation.  The adoption of lower price for finished products for sale by primary producers are also causing concern to secondary steel sectors so the main producers should be permitted to sell only higher sections steel products like
25 mm plus Rounds, Tor and items like 65 10 mm plus structurals and rest should be left to secondary Steel Industries.  Moreover secondary producers should be permitted to supply to Government directly and the export policy should enable them to supply to the foreign markets,
besides making custom duty a tool of level playing field.  Association wanted further concessions for granting MODVAT benefit on the raw materials used in the excisable end products.
            Association wanted concession in Sales-Tax from State Government which is triple system 11% (4% + 2% + 4%) for the same product.  Moreover the rules of consignment sales outside the State should be allowed freely.
SALEM STEEL PLANT (SSP)
 
The Sub-Committee visited Salem Steel Plant, the youngest steel unit of SAIL, based upon the principle of reverse integration. At present SSP has two cold rolling Sendzimir Mills, state-of the art hot rolling Steckel Mill and a blanking line. The first stage of the plant

SPONGE   IRON INDIA LIMITED (SIIL)
 
            The Sub-Committee visited Sponge Iron India Limited (SUL), on 12.10.1998. and came across the problems and prospects of the first coal based Demonstration Sponge Iron Plant in South East Asia. Initially, SUL was incorporated as public Ltd. Company in March 1975 with
a capacity of 30,000 tonne per annum with UNDP/UNIDO assistance to establish the techno-economic feasibility of manufacturing Sponge iron suitable for steel making using indigenously available ores and non-coking coal. The rationale behind setting of SIIL was the problem of
avail-ability of coking coal and the fluctuating trends or availability of ferrous Scrap affecting the steel production in the country. Several improvement and modification were effected in the Sponge Iron Plant based on Rotary kiln process to suit the local raw-materials and operating
conditions paving the way for development of the Sponge Iron industry in the country. Being a Demonstration plant it is designed to be operated on a product and for R&D work. Government of India sanctioned in 1982 a second unit resulting into doubling the plant capacity from
30,000 tonne to 60,000 tonne per annum which went into regular production from October, 1985. The company has also successfully designed and built a plant for briquetting of Sponge Iron fines  and the briquette was commissioned during October, 1987 and is operating to capacity.
A new and innovative project aimed at conservation of energy was commissioned with effect from 1.3.93 for effectively utilising the sensible heat in the kiln off gases for generation of electric power. The SIIL has gone further for up scaling the  kiln' capacity and has developed
detailed design for larger kiln of 60000 to 75,000 tpa capacity. The sub-merged Are Furnace project with an installed capacity of 45,000 tpa has been set up by SIIL for smelting Sponge Iron into high quality pig iron.
            The authorised share capital of the company is Rs.40.00 crore as on 31.3.98 with paid up capital Rs.32.59 crore (Rs.31.75 crore held by Government of India and the balance of Rs.0.83 crore by the Government of Andhra Pradesh i.e. the order of 97% : 3%).
Meeting with workers of SIIL
The Sub-Committee interacted with the workers of SIIL who expressed deep thanks to the Sub-Committee as this was the first Parliamentary Committee to visit the languishing plant which is located at a far-flung place and is difficult to access. The Sub-Committee started the
interaction with highlighting the pivotal role of workers in the industrial development of the nation.
            The workers informed the Sub-Committee that prior to the liberalisation the plant's financial and economic performance was sound &. Made profit upto 1992-93, the highest of Rs.291 lakh being in 1992-93 but later on due to high cost of production and low realisation of price
of Sponge iron because of import of Sponge Iron at cheaper price, whereby, the plant proved internationally less competitive and therefore suffered net losses of Rs.245 lakhs in 1993-94 and 198 lakhs in 1994-95.
            The Workers highlighted cost assessment study made by Mis Kirlosker consultants - the maximum selling price that the quality of pig Iron proposed to be in the market is only Rs.7000/- per tonne. Whereas the actual cost of production works out to be Rs. 10,500/per tome and
the direct cost is itself Rs.8,500/- per tonne. The price remained the same but the      cost has gone up substantially for raw-materials and power.  The shortage of availability of power in the state involves a power cut to the extent of 60% and whenever power is available it cost is
Rs.3.25 per unit as against Rs.2.15 of project report. The workers informed the Sub-Committee that the power generation cost at the plant is Rs.1.80 and the plant gives the power to APSEB at the lower cost.
 
            The workers informed the Sub-committee about the drain of plants finance on the maintenance of CISF. The numbers of CISF are quite high & the plant has to incurr loss on account of stretched financial expenses. The Sub-Committee was requested to recommend for the
reduction of the expenses on the maintenance of CISF, particularly when the industry & plant are facing financial constraints.
            The Sub-Committee came across the problems of marketing of Sponge iron. The closure of M/s Andhra Pradesh steels limited, adjacent to SIIL consuming 40% of the total production of Sponge Iron, created the problem. With closure, SIIL has to search for raw materials
located outside Andhra Pradesh, incurring high transport cost resulting into scaling down of realisation. 
            Representatives from Sponge Employees & contract workers Unions expressed the hope to make the company profit-oriented by following measures.
1.
      Sanction of Rs.1.00 cores for Sponge Iron India Limited to increase the production capacity upto 1,20,000 TPA and to establish downstream Plants &. conversion of Rs.32 crore on Submerged Arc Furnace (SAF) into equity.
2.      Declaration of Steel Industry as infrastructure industry and imposition of 30% dumping duty on imported Scrap to provide protection for Sponge Iron industry.
3.      Removal of Central Sales Tax (CST) on the product of Public sector Sponge Iron Plant i.e. SIIL.
4.      Reduction of Excise Duty on Sponge Iron from 15% to 5% to promote DR-EAF technology.
5.      Provision of MODVAT facilities for Induction Furnace and Re-rolling mills to encourage Sponge Iron Consumption and save foreign exchange.
6.      To overcome the marketing problems of SIIL, Ministry of Steel, Government of India and the management of Vizag Steel Plant be convinced to take 20,000 ton Sponge each year
7.      Provide participation of workers in the Board in all public undertakings in general and SIIL in particularly for better results.
8.      Constitution of Tripartite committee on Sponge Iron Industry with the representation of management, Union and the Government to discuss the problems and to get solutions.
9.      Establishment of Independent Public Sector Development Fund with 50% amount of public sector disinvestments  for improving the public sector industries all over the country.
            The Sub-Committee was further appraised of the problems of SIIL arising out of locations of its registered office & technical Staff of registered office at Hyderabad are permitted to table work, so site office is losing the services of the technical officers. Moreover, as registered
office is a separate office establishment, expenditure on phone, Fax, Tours and other administrative expenses are very high causing additional financial burden on the company. Besides additional expenditure, the delay in decision making process is an added disadvantage, besides
creating communication dead lock.
            Representation on behalf of SIIL employees union, SIIL Supervisors Association, Sponge Iron Employee's and contract labour union and Sponge Iron employees and contract labour Union affiliated to INTUC, suggested the merger of SIIL with SAIL, approval of expansion
and down stream proposals, conversion of investment on SAF equity, shifting of registered office from Hyderabad to site-office for quick decision & reduction of expenditure and on the spot acquaintances of problems faced by SIIL. Moreover, price reduction measures on raw
materials through rational & consistent pricing policy on the part of NMDC & SCCL and commitment of Visakhapatnam Steel Plant to purchase 50% of production of SIIL are essential for substantial and profitable condition of the company. Moreover, Governmental initiative for the
resources of Central Sales Tax and reduction of excise duty on Sponge Iron; imposition of 25% dumping duty on imported scrap and withdrawal of CISF. The Sub-Committee expressed its happiness over harmonious  & cooperative relationship between Union and management with
high work culture & timely payment of salary.
Meeting with SIIL management
            The Sub-Committee met with the management of SIIL which informed the Sub-Committee that India stands second in the production of Sponge-Iron in the world after, Venezula. Sponge is a part substitute for ferrous scrap used by steel-melting electrical are furnaces, Steel
plant and indirect furnaces. In many western countries Electrical Steel melting process is based on Sponge-Iron. SIIL is the first plant in the world in which non-coking coal- is used as a reluctant.
            Being a pioneer in coal based Sponge Iron technology & because of its extensive expansion under actual operating condition in excellent laboratory facilities available at the plant SUL has given technology consultancy to five units in the private sector. On the global front the
company has undertaken several consultancy assignments for testing of new materials for various countries such as Niger, Pakistan, Zambia, Vietnam etc. for establishing the suitability of their raw materials for manufacturing of Sponge Iron. The company has given extensive
consultancy work covering supply of critical equipment, deputation of technician, imparting training for Vietnam Sponge Iron Plant under a UNDP/UNIDO assistance programme. It had entered into an agreement with Peruvian Steel Co. to provide technical assistance covering
equipment and commissioning services.
            The management talked about the conversion of the Sub-merged Arc Furnace (SAF) plant to take up  the  manufacture of  SILICO Manganese.  SAF installed at  actual cost of  Rs.23.90 crore  or manufacturing of Special grade Pig Iron could not be continued due to non
availability of required quantity of power at 4 MW and negative economic viability as the selling price presently prevailing in the market for the special grade pig iron was not covering the direct cost of production. At this junction M/s MN Dastur & Company advised that the existing
infrastructure with modification could take up the manufacture of SILICO Manganese at the cost of Rs.2.0 crore with projected installed capacity of 8700 t.p.a The modification of SAF is complete and ready for production of Silico Manganese.
            Despite the diversification of SAF plant for manufacture of Silico Manganese, SIIL's performance is not upto the expected performance due to low break-even point i.e. 7000 tonne at selling price -of Rs.7500/- per tonne. And as the income from consultancy continues to be
sporadic, the expansion of the existing installed capacity for manufacture of Sponge Iron is the only left Strategy for lasting stability and viability. ,k detailed technical analysis shows that the present capacity of 60,000 tonne be doubled to 1,20,000 tonne by installing one additional
kiln. of 60,000 tonne, at the total cost of Rs.46.95 crore. Due to high brand endowment, additional manpower available, sufficient layout and infrastructure, comparatively lower capital cost of new plant and additional power generation through the second captive power plant, the
strategic solution to the problem of SUL is the expansion of existing capacity.

            The authorised capital of NMDC as on 31.3.98 is Rs.150.00 crore with paid up capital of Rs. 132.16 crore; cumulative reserves and surplus Rs.591.55 crore & net worth of Rs.717.08 crore and there is no outstanding loan to be paid by the compa ny, so, NMDC is a zero debt -
