The Committee was further informed that the magnitude of NPAs and sickness in the 
SSI sector is comparatively large particularly in industries like engineering, textiles and 
chemicals. However the Bank of India have finalised rehabilitation package in viable units with 
the following strategies:-
(i) Arresting slippages by replacement/rescheduling/installments/interest in genuine 
cases affected due to natural calamities/project failure/delay in implementation 
etc. and for reasons beyond the control of the borrowers/entrepreneurs. 
(ii) Intensive drive for recoveries in doubtful accounts. 
(iii) Timely action for revival of units, right at incipient sickness stage and provide 
rehabilitation to such units. 
(iv) Re-examination of the units earlier identified as sick non-viable and to take 
appropriate rehabi I itation/recovery measures. 
Explaining the causes of NPA in the SSI sector the officials attributed to the delay in 
commissioning of projects leading to cost over-run, diversion of funds by small scale enterprises 
in other activities, non-payment of dues by large corporate/MNCs specially during recession 
leading to huge blockage of working capital funds and delay in providing second charge by 
SFCs/Fis. 
However the Bank of India has outlined area specific strategies to be adopted by 
zones/regions to achieve targets, set in SSI financing which inter-alia include identification of 
potential centers in zones for quantum development in SSI business and close monitoring of 
identified branches alongwith specilised SSI branches; arranging workshops/seminars to 
motivate specilised SSI branches and key branches having potential for SSI financing; 
enhancement of credit flow to tiny enterprises, artisans, village and cottage industries; exploring 
possibilities for take over of good rated accounts from other banks; timely review of existing 
accounts and considering additional need based limits to the borrowers; expeditious processing 
of proposals at all levels and quick disbursement of new limits; liaison with chamber of small 
Industries, Federation of Association of Small industries of India (F ASSI), NGOs and SHGs for 
prospective potential business; holding of SSI customers meets regularly by zonal managers 
with display of products of SSI units financed by Bank of India in the zones.

Maharashtra State Financial Corporation 
During the course of interaction the Committee came to know that Maharashtra State 
Financial Corporation (MSFC) was established in /\ugust 1962 under the enactment of State 
Financial Corporations Act, 1951 with the follm\ in g. ubjectives:-
(i) Function as development agency to promote and accelerate industrial growth in 
rural and backward areas of the State. 
(ii) Promote first generation entrepreneurs. 
(iii) Reduce socio-economic imbalance and create employment opportunities. 
The cumulative sanctions of the Corporation as at the end of March 2000 are Rs. 3312 
crores and cumulative disbursements of Rs.2380 crores. The share of the SSI sector in these 
cumulative sanctions works out to about 75% i.e. at around Rs.24 76.81 crores. Further, this 
assistance has created employment opportunities to about 14 lakhs persons. 
The Committee was informed that the initial developmental role played by the 
Corporation has now created certain situational weaknesses in the changed economic scenario. 
The following salient features of post-liberalisation era have largely affected financial position 
of this Corporation:-

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 
OF THE COMMITTEE 
The Committee is of the view that although Industry as a whole plays crucial role in the 
process of economic development, employment generation, equitable distribution of national 
income, mobilization of capital and entrepreneurial skills and contribution to export earnings of 
the country but SSI sector occupies an important position in the industrial economy of the 
country because of its advantages in terms of low investment, high potential for employment 
generation and wider dispersal of industries in rural and semi-urban areas. This sector offers a 
method of ensuring a more equitable distribution of national income and facilitates effective 
mobilization of resources of capital and skill which might otherwise remain unutilized. It 
further stimulates the growth of industrial entrepreneurship and promotes and diffuses the 
pattern of ownership and location. SSI sector is one. of the most vibrant and dynamic sectors of 
the Indian Economy. Over 40% of the gross turnover in manufacturing activities as also around 
35% of our exports, are contributed by SSI sector. In the area of employment generation, 
significant contribution is made by SSI sector which accounts for employment of over 1.6 crore 
workers. 
SSI sector has consistently displayed a high growth potential and employment 
generation capacity. Recognising SSI sector as a core area for growth and development of the 
Economy, the Government has from time to time taken steps to remove bottlenecks and pave the 
way for accelerating the growth of this sector by various measures, chief among them being 
streamlining the flow of Bank Credit to this sector. Public Sector Banks, on their part, have also 
made important contribution in ensuring that adequate fund flow is ensured to this sector. 
The SSI sector constitutes a major portion of the priority sector to which almost 40% of 
the bank credit is diverted. Even though no specific benchmarks are stipulated for SSI within the 
priority sector, it is ensured that out of total finance available to SSI sector 40% is granted for 
units with investment in plant and machinery. 
The Committee is happy to note that RBI has done commendable job for ensuring 
smooth credit flow to SSI sector . RBI has set up Nayak Committee in 1991 to deal with the 
aspects of adequacy and timeliness of credit to SSis and the same Committee submitted its 
report in September, 1992 with several recommendations which inter-alia include granting of 
working capital credit to SSI units computed on the basis of a minimum of 20% of their 
projected annual turnover ; giving preference to village industries, tiny industries and other 
small scale units while meeting credit requirement sector; extension of single Window 
Scheme of SIDBI to all districts; avoidance of delay in sanctioning and disbursement of 
credit to SSI sector; non-insistence on compulsory deposit as a quid-pro-quo for sanctioning 
the credit limit; opening of specialised branches; identification of sick units and urgent action 
to put them on the nursing programme; the standardized loan application forms to be used by SSI 
units; imparting of necessary training to Bank staff to handle the SSI clients. As a follow up 
of Nayak Committee recommendations , Finance Minister in the budget speech of 1995-96, 
announced seven point Action Plan for improving the flow of credit to small scale sector 
consisting of time bound action for setting up specialised SSI branches in 85 identified 
districts; at least 100 such dedicated branches to be opened before the end of 1995-96; Adequate 
delegation of powers at the branch and regional levels; Banks to conduct sample surveys of their 
performing SSI accounts to find out whether they are getting adequate credit; steps to be taken 
to see as far as possible that composite loans (covering both term loans and working capital) are 
sanctioned to SSI entrepreneurs; regular meeting by banks at zonal and regional levels with SSI 
entrepreneurs; need to sensitise bank managers and reorient them regarding working of the SSI 
51 

sector; simplification of procedural formalities by banks for SSI entrepreneurs. Accordingly, 
RBI issued instruction to banks for taking appropriate action for effective implementation of the 
seven point action plan and to keep their respective boards, apprised of the progress and also 
forward to RBI a copy of the note put up to the board. 
Concerned with the continuing problem on credit to SSI sector, RBI had set up a High 
Powered Committee in December, 1997 under the Chairmanship of Shri S.L. Kapur, Member, 
BIFR and former Secretary (SSI& ARI) to review the working of credit delivery system for 
SSis. The Committee submitted its report to RBI on 30
1
h June, 1998 and the same report contains 
126 recommendations and some of them are special treatment to smaller among small 
industries; enhancement in the quantum of composite loans; removal of procedural difficulties in 
the path of SSI advances; sorting out issues relating to mortgages of land including removal of 
stamp duty and permitting equitable mortgages; allowing access to low-cost funds to Small 
Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) for refinancing SSI loans; Non-obtention of 
collaterals for loans up to Rs.2 lakhs; setting up of a collateral reserve fund to provide support 
to first party guarantees; setting up of a Small Industries Infrastructure Development Fund for 
developing industrial areas in around metropolitan and urban areas; change in the definition of 
sick SSI units; giving statutory powers to State Level Inter Institutional Committee (SLIIC); 
setting up of a separate guarantee organization and opening of 1,000 additional specialised 
branches; and enhancement ofSIDBI'S role and status to match with that of national Bank for 
agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD). RBI has accepted 64 recommendations of 
Kapur Committee and advised banks to implement 48 of these recommendations. During the 
course of interaction with the officials and management of various commercial banks the 
Committee was informed that the public sector banks are conforming to the recommendations 
of Nayak Committee and Kapur Committee. 
The Standing Committee on Industry, while endorsing the recommendations of the 
Nayak Committee and Kapur Committee, opines that timely and adequate credit flow to SSI 
units is the need of hour for rapid industrialization and growth of the national economy. While 
a host of issues were raised during the three days meeting at Mumbai, however, at this juncture 
the Committee while taking note of various issues to deal with at appropriate time, decided 
to dwell upon only with the credit related issues. The Committee feels that the Government 
may act promptly on following issues for continued credit flow to SSI units:-
1. MEETING OF WORKING CAPITAL REQUIREMENT 
The Committee notes the recommendations of the Nayak Committee and Kapoor 
Committee and guidelines given by RBI on the issue of the availability of working capital credit 
to SSI and the Committee is pleased to note that Government is working in right direction 
to ensure the smooth credit flow to SSI Units but at the same time the Committee is 
constraint to express in concern over the "credit gap- situation" due to non-availability of 
sufficient working capital requirement . The Committee is unhappy to note that although the· 
SSI production increased by 3.4 times but the credit availability by the banks to the units 
increased by 2.9 times only. The sordid state of affair is that despite the fact of 
recommendations made by various Committees for providing 20% of working capital 
requirement and issuance of necessary guidelines by the RBI to improve the situation in this 
regard, the availability of working capital credit has not shown any significant improvement 
and the same is bottom I ined at 7-8% . Therefore the Committee recommends that steps 
should be taken to ensure credit facilitation to SSI units upto 20% ofSSI production/turnover. 
52 

2. SUSTAIN ABLE RATE OF INTEREST 
Since the SSI units have not only to compfie with medium and Large Scale units 
but also to compete with MNCs due to ongoing liberalization and globalisation process it is 
pertinent on the part of Government to render credit facilities to SSI units at sustainable and 
oompetitive rate. The general impression of SSI associations and entrepreneurs are that 
SSI units have been exposed to phantom MNCs units without taking into account the fact of 
comparatives competitive edge and resilience which is being nurtured and nourished by 
credit facilities. During the course of interaction with SSI association the Committee came 
across that while industrial units in other countries gets credit at the rate of 4-5% per 
annum but in India SSI units is getting loan at the rate of 12 to 13% per annum. The 
Committee understands the problems of commercial banks to extend credit to SSI units at 
such a low rate of interest. Since RBI has given autonomy to Commercial Banks to decide 
their respective rate of interest the Committee feels still there is scope for lowering of rate of 
interest to some extent. The Committee not only hopes that the Commercial Banks will lend 
credit to SSI units at sustainable rate of interest but hopes strongly that Government will 
chalk out adequate measure. Incentive to induce commercial banks for extending loan at 
sustainable rate of interest. 
3. JOINT MECHANISM FOR APPRISING TERM LOANS AND WORKING 
CAPITAL 
The Committee came to know that there is no single agency for lending the term loan and 
\Vorking capital to SSI units requirement exceeding Rs 10 lakhs which leaves the SSI 
entrepreneurs to run from pillar to post. Under the circumstances, the Committee feels that 
situation may improve a lot if there is a mechanism for joint appraisal of term lending and 
working capital loan for higher amount ( about Rs.l 0 lakhs) so that there is no gap in the sanction 
of two types of loans. The measures, if undertaken, not only will save the time but also the 
money of SSI entrepreneurs, the Committee feels. 
4. WIDER ACCESS TO BANK FINANCE 
The Committee is at loss to note that only 15 to 20 percent of SSI units have access to 
Bank finance and the same findings was highlighted by a study conducted by the office of the 
DC (SSI) and Kapur Committee which caste a shadow over the credit facilities available to SSI 
Units in the country. The Committee feels that narrow access to bank finance are due to 
cumbersome procedure to access bank finance and the comprehensive conditions prescribed by 
the bank. Whatever the case may be, prevailing access to Bank finance seems to be 
narrow which must have been affecting the productivity of units engaged in SSI activities. 
Therefore, it is indispensable for credit facilitation to make adequate in conducive 
atmosphere for accessing bank finance. The Committee feels that the Government should 
undertake following measures for enabling SSI units to have access to bank finance::-
(ii) Undertaking of orientation course and adequate training for staff/officers of 
commercial banks for a change in the attitude for lending to SSI sector; 
(ii) Simplification of procedures for obtaining credit from Banks. Arrangement 
may be made for land mortgage instead of stamp duty for enabling SSI units to 
obtain credit from bank against land mortgage ; 
(iii) Government should create conducive climate for development of factoring 
services through appropriate policy prescription/legislative changes to ease 
the problems relating to stamp duty, registration for, assignment of Def'artment. 
53 

(iv) Recapitalisation and revamping of State Financial Corporation (SFCs) with the 
help ofSIDBI and lOBI enabling SFCs to lend fixed capital to SSI units; 
(v) Since Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) are most widespread with branches 
even in rural areas so well-performing RRBs may be encouraged to lend term 
loan and working capital to SSI units. 
5. POPULARISATIONOF VENTURE CAPITALFUND 
The Committee observes that assistance under venture capital fund has assumed 
importance as the liberalized regime has opened the door for a large number of 
entrepreneurs to embark upon setting up of ventures with innovative technologies and their 
commercial applications being a high-risk-high-return profile. In this regard the Committee 
would like to congratulate SlOB I for being the first financial institutions to set up a Rs.l 00 
crore National Venture Fund as a three tier strategy for development of SSis in software/IT 
industry (NFSIT) in collaboration with Ministry of Information Technology and Government 
of India. The Committee feels that the Commercial Banks should come forward in launching 
venture capital funds in all its comprehensiveness so as to effectively integrate and enhance the 
opportunities for Small Scale Industries in domestic and international market. The banks 
should endeavour to set up more and more such venture capital fund not only in software/IT 
industry but also for high growth sectors such as bio-technology and food processing. 
6. SETTING UP OF TECHNOLOGY UPGRADATION AND DEVELOPMENT 
BANKS 
The Committee observes that of obsolescence of Technology is one of the major 
problems of Small Scale Industries which has not only affected the manufacturing system and 
quality standard but also the economies of scale. Although SIDBI has come forward with 
technology development and Modernisation Fund (TDMF) Scheme in order to assist SSis at its 
prime lending rates but the Committee, taking into account the magnitude of the problem of 
technological obsolescence in SSI sector, feels that Government should come forward to set 
up Technology Upgradation and Development Banks to take stock of ground realities of 
sickness of SSI units due to obsolescence of technology and assist the units by ensuring 
credit facilitation at appropriate time and thus save the sick but potentially viable SSI units 
before dying out. 
7. EXTENSION OF NON-FINANCIAL SERVICES 
The Committee is of the view that banks have to take on a proactive role in extending 
non-financial services in the areas of technology upgradation, management training, skills 
upgradation, quality improvement, environment management, information about markets, 
regulations and clients, etc. Commercial banks and SFCs can study the package of non-financial 
services offered by the Business Development Bank of Canada (BDC), SIDBI etc., and adopt 
them with such modifications as are considered appropriate. The Committee is of the view that a 
loan application should be given along with "Small Business Growth Kit" with a guide to prepare 
business plans and a series of financial ratio calculators followed by a free consulting session of 
personalized solutions to meet the needs of small and medium sized business at every stage in 
their development including export solutions and quality solutions. Moreover, banks should come 
forward for finding foreign buyers by identifying possible export markets, undertaking market 
research projects, identifying the barriers to entry and to promote products to trade fairs and 
foreign missions. Financial Institution should also facilitate the product for the foreign market and 
outlining the national logistics such as transportation, shipping, insurance and documentation and 
developing the network of physical distribution of the product besides arranging to provide the 
legal and accounting service in the target market. Not only this, financial institution should also 
54 

provide assistance to small scale entrepreneurs in risk management by obtaining credit 
information on foreign buyers. helping insurance against commercial and political risk of non­
payment. helping finance foreign receivable and providing assistance when the small business has 
to issue a bond or a performance guarantee. That is to say, banks need to play the role of a friend, 
philosopher and guide to their SSI clients. 
8. PRIME MINISTER'S ANNOUNCEMENT OF PACKAGE FOR SSI SECTOR 
The Committee observes that the Government is really serious about removing the 
problem . specially credit related, of SSI Sector . The Committee feels that the Composite 
Loans Scheme wherein the loan limit has been raised from Rs.l 0 lakh to Rs.25 lakhs will go a 
long way in meeting the credit requirements of tiny units through single financing agency. 
Similarly, the enhancement in investment limit. of industry related services and business 
enterprises from Rs.S lakhs to Rs.l 0 lakhs will enable large number of enterprises to have 
access to priority sector credit. Moreover the Committee is happy to note that the Government 
is taking required steps for technology upgradation and therefore announced a Capital subsidy 
of 12% for investment in technology upgradation. Presently, the Government has given the 
capital subsidy in select sectors. The Committee feels that the Ministry of SSI and A&RI 
should examine whether such capital subsidy is required in other sectors of SSI for technology 
upgradation and if so, the Ministry should take up the issue at the appropriate level. The 
Committee is happy to observe the enhancement of project limit under National Equity Fund 
of SIDBI from Rs. 25 lakhs to Rs.SO lakhs which will further help the tiny sector because 30% 
of investment under NEF Scheme has been bracketed for tiny sector . The Committee is 
also pleased to observe the announcement of Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme, operated by 
Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Small Industries (GIS!) jointly set up by the Government of 
India and SIDBI, with the corpus of Rs.125 crore (contributed Rs.l 00 crores by 
Government of India and Rs.25 crores by SIDBI) and hopes that SSI units will have access to 
bank credit without collateral fee and third party guarantee. 
The Committee would like to extend its congratulation to SIDBI & NSIC for their 
continuance to give concessional rate of refinance/finance to tiny sectors. The Committee 
feels that Government would take urgent steps to revitalize/restructure State Finance 
Corporation enabling them to lend term loan to SSI units. The Committee also hopes that RBI 
would take concrete steps to strengthen and popularize factoring services to encourage bill 
culture in order to remove the problems of delayed payment ofSSI units. Once the problem of 
delayed payment is solved SSI units would be in a better position to recycle their profit into 
capital and in a way solve the problem • of working capital, the Committee feels . The 
Committee further observes that since sickness of SSI units is a chronic problem, a serious 
thought and timely action is required for rehabilitation of currently sick but potentially viable 
SSI units . The Committee hopes that RBI will be successful in its current efforts to draw a 
detailed , transparent and non-discretionary guidelines and same will be issued for effective 
implementation before the sick but potentially viable SSI units go beyond the point of no 
return. 
The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Government and feels that 
policy/package which have been envisaged/extending to SSI sector will not suffer the problem 
of implementation gap. While appreciating the steps taken by the Government to ensure the 
smooth credit flow to SSI sector, the Committee hopes that all the policy and programme 
will see the light of the day and the Government and its machinery should be equally 
enthusiastic in implementing the package . In this regard the Committee recommends that 
the Ministry of SSI and A&RI while furnishing the Action Taken Note on the 
recommendations contained in the present Report will give detailed note with regard to 
55 

Action taken and its impact of each and every scheme under the present package for SSI 
units. 
9. SHRIMAHILAGRIHUDYOG LIJJAT PAPAD

th July, 2000  to have interaction with the workers
and the Management on the problems being faced by this PSU.  The Sub-Committee was taken around its factory at

products,technical know-how, existing manpower, its contribution to various sections of  the economy etc. While 
interacting   with the   representatives   of the workers’ union andthe Management, the following points emerged during
the course of the discussion :-
 
Points raised by the Workers’ representatives
 
1.
                  Sub-Committee was informed that the restructuring   of the   Company has been pending  since  1991
due to  various conditions imposed by the  Ministry of Finance.
 
2.
                  The workers expressed their  view that workers to officers ratio in the Company is inappropriate.  There 
should be  parity in the  ratio.
 
3.
                  The Government has adopted a  lackadaisical approach  in  releasing  the  required funds under its
restructuring plans  even after the submission of  the worker’s demands  on 8th April 2000  which  is still 
pending with  the Government.
 
4.         The Company is facing lack of work-orders  which has resulted  in  some of the work-force  sitting idle .
 
5.         Revival  package  needs  to be implemented  seriously & expeditiously.
 
6.         The  Company needs to be  modernised  with the latest  technology so as to   face  the private sector in
the field.
 
Points raised by the Management
 
1.
                  The Management reiterated their demand for exploring financial restructuring of the Company and
urged the Sub-Committee to release the adequate funds under  restructuring plans of the Company.

OBSERVATIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS
 
 
            As is evident from the subject of study assigned to the Sub-Committee, it was required to review the
performance of Central Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) under the administrative domain of the Department of
Heavy Industry, Ministry of Heavy Industries  and Public Enterprises.  Accordingly,  the Sub-Committee embarked
upon the most talked issue, namely, the performance of the Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs)  in the changed scenario
of the Indian economy.  The Sub-Committee, while having interaction with the Workers and Management of select 6
subsidiary companies  of the Holding Company, i.e.,  Bharat Yantra Nigam Ltd. (BYNL), had an opportunity to analyse
the factors responsible for the present state of decline of some of these PSUs.  These PSUs, for long, had lived under a
protective regime and the opening up of the economy had meant opening of floodgates of unforeseen  problems for
some of them.  Transmission from a closed economy to a free economy has caught them and exposed their
vulnerability.  There is a host of reasons which culminated into present crisis.  State protection can no longer be there to
shield them against the onslaught unleashed by  their rivals in the present competitive and consumer-oriented market.  
It is apparent that the present crisis in some of these PSUs  is a simple case of gross managerial inefficiency and sheer
lack of  foresightedness on the part of those who have been at the helm of affairs. 
 
The first major problem, which warrants the attention of this Sub-Committee, is the delay in approval of the
restructuring of the subsidiary companies of BYNL .  It is felt that Department of Industry, Ministry of Heavy
Industries  and Public Enterprises seems to have a very indifferent approach towards the preparation, approval and
implementation of the restructuring packages for these subsidiary companies.
 
The Sub-Committee feels that any delay on the whole process involving the restructuring of a Company smacks
of lack of commitment  on the part of the Government.  Therefore, the Sub-Committee recommends that the Department
of Heavy Industry , Ministry of Heavy Industries  and Public Enterprises, should make conscious  efforts to help these
subsidiary companies by approval , timely preparation, and implementation of their restructuring- packages.

44th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/44threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:12:21]
 
            The issue of  timely payment of arrears and strategy to reduce  the employees of these subsidiary companies
merit the Sub-Committee’s serious consideration as it has a direct bearing on the well-being of thousands of employees.
For years together, there has been no wage revision in some of these  PSUs as a result of which the moral of the
employees has touched its  nadir.  Some of these PSUs have  also defaulted in the payment of  statutory dues  like
gratuity, PF, etc. of the employees because of shortage of funds.  The argument advanced by the Government  for non-
payment of wage etc. was that the responsibility of payment to employees lies with the  companies  themselves and the
issue is being examined by a Group of Ministers. 
 
            The whole issue is a sensitive one and it affects the employees in various ways.  The Sub-Committee, therefore,
recommends that arrears and statutory  dues  should be paid  to the employees forthwith by earmarking separate funds
for this purpose .  The Ministry merely becoming a helpless spectator  in the matter  by saying that the matter is being
examined by a Group of Ministers does not end the responsibility of the Administrative Ministry. The Ministry  should
own the responsibility in this regard and take up  the matter  seriously with the Government at appropriate forum for the
release of  funds for the payments of wage arrears, statutory dues, etc. by arranging some separate fund for the purpose,
if necessary,  in conjunction with other Ministries  whose  PSUs are also not able to pay  salaries to their employees.
During the visit of the Committee to various subsidiaries companies it was found that there was not enough work
order with these subsidiaries as a result of  which  the entire  activities of  these subsidiary companies may come to a
grinding halt at any moment.
 
            The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Heavy Industry, Ministry of Heavy Industries
and Public Enterprises, should   take up the matter with the Union Cabinet and necessary instructions should be  issued
for those customer-PSUs and Departments for placing adequate orders on these  subsidiaries of  BYNL.
 
 Many subsidiaries are having excess manpower that has proved a handicap to function in the post liberalization
era . Although planned rationalization of manpower by offering attractive packages   could solve the problem,  the flow
of funds for the implementation of  Voluntary Retirement Schemes  (VRS)  still remains far below the required mark. 
The Sub-Committee, therefore, recommends that  wherever the  planed VRS can facilitate a firm ground , the
Government should make requisite financial support available to that particular  PSU  without delay.
 
 During the interaction with the Officials of the customer PSUs/ concerned Departments of these  PSUs the Sub-
Committee was informed that the delivery record of these PSUs is very poor. The Sub-Committee, therefore, 
recommends the need for timely execution of orders / projects in order to avoid subsequent delay in completion of the
projects of the customer PSUs / Departments as it ,in turn, helps them to avoid cost and time over-runs.  The Sub-
Committee, therefore, recommends that all PSUs should evolve a proper workable mechanism to meet the deadline for
supply of orders.  The Sub-Committee further recommends that in case the delivery is before the deadline, there should
be some provision for rewarding the supplier PSU in some form.
 
Through the interaction with various PSUs it also came to the notice of the Sub-Committee that fair amount of
money of various PSUs is locked-up with the State Government Agencies like State Electricity Board, Power houses,
State Irrigation Department, State PSUs, etc.  As a result the Company is not able to make payments to their suppliers
and it is also not in a position to pay  monthly wages to their employees.  The Sub-Committee is perplexed to see such a
helpless situation.  The Sub-Committee , therefore, recommends that the Department of Heavy Industry should take up
the matter with the State Governments for release of such dues .Otherwise, in the alternative , they should take up the
matter with the Planning Commission and inform them the details of dues yet to be released by the State Government
agencies and to impress upon the Planning Commission to consider this aspect before  allocation of funds to the State
Governments.       It has also come to the notice of the Sub-Committee that earlier these PSUs were getting orders from
the State Government Agencies but now the State Governments have started  placing their orders with their own PSUs
or any other private agencies for its requirements. The Sub-Committee feels that like the Central PSUs which are giving
some purchase preference to the Central PSUs, the State Government may also be requested to give some purchase
preference to the Central PSUs and the Central PSUs may also give  some purchase  preference to the State PSUs.  The
placement of work-orders   by State PSUs  to Central PSUs  and vice-versa will take Government PSUs  a long way in 
post  liberalization period  which will  usher in a  new chapter in the   relationship between the Central and State
Governments.

BRIDGE AND ROOF COMPANY(INDIA) LTD.
 
1.         The capital-restructuring proposal of Bridge and Roof Company  has been pending since 1991. The Capital
restructuring proposals of Rs.42.57 crores  has already been submitted to the Government.  However,  proposal  has not
been approved   by the Government   till date.  This inexplicable delay in the approval of the proposal is coming in the
way of the companies’ efforts to borrow from the open market to meet the total capital requirement. 
The Sub-Committee has taken a serious note of this undue delay and recommend that capital restructuring of the
Company should be approved by the Government at the earliest.
  2.       Bridge and Roof Company  was  awarded  a contract for `Design, engineering, supply, installation and
commissioning of storage facility at four locations,viz., Thankot, Amlekhgunj, Kathmandu and Pokhara in Nepal, by
Nepal Oil Corporation Limited (A Nepal Government Undertaking) valued at Rs. 17.77  cores in March, 1994. Out of
four sites works at three sites have been completed and Fuel has been stored in all the Tanks.  The work was
accomplished despite a lot of constraints and delay faced by Bridge and Roof Company  due to reasons beyond the
Company’s control . Fourth terminal at Pokhara has been abandoned/foreclosed by NOC on their  own due to local
villagers’ problem/land  dispute.
 
            Since commissioning of the storage facilities built by B&R NOC has been using  three  terminals for storage of
Fuel and other purposes, formally taken over the sites and issuing  substantial completion certificate as  per the  contract
condition.  They have also not  taken-over the fourth terminal at Pokhara though they have foreclosed the same. NOC
are not paying dues of approximately Rs.12.90 crores comprising schedule bills, extra work bills, escalation bills and
claim.
 
            Due to above situation, B&R’s Bank-Guarantees towards (a) Mobilisation Advance ((Rs.2.69 crores) and (b)
Performance Guarantee (Rs.3.54 crores) are blocked. As a result this, Bank-Guarantees have to  be extended a number
of times draining Rs.30 lakhs annually due to bank charges only. Consequently, Bridge and Roof Company  has to
perforce maintain the establishment at Nepal since they can not abandon the project unless the terminals are formally
taken over by NOC.  This involves  recurring expenditure around Rs.6 lakhs per month.  If Bridge and Roof Company 
do not continue to extend the   Bank-Guarantees  as demanded by NOC or decide to leave the project now, NOC is
likely  to encash  Bank-Guarantees and foreclosed  outstanding- payments.
The Sub-Committee, therefore, recommends that Department of Heavy Industry should used the Good Offices
of the Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of External Affairs to help release of payments by Nepal Oil Corporation to
Bridge & Roof Company.

3.
 
RECOMMENDATION
 
                        Closely linked with it is the disturbing fact of which the Sub-Committee has taken a serious note,
is the inexplicable dithering on the part of the Department of Heavy Industry when it comes to supporting the
revival package of a sick company. The Sub-Committee came across a number of cases wherein the Department
backed out at the eleventh hour in the proceedings of the BIFR by expressing its inability to support the revival
plan of a PSU referred to the BIFR.  This ambivalence in the approach of the    Department leads the Sub-
Committee to conclude that  it has acted like a fair weather friend with an ulterior motive to ultimately wash its
hands off those PSUs who are  in the moribund state.
               The Sub-Committee, therefore, recommends to the Department of  Heavy  Industry  to  take the revival
packages of the sick PSUs to their logical  conclusion  by  assuring  the  BIFR  of providing full financial
backing to any such revival plan.
 
COMMENTS
 
               Govt. is committed to the revival of sick PSUs, if a credible and viable revival plan emerges. 27 sick
PSEs under DHI have been referred to BIFR. Rehabilitation schemes have     been sanctioned by BIFR in the
case of 12 PSEs which are under implementation for which Govt. have provided fresh infusion of funds to the
extent of Rs.637 crores and financial restructuring of Rs.2063 crores. No time is lost in release of funds and
issue of necessary sanctions for conversion of loans into equity etc. once a BIFR revival package is sanctioned.
 
FURTHER COMMENTS
 
         A list indicating the name of PSUs and their date of reference to BIFR is given at Annexure-I.
 
         In the case of 8 PSUs, the revival plans are awaiting recommendations of BIFR.  Govt. has been
extending financial assistance for meeting working capital requirements including  payment of salary and wages
and for Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS)  to these PSUs besides funds for investments under plan..  Details
of  assistance provided by the Govt. during  the years 1998-99, 1999-2000 & 2000-01 (upto 31.1.2001) in case
of these 8 PSUs, and their  present status are given at Annexure - II.

               The  issue of non-payment of arrears and statutory dues of the  employees  of  these  PSUs  merits  this 
Sub-Committee's serious  consideration  as  it  has  a  direct  bearing on the well-being of thousands of
employees.  For  years  altogether, there has  been  no wage revision in some of these PSUs.  As a result, the
morale of the employees has touched its nadir with a clear reflection on their productivity and motivation. This
apart, a majority of these PSUs have  also  defaulted  in  the payment  of statutory dues like gratuity, provident
fund, etc. of the employees.  In some cases where the wage  revision  has been  effected, employees have not
been paid arrears for long.                
               The whole issue is a sensitive one as it affects the employees in different  ways.    Hence,  the  Sub-
Committee  has taken a sympathetic note of it. Accordingly, the Sub-Committee recommends that arrears and
statutory dues of the employees should be  paid  forthwith  by earmarking separate  funds  for the purpose.  A

RECOMMENDATION
 
              As described elsewhere in this Report, these  PSUs  have  long been nurtured  in the shadow of state
protectionism.  With the change in the overall industrial economic scenario, they  have become the  victims  of
circumstances.  There was a time, when they did not have to toil hard to  get  work  orders  to  keep their
workshops running as they were assured of regular orders from their  customer  PSUs/Departments.   Things  
are no  longer   the   same  as   they  once  used to be.  Hence, the present critical order book position. Now,
these PSUs are not only facing stiff  challenge  from the  indigenous  private  sector  companies  but also from
the multinationals.    The   change-over   from   the   days    of `no-competition' to an era of `fierce competition'
is the bane of all the woes of these PSUs. That is why, this Sub-Committee strongly feels that these PSUs
deserve a  thoughtful  consideration.  Any attempt to downplay their importance could  have  serious 
ramifications  for  all concerned.   In  the  opinion of the Sub-Committee, these PSUs should be given enough 
elbow  room  to  adapt  themselves  in accordance with  the  new realities.  For this, they need some degree of
protection by way of reserving a fixed percentage of work orders of the  customer  PSUs/Departments  for  at 
least another  four  to  five  years  so  that they are able to grow enough teeth to take on their rivals.
 
               Therefore,   the   Sub-Committee   recommends   that   the Department  of  Heavy  Industry  should 
prepare  a   detailed PSU-wise  note  giving  each  company's order book requirement from the customer PSUs
and the Departments of the  Government. Any  such  note,  then  be placed before the Union Cabinet for  
having   necessary instructions issued for  all  those  customer  PSUs and Departments for placing adequate
orders on these PSUs of the  Department of Heavy Industry.  The Sub-Committee hopes that Department of
Heavy Industry would not be  found  wanting in its endeavour to pursue this line of action vigorously.

RECOMMENDATION
 
               During the course of its study, the Sub-Committee had a close look at the managerial aspect of these
PSUs and the need for granting functional  autonomy  to  them.  It was informed that lack of  professionalism 
amongst  the  Management  is  mainly responsible for  the  sickness  of  these  companies.    Inept handling of
the affairs has brought these PSUs to such a pass. Lack of functional  autonomy  also  aggravated  the  state  of
affairs. Therefore,  in  the  opinion of  the Sub-Committee, the need of the hour is to appoint full-time and
seasoned professionals to run the affairs of these companies and  give  them  greater functional  autonomy  to
enable them to deal with new emerging challenges with boldness and in a professional manner. At the same
time, Government should also find out, apart from the extraneous reasons, the administrative and managerial
failure in respect of these PSUs and fix accountability and responsibility.
 
 
COMMENTS
 
               Govt. has been giving more and more functional autonomy to PSUs to enable them work on
commercial lines and improve their viability. In the past 696 Govt. guidelines which were applicable for Central
PSUs have been scrapped. Greater autonomy is being given for MOU signing companies. Some of the
companies have been identified as Navratnas  (BHEL) and Mini-ratnas (HNL, HMT (I) and REIL) which entitle
them to additional autonomy in the area of investments, personnel policies, raising capital from domestic and
international markets and entering into joint ventures etc. So far as accountability is concerned, the Chief
Executives are being appraised with reference to objective parameters of performance and efficiency that takes
into account achievements of various targets, control over the organization etc.
 
 
FURTHER COMMENTS
 
               During the last three years no additional autonomy has been given to the MOU signing companies in
the area of capital investments, personnel policies, raising capital from domestic and international market and
entering into joint venture, etc.

RECOMMENDATION
 
               Rationalisation of  excessive  manpower  is  another  area  of concern for these PSUs.  As stated earlier,
one of the motives behind  these  companies,  being  in the public sector as they are,  was  to   generate  
adequate   number   of   employment opportunities   for  the  growing  populace  of  the  country. Accordingly, it
was in  the  fitness  of  things  to  adopt  a liberal recruitment  policy.   However, the negative result of  this
liberal policy began to be felt with the onset of economic liberalisation which caused depletion of  profit as it
was now beyond the reach of these PSUs to sustain their large workforce.  In case of a number of these PSUs,
the presence of excessive manpower is proving  to  be  a major  stumbling  block  in their attempt to regain their

RECOMMENDATION
 
Of these problems, one major problem whose tentacles are spread over just about every PSU, is the loans
given to them by the Government.  Conversion of these loans into equity would not only  reduce  the  burden of
debt and the interest  accrued on it but would also enable these beleaguered PSUs  to embark on  a  major 
financial  restructuring.  Besides, these companies will be in a position to get commercial borrowings to meet
their immediate requirement for working capital. It  is,   therefore,   the   considered   view   of  this Sub-
Committee that the Department  of  Heavy  Industry  should prepare a comprehensive  financial restructuring
package for all these PSUs so that they  are  able  to  bounce  back  with vigour and  vitality.  This package
should also address itself to the interest accrued on the loans, as  mere  conversion  of loan into equity would not
serve any meaningful purpose in the absence of waiver of interest.
 
 
COMMENTS
 
The financial restructuring proposals include write-off by the Govt. for interest/loan, fresh infusion of
funds, Govt. guarantees apart from conversion of loan into equity/debenture. These proposals are formulated and
approved after careful consideration by various agencies. Amongst the BIFR referred companies, revival plans
have been sanctioned by BIFR in case of 12 PSUs. In these cases write off of interest/loan is to Rs.1616 crs. And
conversion of loan into equity/debenture amounts to Rs.447 cr. In addition revival plans include fresh infusion of
funds of Rs.637 crs. and Govt. guarantees for Rs.625 crs. Details are attached at Annexure-VII.

RECOMMENDATION
 
                        During its interaction with the officials  of  customer  PSUs/ Departments of these PSUs, the Sub-
Committee was informed that the delivery   record  of  these  PSUs  is  very  poor.    The  Sub-Committee
recognises the  need  for  timely  execution  of orders    in    order   to   avoid   the    subsequent   delay    in    the
completion of the projects of the customer PSUs departments as it, in turn, helps them to avoid cost and time
over-runs. The Sub-Committee has  come  to the   conclusion that delivery track record  of  these  PSUs  is  not 
very satisfactory and requires a major improvement.   Therefore,  the  Sub-Committee recommends that all these
PSUs should evolve a proper workable mechanism  to  meet  the  deadlines  for  the supply of orders placed on 
them.    Accountability   should   be   fixed   for non-adherence to the delivery schedules.          
 
 
COMMENTS
 
               All the PSUs under DHI are being advised to evolve a proper workable mechanism to meet the
deadlines for the supply of orders placed on them and fix accountability for non-adherence to the delivery
schedules. This seems to be showing results in a few cases like HEC where the delay percentage has been
brought down from 55% to 20% during the year 1999-2000.
 
 
FURTHER COMMENTS
 
PSUs under the Department of Heavy Industry are engaged in manufacture of large number of products
ranging from heavy machinery, with manufacturing cycle of 2-3 years, to manufacture of consumer goods like
paper, cement etc which have a small manufacturing cycle and are mostly supplied off the shelf. Collection of
data for delivery schedules for all the products will be voluminous and time consuming. In-order to appreciate
the problem of delays in delivery schedules the PSUs are being asked to furnish information on contractual and
actual deliveries for equipment / services with a value of Rs.5 Cr. and above. Information on these lines is being
collected and will be placed before the committee shortly.

RECOMMENDATION
 
               One such company which has successfully withstood the changes brought about by the liberalisation of
Indian economy. The impressive track record of it calls for a special mention of its achievements. As a matter of
fact, BHEL is a role model for other PSUs of Ministry of Heavy Industry. For, it has managed to stay in the race
despite the odds faced by it as a result of stiff competition unleashed by the multinational giants operating in its
field of  specialisation namely, manufacture of power plants. Though, BHEL has managed to sustain its viability
yet it is facing some unfair challenges. The absence of a level playing field vis-à-vis its multinational
competitors has been posing stiff challenges to the company. This is leading to an ever increasing pressure on
the profitability of  it. Despite this, the company has been constantly upgrading its technology and has also been
successful in acquiring state of the art technology used in HVDC power projects. This reflects the commitment
of the company as a whole to serve the nation even when the odds are stacked against it. Therefore, what this
company requires is little help from the Government in the form of suitable policy measures. In this regard, the
Sub-Committee draws the attention of the Government to the issues of price and purchase preference to BHEL,
and import duty concessions to the foreign companies. Though, in some cases price and purchase preference is
granted to the PSUs, the positive results of this measure are negated by the import duty concessions extended to
the foreign companies by the Government. These concessions and exemptions are precisely the reasons for the
playing field not being level for domestic companies or for that matter PSUs as the bids offered by foreign
players are much lower in comparison to the ones offered by PSUs. In other words, the competition is killed well
before it begins. The Sub-Committee believes that the need of the hour is not to go back to the days of
protectionism rather to provide a level playing field to all the players for the sake of  healthy competition.
 
               In view of the above, the Sub-Committee has come to the conclusion that the Government should take
necessary policy measures to extend 15%  price and purchase preference to BHEL vis-à-vis its bids for domestic
power projects. It also recommends that the Government should review its policy of giving duty concessions to
the foreign companies inasmuch as it leads to disadvantages to the domestic companies especially the PSUs. It is
the considered view of the Sub-Committee that foreign companies should not be shown favour at the expense of
domestic companies.
 
 
COMMENTS

Commerce:-

1999-2000;

funded projects irrespective of the rate of customs duty;
 
Alternatively…
      Equipment  imports in the case of projects funded by UN/World Bank/ADB should attract customs duty
of at least 15%.

2.         At the outset, the Convenor welcomed the Members of the Sub-Committee and apprised them about the Action
Taken Note (ATN) received from the  Ministry  of  Heavy  Industries and Public Enterprises on the recommendations 
of the 36th Report on PSUs of  Heavy Industry – Disinvestment, Sickness and  Revival  to be taken up in the meeting.
 
3.         The Convenor requested the members present in the meeting to express their views on the Action Taken Note
and the pathetic condition of some of the Public Sector Enterprises  under the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public
Enterprises.   One member  inquired about the fate of the revival plan  of  Bharat Ophthalmic Glass Ltd. (BOGL) 
submitted  by the Operating Agency to BIFR.   He asserted that  some of the arrangements should be made to infuse
funds in BOGL  and implement  VRS in the company so as to enable the company to come out of the financial crisis.
In this regard,  The  Director, Rajya Sabha Secretariat, stated that as per the latest information received from the
Ministry  the revival scheme recommended by the expert group has been forwarded to  the BIFR  and the operating
agency for the preparation of Draft Rehabilitation Scheme which was yet to be finalized by BIFR.
 
4.         The Member  further inquired about the Burn Standard Co. Ltd.,   Mining & Allied Machinery Corp. Ltd.
(MAMC)  and  Andrew Yule & Company  (AYCL).  He asked   whether   the funds   sanctioned  for the revival plans  
were   really being  used for  the purpose ?     He further asked  whether  there was  any provision   in the   Central 
Budget  for  2001-2002,  for  VRS  being introduced in  MAMC  and   AYCL. The  Director of the Secretariat  stated
that in the budget  there was no provision of grants for VRS  in respect of   MAMC and  Burn  Standard
 
Co. Ltd.  He stated that as per the latest information available from the Ministry it has been decided   to  close  
MAMC     which     has     been    considered    unviable   after    considering 
recommendations of the Expert Group  set up to explore the possibilities of revival. Regarding  Andrew Yule &
Company, he disclosed that it was making  profits after the implementation of the  revival plan. The Balance Sheet of  
the company indicates that in the coming days it would be one of the blue chip  companies. He further revealed that
whether revival plans are implemented in accordance with the guidelines was a responsibility of the Ministry.  He,
however, promised to write to the ministry requesting them to furnish the latest status of these companies.
 
5.         Another Member sought to know  the budgetary provision for Scooter India Ltd. The Director of the
Secretariat  giving  details of the budgetary provision stated that there was  no provision for VRS for the company.
Further, he revealed that an amount of Rs.8.00 crore have been allocated for the plan investment for the company. Shri 
Manjay Lal inquired about the status of Hindustan Engineering Corporation  (HEC) and the budgetary provisions
therefor. In this connection  it was explained  that the company had been referred to BIFR which, in turn, has directed
for the appointment of consultants for preparing feasibility study for revival of the company. He further added that
Rs.36.74 crores and Rs.22.92 crores have been allocated to the company as interest subsidy and non-plan loans
respectively in BE 2001-02  to enable  the company come out of financial crisis.
 
6.         The Convenor of the Sub-Committee informed  the members present that the Department of
Telecommunications (DoT) had promised to give atleast 10% work orders to Hindustan Cables Ltd. (HCL). Regarding
Bridge & Roof Company Ltd. (B&R) he said that the company had started earning profits after the implementation of
revival plan.
 
7.         The Convenor then requested the Members to send their suggestions, if any, on the Action Taken Note in two-
three days so that the Action Taken Report could be finalized. The Sub-Committee, thereafter, authorized the
Convenor to finalise the Action Taken Report and forward the same  to the Main Committee for consideration and
adoption.
 
8.         The Sub-Committee then adjourned at 5.00 P.M.

System in Telecom Sector  pertaining to the Department Public Enterprises,  Ministry of  Heavy Industries and Public
Enterprises

of Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, Ministry of Communications and Department of Defence
Production & Supplies, Ministry of Defence,  on the  6th  and 20th December,  2000 respectively.

4.      The Committee in its meeting held on  the 14
th May, 2001 considered and adopted the Report.
 
 
 
                                                                   RAMDAS AGARWAL
                                           Chairman
NEW DELHI;                                                                                         Department Related Parliamentary
  14  May, 2001                                                                                         Standing Committee on Industry 
REPORT
 
I.          Introduction
 
1.1
              The Department Related Parliamentary Standing  Committee on Industry in 2000, appointed the following Sub-
Committees for detailed examination of Annual Reports:
 
            (i)         Sub-Committee I
            (ii)        Sub-Committee II
            (iii)       Sub-Committee III
                       
1.2       The Sub-Committee on Heavy Industry and Public Enterprises, as part of  examination of the Annual Report of
Ministry of Heavy Industry and Public Enterprises took up the examination of MoU system.
 
1.3       The Sub-committee, for a detailed study of the   MoU system and its effectiveness with regard to the
performance of the PSEs  took up PSEs of  various sectors.  However, in this Report, the Sub-Committee dealt with
some of the PSEs of Telecom Sector. The Sub-committee examined the MoUs of the following PSEs of Telecom. 
Sector:
 
(i)
                  ITI,  Bangalore
(ii)                BEL, Bangalore
(iii)               HTL, Chennai
(iv)              TCIL, New Delhi
 
1.4       As a part of examination of MoUs of PSEs of Telecom Sector, the Sub-Committee visited the PSEs (ITI, BEL
and HTL) to have first hand information on the implementation of MoUs from 19 th to 21 th September 2000 at
Bangalore and Chennai.  The Committee also visited TCIL on  31st October, 2000 at Delhi.  Extensive discussions were
held with the Chief Executives of selected PSEs and the Officials concerned with the MoU  system.  The Sub-
Committee also heard the oral evidence of the Secretaries of Department of Telecommunications, Ministry of Heavy
Industries and Public Enterprises and Defence Production & Supplies  at its meetings held on 20 th December , 2000
(Annexure).

II.         Background Of MoU System
 
2.1       The Department of Public Enterprises in their Background Note on the MoU system have stated that as a major
policy initiative, the MoU system was introduced by the Central Government as an important tool to improve the
performance of the Central Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs).  The New Industrial Policy of 1991 laid greater emphasis
on the MoU system requiring all PSEs to be brought under the ambit of the MoU system.  Beginning with 4 PSEs in
1987-88, the MoU system has now been extended to a large number of PSEs during the course of time and during the
year 2000-2001, 108 PSEs have signed the MoUs (Annexure).
 
2.2       It was stated that the main objectives of the MoU system are to improve the performance of the PSEs by
imparting increased autonomy and accountability and to provide a method of evaluation of the performance of the
managements of the PSEs in an objective and transparent manner.  Further, the objective of providing clarity of goals to
be achieved by PSEs is another dimension of the MoU system.
 
2.3       The Committee has noted that there is a High Power Committee (HPC) at the apex level, headed by the Cabinet
Secretary which is basically a policy making body for the MoUs.  This HPC consists of Secretaries of all nodal
Departments of Government such as Finance, Expenditure, Planning Commission and Programme Implementation, etc. 
The HPC undertakes the evaluation of the performance of the PSEs and in addition the HPC also provides a forum to
resolve inter-ministerial issues.
 
2.4       To assist HPC in this task and also to provide the technical inputs and to finalise the MoUs, there is an Advisory
Body called Adhoc Task Force (ATF), it was stated.  The members of the ATF are drawn from various fields having
vast experience in their areas and include retired Secretaries, Chief Secretaries, top experts in different disciplines like
finance, management, science and technology, and prominent academicians.   This body provides the neutrality and
objectivity to the MoU system.
 
2.5       The Department have also informed that under the present set up there is a small MoU Division under the
Department of Public Enterprises, Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, which co-ordinates the entire
exercise of finalising the MoUs in respect of all the PSEs numbering 108. In addition to finalising the MoUs, the MoU
Division is also responsible for the evaluation of performance of PSEs, both on the basis of the provisional results as
well as the audited results.
 
2.6       Explaining about the process of preparing MoUs, the Department have stated that the MoU process starts with
the issuing of guidelines by the DPE to the PSEs/Administrative Ministries for drafting the MoUs.  The PSEs prepare
their MoUs on the basis of these guidelines and these draft MoUs are then discussed with the Administrative Ministries
and in the Boards of the PSEs and are then submitted to the DPE.  DPE prepares background papers and its comments
on each draft MoU keeping in view the past performance of the PSE, its future potential, the industry scenario and the
economic environment of the PSE, it was added.  It was further stated that these draft MoUs are discussed in the MoU
negotiation meetings where the ATF members, managements of the PSE, officials from the Administrative Ministries
and the representatives from nodal Government Agencies like Ministry of Finance, Ministry of Statistics and
Programme Implementation and Planning Commission are also present.  The MoUs and the targets are finalised in these
meetings through mutual discussions.
           
 
III.
       Performance of MoU System in Telecom. Sector
 
            The Sub-Committee now deals with the  performance of MoU system of ITI, BEL, HTL and TCIL in the
succeeding paragraphs:
 
IV.       Indian Telephone Industries  Ltd.
 
4.1       ITI Ltd. was formed in 1948 and was the first Public Sector Undertaking to be set up by the Government of
India.  The Company has seven manufacturing units located at Bangalore (two units), Naina, Rae Bareli, Srinagar,

46th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/46threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:12:24]
Palghat and Mankapur and Network Systems Unit with headquarters at Bangalore to provide value added services like
paging, e-mail, voice mail, etc.
 
4.2       ITI manufactures a wide range of equipments, which include electronic switching equipments, transmission
equipments, VSAT equipments and telephone instruments of various types. ITI is also providing value added services
like VSAT, MRTS, etc.  The Company has been responsible for building around 70% to 80% of the country’s telecom
infrastructure.  This has been possible through its countrywide service network and state of the art technology.
 
4.3       Major customer of Company’s products is Department of Telecommunications.  ITI is also supplying telecom
products to Railways, Defence and Corporate Sectors.ITI has exported its products to  foreign  countries  aMoUnting  to
Rs.703.41 lakhs  during 1998-1999.
 
4.4       ITI Ltd. has been signing MoU since 1991 with the Government of India.  The ITI Ltd. has been
manufacturing/supplying various kinds of equipments to the Telecommunication Sector ranging from telephone sets to
small/medium exchanges, large exchanges, digital radio and optical fibre, etc.  The PSE has gone through different
phases in the past especially after the introduction of economic reforms in the country and it has stabilised its operations
during the recent years.  It has been able to develop a very strong infrastructure for supply of products/technologies in
the field of telecommunications. The increased competition due to globalisation has posed a new threat to the ITI Ltd.,
but at the same time with the fast growth of this sector, new avenues of growth are also available for the Company.  It
can become a major player in the sector through diversification of its activities, improving the quality through
introduction of new technologies and by improving the efficiency.  The performance of the Company under the MoU
system is being evaluated under the major parameters details of which are as under:-
 
 
4.4.1
        Financial Performance
 
            The financial performance in respect of this PSE is evaluated against two parameters namely Gross Margin and
the Ratio of Net Profit to Capital employed.  Both the parameters have been assigned significantly higher weight
ranging between 50% to 60% since 1994-95.  Because of competition, the PSE faced the worst situation in 1995-96
when it incurred an operating loss of Rs.88 crores.  In view of this situation, a very modest target of Gross Margin of
Rs.31 crores and Rs.19 crores was kept for the years 1996-97 and 1997-98.  But the performance was much better than
expected.  From 1998-99 onwards it has stabilised its operations and there has been a steady growth in Company’s gross
margin.  The other financial parameter i.e. ratio of net profit to capital employed also indicates that year 1995-96 was
the worst year for the PSE so far as its performance is concerned.  This ratio was negative during 1995-96 and 1996-97. 
But it recovered in the subsequent years and this ratio improved to the level of 3.01 during 1999-2000.
 
 
4.4.2
        Net Sales
 
            Net sales is another parameter to evaluate the performance of the ITI Ltd. under the MoU system.  The weight
assigned to this parameter has varied from 4% to 10% during the period.  The trend in performance of the PSE under
this parameter has been similar to that  under financial parameters.  Its sales were just of the order of Rs.783 crores
during 1995-96.  Since 1997-98, the PSE has shown a turnaround and has been able to exceed the targets under this
parameter.  The sale during 1999-2000 was of the order of Rs.1824.44 crores.
 
 
4.4.3
        Physical Parameter
 
The performance of the PSE under the physical criteria is evaluated against four major parameters, which are as
under :-
 
a)      Supply of small and medium exchanges (KL) – This has been a performance criteria for the evaluation of the
performance of the PSE under the MoU system except during 1995-96 and 1997-98.  The weight assigned to
this parameter used to be 5% and it has been reduced to 2% since 1996-97.

46th Report

b)      Supply of large exchange (KL) – This parameter has also been assigned a weight of 2% since 1996-97.  The
performance of the PSE under this parameter has also been very encouraging and always exceeded the
targets.
c)      Digital Radio – under this parameter the performance of the PSE has been much below the targets till 1998-
99. However, in 1999-2000, the PSE was able to exceed the targets.  This parameter has also been assigned
the weight of 2% since 1996-97.
d)      Optical fibre (PDH/SDH) Terminals – This parameter included in the MoU document also continue to get
the weight of 2%.  The PSE has not been able to achieve the targets under this parameter.
     Thus total weight assigned to the physical parameters works out to be 8%.
 
 
4.4.4
        Non-Dot Business
 
(i)         As mentioned earlier that after introduction of economic reforms, ITI Ltd. has faced tough competition in the
market and its performance has suffered significantly because of the changes in procurement policy of
telecommunication equipments by Department of Telecommunications which has been the main customer of the
products supplied by the PSE and increased competition.  In 1997-98, DOT provided the requisite support and the PSE
could get sufficient orders, which improved its position.  ITI Ltd. has been making efforts to expand its business and
there has been a steady progress in this regard.  During 1995-96, the target for getting non-DOT business was Rs.200
crores and against this the PSE could get business only of the order of Rs.93.35 crores.  However, in the subsequent
years, the non-DOT business in terms of rupees has increased to Rs.202 crores in 1998-99 and to Rs.226 crores in 1999-
2000.  During 1998-99 and 1999-2000, the Company could exceed the targets under this parameter.  The weight
assigned to this parameter under the MoU has been between 2% to 4%.
 
(ii)        It is pertinent to mention here that during 1995-96 and 1997-98, there were no targets for the physical
parameters. The other parameters, which are included in the MoU are Research and Development, HRD and project
implementation.  For project implementation, the weight is assigned keeping in view the number of projects being
implemented by the PSE and their respective importance.
 
(iii)       The performance of the Company has been rated as excellent under the MoU system since 1991 except during
1994-95 and 1995-96 and 1996-97 when the performance of the Company was rated as Good, Fair and Very Good
respectively.  In fact, as stated earlier, the Company was facing a tough competition because of opening of the
economy.  The year 1996-97  was a turnaround year for the PSE.
 
 
V.        Bharat Electronics Limited
 
5.1       Bharat Electronics Limited (BEL) was established at Bangalore by the Government of India under the Ministry
of Defence in the year 1954.  Presently, it is the country’s premier electronics manufacturing company having 9
operating units.  The authorised and paid up share capital of the Company as on 31.3.99 were Rs.85 crores and Rs.80
crores respectively.
 
5.2       BEL meets the bulk of the electronic equipment needs of the Indian Defence Services, Paramilitary Forces and
other Government users like All India Radio, Doordarshan, Department of Telecommunication, Police Wireless, Airport
Authority of India, Meteorological Department, Railways etc.  BEL is also the premier source in India for Professional
Electronic Components catering to the needs of a variety of customers in the consumer electronics sector viz. the Radio
and TV manufacturers as well as original equipment manufacturers involved in the manufacture of all types of
electronic equipments.  The Company has a very wide product range and makes over 350 different products.
 
5.3       Around 70% of BEL’s turnover today is from products designed in-house/ indigenously.  BEL is also making
export promotional efforts like appointment of overseas agents, participation in foreign exhibitions etc. BEL is also
concentrating on widening the product market in certain sectors.
 
5.4       BEL is signing MoU since 1990-91 and has a good track record of performance.  Amongst the major objectives,
the Company has set for itself include the generation of internal resources for the growth of the Company to achieve
self-reliance by indigenisation of critical material and components and remain a leader in the technology so far as the
requirement of the defence and other selected fields of professional electronics is concerned through Research &

46th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/46threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:12:24]
Development.  Keeping in view the above objectives, efforts are made to translate them into performance indicators and
set some quantitative targets.  The major parameters followed for evaluation of the performance of the Company are as
under:-
 
 
5.4.1
        Financial Parameters
 
            As per DPE guidelines, 60% weight is assigned to the financial parameters namely gross margin and ratio of net
profit to capital employed.  During 1994-95 and 1995-96, the Company was not able to achieve the targets under this
parameter.  In fact, the gross margin during 1995-96 was lower than that of 1994-95. But since 1996-97, BEL has
shown an impressive improvement over the previous years and the achievements in 1996-97 was Rs.203.92 crores
against the target of Rs.158.03 crores.  In the subsequent years, the Company maintained the trend of steady growth of
gross margin.  However, during 1998-99 there was a significant reduction in the gross margin and was Rs.189.39 crores
against the target of Rs.200 crores.  This was mainly due to the economic sanctions, which the country faced during this
period.  However, during 1999-2000 there was a significant improvement in the gross margin of the Company and it
was Rs.235.76 crores against the target of Rs.190 crores.  The other financial parameter which also carries 30% weight
is ratio of net profit to capital employed.  BEL has registered a very impressive improvement under this parameter.  The
return on the capital employed which was just 3% during 1994-95 has increased to 17.5% during 1999-2000.  In fact the
performance under this parameter has been improving consistently over the years. The rate of return of 17.5% on capital
is quite impressive by all means in commercial terms.
 
 5.4.2
        Physical Criteria – Turnover
 
            The performance of the Company under this parameter has shown consistent improvement over the years except
during 1998-99 when there was a decline in the turnover (due to economic sanctions).  The turnover, which was just
Rs.938.50 crores during 1994-95 increased to Rs.1496.40 crores during 1999-2000.  The weight assigned to this
parameter was 20% during 1995-96 and 1996-97.  From 1997-98 onwards, the weight to this parameter has been
reduced to 10%.  The other physical criteria applied to evaluate the performance of the Company is exports.  The weight
assigned to this parameter has been 5%.  Though high targets were given to the Company every year,  it has not been
able to achieve the targets under this parameter during all the years.  However,  it is worth mentioning here that its
performance under this parameter has shown a consistent improvement over the period.  The exports which were just of
the order of US$3.74 millions increased to US$7.36 million in 1998-99 but during 1999-2000 it was just US$5.01
million.
 
 
5.4.3
        Efficiency Criteria
 
            Inventory management and value addition have been adopted as efficiency criteria in respect of BEL.  Under this
parameter the Company has been able to improve its performance over the years.  Since 1998-99, the criterion of value
addition was also included as once of the parameters to evaluate the performance of the PSE.  During 1998-99, the
weight assigned to this parameter was 2% and from 1999-2000 onwards the weight has been increased to 5%.
 
 
5.4.4
        Dynamic Parameters
 
(i)         Under dynamic criteria, the parameters such as development of new products and HRD are included. 
Development of new products, which indicates R&D efforts of the Company, has been generally assigned for
production of new products.  The performance of the PSE is evaluated against the time schedule set for development of
these products.  Similarly, under HRD, a 5% weight is assigned, which is quite significant.  Under this criteria the
efforts of the Company to equip its staff with new skills and training is evaluated.
 
(ii)        On the basis of the composite score under MoU, the Company was graded as excellent during 1990-91. 
It was only during 1992-93 when the rating of the Company was fair.  But over rest of the years it has been rated as
either Very Good or Excellent.
 
 
VI.       Hindustan Teleprinters Limited
 
6.1       HTL has been signing the MoU with the Government of India since 1991-92.  The operations of the PSE are
related to production and supply of equipments for telecommunications and other related areas.  The main objectives of

46th Report

the PSE are to become a potential manufacturer and supplier of telecommunications equipments and software, promote
research and development efforts by acquiring technology from the global leaders in the field, besides manufacturing
Digital Switching System, Transmission Equipment, access products, data products and other terminals and provide
value added services in the field.
 
6.2       The main strength of the HTL is its good infrastructure both in terms of physical as well as manpower.  In the
field of R&D, the PSE has the advantage of the availability of trained manpower.  It has also the advantage of expertise
in switching, besides data and transmission.  Department of Telecommunications and MTNL are the main customers of
the Company.  Though there is a tough competition, the fast expanding telecom sector provides good avenues for the
Company to grow at a faster rate.
 
6.3       The performance of the PSE has been evaluated as per the guidelines issued by the DPE for the MoU signing
PSEs.  The details of the major parameters under which the performance of HTL is evaluated as under:-
 
 
6.3.1
        Financial Parameter
 
            As part of the general policy, 60% weight is assigned to two financial parameters namely gross margin and ratio
of net profit to capital employed.  With respect to the gross margin, the performance of the PSE has not been very
encouraging till 1997-98.  For example, during 1994-95, the achievement was only Rs.7.67 crores against the target of
Rs.11.45 crores.  Similarly, in 1996-97, the target was Rs.11.88 crores but the achievement was only Rs.2.15 crores. 
But since 1997-98, the performance of HTL improved significantly and the gross margin increased to Rs.15.36 crores
against the targets of Rs.21.40 crores which was significant keeping in view the achievements during 1996-97.  In 1998-
99, the PSE was able to achieve the gross margin of Rs.17.80 crores against the target of Rs.16.24 crores.  Similarly in
1999-2000, the gross margin of Rs.30.50 crores was against the target of Rs.16.99 crores.  Similarly under the other
financial parameter i..e. the ratio of net profit to capital employed, the performance trend was similar to that of gross
margin.  It was as low as 1% during 1994-95 and 1995-96.  In fact during 1996-97 it was negative which means the
Company was incurring operational losses.  But after that there has been a considerable improvement in the ratio and
this ratio improved to 12.27 during 1999-2000.
 
 
6.3.2    Physical Parameter
 
(i)         Under the physical criteria, sales turnover has been adopted to evaluate the performance of the PSE. 
During 1994-95, the weight assigned to this parameter was 15% and from 1995-96 onwards the weight was reduced to
10%.  Under this criteria also, the PSE has performed well only after 1997-98.  The sales turnover which was just
Rs.118.85 crores in 1994-95 has increased to Rs.402.46 crores in 1999-2000 which is an indicator of an impressive
performance by HTL.
 
(ii)        Other related parameter to measure the performance of the PSE includes the Inventory Stock
Management, Quality Control, Project Implementation and Research and Development.
 
(iii)       The weight assigned to Inventory Management has been between the range of 4% to 5% which was used
as an efficiency criteria.  The quality control has been assigned a weight of 6%.  In fact, during 1997-98 this criteria was
assigned 9% weight.  Similarly, for Research and Development which is very crucial for the growth of the Company,
the weight assigned has been between 6 to 7%, which is quite significant.
 
(iv)       Though the actual performance of the Company was not very satisfactory till 1996-97 but still the
company was rated as Excellent keeping in view the managerial efforts which were acknowledged by the DPE.  From
1997-98 onwards, it was a turnaround case because of the managerial efforts.  There was totally a lack of demand of
their traditional products i.e. teleprinters, etc. and the management took the initiative to diversify its operations and the
results of these initiatives were seen from 1997-98 onwards.  Since MoU system basically reflects the evaluation of the
performance of the PSE, therefore, the factors which were beyond its control of the management were given due
consideration and accordingly the rating were adjusted by the ATF.
 
 
VII.      Telecommunications Consultants India Limited
 
7.1       Telecommunications Consultants India Ltd. (TCIL) was set up as a Public Sector Undertaking under the
Department of Telecommunication in August 1978 for providing globally know-how in all the fields of
